paragraphs.text: Ramathaim-Zophim: this is the city of Ramah, which lies about ten miles north of Jerusalem. It was the home of Samuel's family, and it was also the city from which Joseph of Arimathea came in the days of Christ. The word Zophim refers to Samuel's fourth forefather, who may have been the first of the family to dwell in this city. There are several cities called Ramah, so the text distinguishes this one by saying Ramathaim-Zophim.

The book begins by introducing to us the person of Samuel's father. It tells us his name, "Elkanah," and his home, the city of Ramah, and it also lists his ancestors back to the great-grandfather, to confirm his identity and his belonging to the tribe of Levi (the Kohathites), who are mentioned in more detail in (1 Chr 6:20-27). The word Ephraimite means that he dwelt in the midst of the tribe of Ephraim, for he lived in the hill country of Ephraim.

Elkanah had two wives, since the Jewish law permitted polygamy. The first was Hannah, the mother of Samuel, who was barren and without offspring, and the other was named Peninnah, and she had children.

Shiloh: a city lying north of Bethel and 17 miles north of Jerusalem. Joshua moved the tabernacle of meeting there from Gilgal, and the tabernacle remained there for about 310 years. Eli the priest and Samuel dwelt there.

As an indication of the piety of Elkanah, the husband and father, we learn that he was religious and constant in worship, and did not neglect to go up to the house of the Lord every year to offer sacrifices for himself, his children and his wives, according to the commandment of the Lord. The Law commanded going to the house of the Lord three times a year, at the feasts of Passover, Harvest and Tabernacles. In that period they had neglected to keep the three feasts, and they used to go only at the Feast of Harvest, as Jewish tradition declares. The house of the Lord at that time was the tabernacle of meeting, which had been set up in the city of "Shiloh." This verse also tells us that Eli was the high priest at that time, and that he had two sons who were priests, "Hophni" and "Phinehas."

Some sacrifices, such as the peace offering, were divided between God, whose portion was burned on the altar, and the priests, who had the front leg and part of the breast. As for most of the sacrifice, it was eaten by the one who offered it, together with the Levites and the poor.

When Elkanah gave portions to his wife Peninnah and her children, he did not wrong them; but he favored Hannah with a double portion. The inspired text makes clear to us the reason for this: that her husband loved her more than Peninnah, who had the children, and perhaps also as a compensation for her and a comfort to her heart for not bearing children because her womb was closed. Elkanah's love for Hannah troubled Peninnah, so she provoked Hannah, as appears from (v. 6). The First Book of Samuel. And Peninnah, with her many children, is a type of the Jewish nation, which had a portion with God, while Hannah is a type of the Church of the Gentiles, which was barren before she enjoyed her heavenly Bridegroom, "Christ," and then became possessed of a blessed offspring greater than that of the first.

Take care to compensate every weak person around you with your tenderness, and encourage him so that he may continue his life with contentment and joy, as Elkanah did with barren Hannah, but with wisdom, so that you do not trouble others.
Provocation: vexation, angering and scheming.

Perhaps because of Elkanah's evident love for his wife Hannah, or because he gave her two portions, "Peninnah" felt jealous, and she kept vexing Hannah with the wounding words of women, taunting her and boasting over her that she was the one with offspring and children, and that the Lord had deprived Hannah of children and motherhood.

This action of "Peninnah" was repeated whenever she went up with her husband and Hannah to the house of the Lord. Consequently the days of the feast and of the joy of offering sacrifices were nothing more than days of sorrow for Hannah, who expressed her sorrow, when it became more than she could bear, by refraining from eating of the sacrifices and from taking part in the celebration of the feast.

Elkanah, the loving husband, sensed the oppression and sorrow that his wife was suffering, so he wanted to relieve her and comfort her heart with gentle words. He told her that, since he loved her and she felt it, was this not enough, and better than her having ten sons?

May you feel for those around you and sympathize with their problems, and try to help them as far as you are able, and offer them kind words that lift their sorrows from them, for in this you offer love to Christ Himself.
A post of the temple of the Lord: beside the door of the temple.

Hannah responded to her husband's kind words and ate with them of the sacrifices, but her heart was still sorrowful and her wound deep. So she went with all her distress, "bitter in soul," to the house of the Lord. "Eli" the high priest was sitting beside its door, and as soon as Hannah arrived she began to pray in sorrow, overcome by her burning tears.
No razor shall come upon his head: one of the features of the law of the vow was that a person was not to cut his hair throughout the period of his vow.

In Hannah's fervent prayer she made a vow to God: that if He would remove her humiliation and give her a son, she would give him to the Lord as a servant and a Nazirite in His house all the days of his life.
The First Book of Samuel

Hannah prayed a long, deep and moving prayer. No one heard her voice, but Eli the priest watched the movements of her lips and thought she was drunk, since he was not accustomed to seeing such a sight in contrite prayer before God.

Eli the priest spoke, rebuking her and disapproving of her state: how could she stand without propriety before the Lord in His house, in a state of drunkenness and immodesty unbecoming to the holiness of the house of God? For her head was moving, and so were her lips, as if she were reeling and shaking from wine, like one who cannot stand with composure and reverence, so he supposed she had drunk much wine.

Eli thought this because, sadly, when they ate of the peace offerings they would drink wine to the point of drunkenness, and this shows the degree of spiritual decline to which they had come at that time.
Belial: the name of a well-known pagan god, and it is a symbol of Satan.

In humility Hannah defended herself, explaining that she was not drunk but broken-hearted and sorrowful, and that she was pouring herself out in contrition before the Lord. She denied that she was a worshipper of Satan or one who despised the house of God, and said that it was her concern and grief that had driven her to speak with God in this manner and for this length of time.

This shows her good manners and humility, for she did not reply to Eli that he was unable to tell fervent prayer from drunkenness, and she did not condemn him for his indulgence toward his sons the priests, who filled the temple with evil by falling into adultery and theft, as will appear in the following verses.

Eli the priest changed his attitude after he heard Hannah's words and her defense and understood her situation, so he prayed for her peace, and that God, the Maker of good things, would give her all that she had asked of Him in her prayer ...
Let your maidservant find grace in your sight: an expression meaning "may you be pleased with me and bless me."

Before Hannah went away, with the utmost courtesy and humility, she asked for the priest's blessing. Having set her problem before the Lord and spoken with the priest, she went back in a different state, for she went to eat, and her face was no longer sad as it had been.
From all that has gone before we learn some useful spiritual lessons, among them:
1- Hannah was a spiritual woman, yet subject to human weakness, and when she could not overcome her anxiety she turned to God and to His house to pour out what was in her heart.
2- Her prayer was long, deep and persistent, and she did not care whether any person heard what she said, but sought God alone.
3- Hannah was a humble woman, and she addressed the priest with these humble expressions: "your handmaid," "your maidservant," "let me find grace in your sight."
4- Eli the priest was also zealous for the house of God, for when he suspected that Hannah was drunk, he did not hesitate to rebuke her. A priest must be moved by a holy zeal for the house of God.

5- How sweet is the word "Go in peace," which the Lord of glory Himself used, and which the priests now use in the Church at the end of dismissing the people, when the last words are "Go in peace ... the peace of the Lord be with you all."

entries.section: (3) The birth of Samuel and his presentation to the Lord

paragraphs.text: At the end of their visit to the temple and their offering of sacrifices, they worshipped the Lord before returning to their town. On their return the inspired text mentions the words "the Lord remembered her," which means that the Lord answered her prayer and the priest's blessing upon her. So Hannah conceived within the same year and bore a male son, and called his name Samuel. The meaning of his name is "asked of God" or "the name of God."

entries.section: (3) The birth of Samuel and his presentation to the Lord

paragraphs.text: The Lord establish His word: God fulfills His promise of accepting Samuel as a Nazirite, as Hannah said in her prayer (v. 11). Elkanah the man and his household went up the following year to offer his sacrifices to God as usual, but Hannah excused herself from going with him until Samuel was weaned, so that there would be one visit in which she would present her son as a Nazirite to God, for she did not wish to go and return without presenting him to the Lord. Her husband "Elkanah" agreed with her opinion that the visit should be postponed until the child Samuel was weaned, and he prayed to God to fulfill His promise of accepting the child as a Nazirite to Him. Here appear Hannah's piety and her great love for God: although this was her only son, she gave him to God to serve in His temple. Her love for God overcame her love for her son, that is, she gave up her motherhood for the sake of God.

entries.section: (3) The birth of Samuel and his presentation to the Lord

paragraphs.text: When she had weaned him: the period of nursing children in those days was about two years.
A skin of wine: a leather vessel like a waterskin, used for carrying liquids.
An ephah of flour: a measure of flour equal to 22.9 liters.

After the little boy Samuel was weaned, Hannah went with her son, and of course her husband, to the tabernacle of meeting at "Shiloh" to fulfill her vow. She took with her three bulls to offer, perhaps to offer them as a "burnt offering," a "sin offering" and a "peace offering" for the boy. She also brought the wine that is poured out on the sacrifices as the Law prescribes, and the flour that is offered as an offering to God (Lev 1, 3, 4). The inspired text mentions that Hannah brought her son up, and not she and Elkanah, to confirm that it was she who thought of presenting her son as a Nazirite to God, and Elkanah agreed to it.

Hannah fulfilled her vow and gave her only son to God. May you be generous in your giving, and give to God the dearest thing you have and the best of what you possess, not only material things, but if your son wishes to consecrate his life to God, may you encourage him and not think selfishly of keeping him for yourself.

entries.section: (3) The birth of Samuel and his presentation to the Lord

paragraphs.text: As your soul lives: an expression meaning "may God give you life."

Hannah stood before "Eli" the priest and spoke in a courteous manner, saying "I ask you, my lord," to request his permission to be heard, and she reminded him that she was the same woman who had stood before him some time before to pray to the Lord that He would give her a boy. She pointed to Samuel, the subject of the conversation, and went on to say that the Lord had accomplished His work and given her what she had asked of Him.

entries.section: (3) The birth of Samuel and his presentation to the Lord

paragraphs.text: I have lent him to the Lord: I have presented him to the Lord.
Lent: a loan or an advance.

Hannah acknowledges God's favor toward her and that He gave her the petition of her heart, and she is here today to present her son to God. Although God gave her a son who belongs to her by physical sonship, and she became also a mother to him, "the mother of Samuel," she lends him as a permanent loan to the Lord, that is, she gave what was hers to the Lord. The expression "as long as he lives" means that she would no longer wish for him or long for him for herself, or regret his separation from her, but she made her son Samuel worship before the house of God. Perhaps in his childhood he did not fully understand what he was doing, but the meaning is very beautiful, that the consecrated one begins by offering his life to the Lord by worshipping Him, as a clear expression of complete submission to His will and purpose.
The First Book of Samuel. The song of Hannah and the sin of Eli's sons
My horn: an expression of Hannah's strength, for she borrowed for it the horn of the animal, which represents its strength.
My mouth is enlarged: I have become able to answer those who taunted me.

In joy after sorrow and brokenness, Hannah stood before God repeating her prayer, her praise and her glorification of the Lord for His gift to her. She began her prayer by declaring this joy, and that it was joy in the Lord's work with her more than joy in her son himself. For He had restored her honor after her brokenness and lifted up her head before those who taunted her, and she regarded what God had done with her as deliverance from her shame and disgrace. The expression "I rejoice in Your salvation" also reminds us of the song of the Holy Virgin, "My spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Lk 1:46). Here appears Hannah's concern to give thanks to God, which many neglect after their troubles are relieved. And although Hannah had prayed in silence during her bitterness (ch. 1), when she gave thanks her voice rose to glorify God. The reason for this thanksgiving is the glorification of God, not the vexing of her enemies. The deliverance of the children of Israel from their enemies the Philistines was accomplished afterward by the hand of Samuel (ch. 7:8-13), and then in the fullness of time Christ triumphed over Satan and bound him by the Cross.
There is none like You, O God, in Your holiness, and no one is able to draw near to it, for there is none like You, and there is no one in Your power, for You are like the rock on which man leans.

"Hannah" addresses the wicked and rebukes them for their pride and arrogance in their speech, and calls them to leave their insolent and mocking talk, because God knows what they think and conceal in their hearts. The expression "by Him actions are weighed" corresponds to "He repays each one according to his work."
The bows of the mighty: the bows of the mighty men.
Were girded with strength: they put on power and courage.

"Hannah" continues describing the works of God. She describes Him as the One who breaks the might of the proud and everything on which they rely, like the weapons of war that the bows symbolize, while the weak and humble He gave strength, victory and courage.

Likewise everyone who boasted of possessing the means of life and luxury .. their condition reached the point that they became poor, so that they worked as hired men and slaves to find the bread they would eat, while the hungry, who have no one but God, have been filled to satisfaction. And the barren one (meaning Hannah) has seven children, a figure of speech for the abundance of her offspring, while she who had many children (Peninnah) has withered, and the glory of her boasting has passed away, because the reason for her boasting was evil, namely the vexing of others.

The First Book of Samuel. The barren woman (Hannah) is a type of the Gentiles who became Christians and whose number has become great, while the Jews who rejected Christ, whom Peninnah signifies, have become weak. The number seven signifies perfection, that is, God gave Hannah sufficient offspring, although she actually bore three sons and two daughters (v. 21).

God alone has the authority to put to death whom He wills and to save whom He wills, and He also makes poor whom He wills and makes rich whom He wills; He brings the proud down and lifts the humble up..; and this is also like the song of the Virgin when she said, "He has put down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly" (Lk 1:52).
The pillars of the earth: an expression that God is the Creator and Founder of the earth, like one who raises a building on pillars.

"Hannah" continues glorifying the Lord in His works. She points to Him in His raising the poor man trodden by people in the dust of the earth, and the needy man despised in the eyes of people, to give them honor and glory, so that their seat is among the nobles, that is, they become among the great, because God is the Founder of the earth, who established it and created it, and He possesses everything on it, and He is the Molder of the creation of people, so He is able to do all things.

God is the Keeper of those who fear Him, and He steadies their feet before hardships, while the wicked end in shame and the darkness of hell. Who then thinks that man's strength is from himself? No one is overcome or victorious unless God is his support and his hope.

Continuing the same meaning: whoever opposes God and is hostile to Him is broken, and God declares His wrath against him from heaven, for He alone is the just Judge of all the earth, and He is the Giver of honor, glory and blessing to those whom He chose of His anointed kings.

It is not hidden from the dear reader that these words are prophetic of Christ, God incarnate. His enemies have been humbled, while glory, honor and power are the attributes inseparable from the glory and divinity of the Son.

This verse refers to Elkanah's return with his family to his dwelling place at Ramah after leaving Samuel in the care of Eli the high priest, so that he might teach him how to serve the house of the Lord.

Let us also learn to plant our children in the Church from their youth to learn the hymns and the melodies, and at the suitable age to present them to receive the blessing of service as deacons, so that they may grow up in this beautiful spiritual and ecclesiastical atmosphere, and this will be reflected on their whole life afterward with blessing and spirituality.
Belial: a Hebrew word meaning without profit, and it was afterward applied to Satan.
Fleshhook: a long fork used in cooking, not like the familiar eating fork.
Laver: a basin containing water, used here to wash the slaughtered meat.
The cauldron: a large copper vessel for boiling water.

Eli the high priest had two sons who were priests, but they turned aside into many evils until they became like sons of Satan. They abandoned the law of God, and were not content with the priests' due from the sacrifices. Rather, when the people offered the sacrifices and ate them in the holy place, that is, beside the tabernacle of meeting, a representative of the two would come by with a fleshhook in his hand The First Book of Samuel and thrust it into the pot of meat, and of course he would choose the best piece, and if anyone objected he would tell him with authority that this was for the priests, and he would be silent for fear of their authority. Thus they fell into the sin of theft by compulsion.

The Law required that the Lord's portion be offered first, before any other portions, and this portion, from the fat, the liver and the two kidneys, was burned on the altar, while the priests' portion was the breast and the right leg (Lev 3:3-5). The priests and the people knew this well, but because of the greed of the priests, the sons of Eli, they were brazenly asking the people to take from the sacrifices before God's portion was offered. And although the simple people warned them not to break the Law, they were thieves, and they took a portion for themselves before God, and if the one offering the sacrifice did not allow this, they took by force what they wanted ... and this is what is now called thuggery.
The young men: what is meant is the sons of Eli the priest.

As a result of the evils of the representatives of Eli's sons in seizing the people's rights, the people were made to stumble by the priests, and they lost their reverence for the temple and its worship and despised the Law.

?No person, however great, is above sin. Here we have priests who are supposed to be the example for the people, yet they sank to the worst level, and this teaches us fear and caution. Let us not rely on the righteousness of our fathers or trust in ourselves, but let us examine all our conduct carefully, especially what concerns God's rights and our duties toward Him, so that we do not fall into contempt and anger God!?!

entries.section: (3) The service of Samuel and God's blessing on Hannah

paragraphs.text: Ephod: a linen garment like a vest, with two bands like a belt with which it is tied around a person's waist. The ephod was among the garments of the Levites and was sometimes worn by the priests. The child and boy Samuel began his service in the house of the Lord, and because of his piety and Eli the priest's love for him, Eli clothed him with an ephod as a mark distinguishing him, despite his young age. His mother kept visiting him as usual every year, and out of her care for her son, whom she had not forgotten, the inspired text tells us that she made him a robe of wool (a tunic) for the boy to wear under the ephod in the days of winter.
Hannah's care for raising her son and instructing him in the spiritual teachings is evident, for she kept him in purity despite the evils of the priests in the temple.

entries.section: (3) The service of Samuel and God's blessing on Hannah

paragraphs.text: Lent: she lent to the Lord and presented her son to Him (see ch. 1:28). Eli admired the piety of Samuel and his parents, especially Hannah, and blessed them from God, and prophesied to Hannah that she would bear sons in place of Samuel whom she had vowed to God. After receiving the blessing, they left Shiloh and returned to their town Ramah.

entries.section: (3) The service of Samuel and God's blessing on Hannah

paragraphs.text: The Lord visited: gave grace.
The years passed and God's promise was fulfilled, and Hannah bore three sons and two daughters, and during these years Samuel was growing in piety before God in His house.

Blessed is he who offers his life or his children to God with a willing heart. Did not the Lord Christ promise him a hundredfold..? God never remains in debt to His children, for in His fatherhood He accepts their gifts, and in His fatherhood He also grants them abundant gifts and reward.
The First Book of Samuel

Eli was very advanced in years, and the people reported to him all that his sons the priests were doing of plundering, looting and seizing the Lord's portions of the sacrifices. Indeed they fell into adultery with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting as volunteers to help in the service (such as washing the sacrifices and cleaning them) before the house of the Lord.

Eli rebuked his two sons for the evils they were doing, and told them that their deeds were not right and caused the people to stumble, since they became an evil example and the people fell into many sins. We notice here Eli's weakness, for he did not rebuke them sternly, nor did he take any action against them, such as preventing them from serving, even temporarily, although they ought to have been put to death, or at least removed completely from the service, according to what the Law commands. This angered God, so He allowed their death, and their father's, in the battle against the Philistines (ch. 4).

If a person sins against another and does not repent and make amends, God judges him; how much more, then, if a person sins directly against God, he deserves a great punishment. This is what the sons of Eli did, so God allowed them to die because of their evil in the battle against the Philistines.

This verse comes as a parenthesis in the context of the account of Eli and his sons. After the review of the evil that had penetrated the souls of the priests, we see a bright picture of the young lad Samuel, who is noted as growing in his love for God, and how God also gave him favor in the eyes of the people, who saw his goodness in the midst of all this evil.

Do not seek an excuse for yourself and fall into sin because of the spread of evil around you. Here is Samuel living in piety in the midst of the evil atmosphere. Indeed God allows your presence among the wicked so that you may be a light to the world, and be confident that He will help you to live in righteousness, whatever the pressures surrounding you.
A man of God: an expression used for the prophets or prominent spiritual figures such as "Elijah and Elisha."

God did not address Eli directly for his great fault in being lax with his sons, but sent him a prophet (whose name is unknown) as a final warning to him to repent before the punishment came upon him. He told him a message, the beginning of which The First Book of Samuel was: "Did I not reveal Myself to your fathers and forefathers (Moses and Aaron) during the humiliation of My people in the land of Egypt in the bondage of Pharaoh.

And I chose the house of Aaron, that is, your fathers, to be priests to Me and to stand before the altar to offer incense to My holy name morning and evening, and I gave them to wear the ephod and all the garments of the priesthood, and I made them heads over the people who accept their sacrifices, and guides to Israel's civil leaders when they come to seek My voice and My counsel through them.

God showed Eli that He had honored him and glorified him with the priesthood, but he despised the holiness of the house of the Lord and its worship, and honored his sons at God's expense. He left them to do evil and was content with reproof, and did not prevent their evils.
God honored the house of Eli with the priesthood as long as they held fast to His Law, but if they despised God and did not honor Him, God would punish them and humble them.

God mentions a second punishment, which is "cutting off the arm." The arm is a figure for strength and for the time of a man's youth, so the punishment is that God will destroy Eli's offspring of priests in their youth, and none of them will remain to old age. Long life in the Old Testament was one of the signs of God's blessing on a person.

Likewise, among the punishments that will come upon "Eli" is that he will see hard days for the house of the Lord, which will be assaulted in his days by the Philistines, who will take the "ark of the covenant" with them to their land. With the disappearance of the ark all the glory of Israel also disappears, and their sense of the presence of their God among them, so the feasts, the sacrifices and the joys disappear, all of which God had ordained as a kindness to His people and for the joy of their hearts.

Among the punishments also coming upon "Eli the priest" is that God will leave some of his offspring as priests serving the altar, but they will be a cause of pain to his soul and weeping to his eyes, because of the evil of their deeds on the one hand, and on the other because of their suffering from afflictions and poverty and their loss of God's blessing and grace in their lives. God also confirms, as He said before, that they will not live long but will die in their youth.
The sign He leaves for him to confirm the truth of His words is that he will hear of the death of his two sons the priests "Hophni and Phinehas" in one day.

We notice that Eli received great honor as high priest, but he did not bear the responsibility of his position; rather he was lax with his sons, so he received a severe divine punishment. As for Samuel, whom the people rejected as the voice of God and asked for a king for themselves, he endured, and then God honored him and he became one of the greatest prophets.

This verse can be interpreted directly: that this is what actually happened when God chose Samuel as His priest to offer sacrifices for the people, although he was not of the offspring of Aaron the priest but of the ordinary Levites, but God alone has the authority. Samuel was indeed faithful and zealous for God and His house, obedient and carrying out His will; and the expression "I will build him a sure house" means that the priesthood will be in his house and to his offspring after him, and he will be a leader of the people and a guide to the anointed king afterward to rule the people.

As for the prophetic meaning of this verse, it was fulfilled perfectly in the person of the Lord Jesus, who has the permanent, eternal priesthood, and whose new house became His Church, and who also became its King, its Guide and its Governor to perfection.

Continuing the discussion of the punishment, everyone who remains alive of the descendants of "Eli the priest" comes to the new priest established according to God's heart, who is Samuel, in humiliation and brokenness to ask for some money or even a piece of bread, and begs him to find a place and a portion in the service of the priesthood so that he may be able to live.

My God and my Lord ... how my heart trembled and my knees shook as I read these severe and just punishments for the one who was lax with Your rights. I beg You, my God, never allow me to neglect Your commands and Your commandments, but make me always watchful and attentive ... and have mercy on me according to Your great mercy.
God's speech with Samuel

This chapter begins by confirming the continuation of the boy's service, which he had begun from his childhood. This service was of course under the supervision of "Eli" the priest, who guided him as his disciple. The inspired text indicates here that visions, prophetic dreams and God's speaking with His people were very rare, because of the people's sins and spiritual dryness, and also the evil of the priests, as we saw in the person of the two sons of "Eli the priest." But God does not leave Himself without a witness, so He spoke to the boy Samuel and prepared him to lead the people. In every generation there is one who fears God and proclaims His voice, like the prophet Moses among the people who went astray and worshipped the golden calf, and Pope Athanasius who preserved the faith despite the deviation of many.

In this time, when the word of the Lord had become precious, "Eli" was sitting in his tent, very near to the tabernacle of meeting, and specifically opposite it, as was the custom of the priests' dwellings. This verse indicates that his sight was very weak and that his eyes could not see as they had, which hindered his service.
The lamp of God: this is the golden lampstand with its seven lamps, which was lit throughout the night and put out in the early morning at the time of dawn.

Of course no one spent the night in the Holy Place, the Holy of Holies or the temple of the Lord. Samuel used to dwell in a tent next to the tent of "Eli" the priest, where he could serve him and hasten to him when he heard his voice, and what is mentioned here is a figure for the nearness of Samuel's tent to the tabernacle of meeting. At about the time of dawn the boy Samuel heard a voice calling him by name. He did not know whose voice it was, but he supposed it was the voice of Eli the priest, so he answered with his voice, before going to him, "Here I am," as one of us might say to another who calls him ("Yes" or "Present"). We notice that the Bible mentions that Eli lay down in his place (v. 2), while Samuel lay down in the temple of the Lord, to declare that righteous Samuel felt the awe and greatness of the house of the Lord, whereas Eli lay down in his body and did not feel the fear of God.
Samuel hurried and ran to "Eli" the priest and said to him: Yes, I am here as you called me. Eli answered him that he had not called him, and told him to go back and sleep.

What had happened was repeated a second time, and Eli the priest sent the boy Samuel back to sleep. Verse 7 makes clear to us that the boy Samuel could not tell that this voice was God, for this was the first time God spoke with him, especially as he was still young. There is a great difference between Samuel's not knowing the voice of God and Hophni and Phinehas's not knowing God because of their evils. But when it happened the third time, the priest, old in days, understood by his spiritual sense that it was God who was speaking with the boy.

So he sent him back a third time to his place, but this time he gave him new advice, telling him that when he heard this voice again, he should answer the One who spoke with the phrase "Speak, Lord, for Your servant hears." The boy Samuel went, obedient to his teacher, with a courage rarely found in a small boy.

God allowed the righteous boy Samuel to learn how to recognize the voice of God from the hand of Eli, the negligent high priest, so that Samuel might learn humility and learning from his elders, which is what boys and youths need in every generation.

Samuel was a righteous boy who loved God, and "Eli" was condemned before God for his shortcoming, his laxity and his lack of decisiveness in depriving his sons as recompense for their evil. Yet God used "Eli the priest" to guide Samuel and inform him that the voice he heard was the voice of God. How much more, then, the priesthood of the New Testament, which works by the Spirit! So, beloved, do not neglect the counsel of your spiritual father when you find it hard to understand God's purposes in your life.
The Lord came and stood: that is, He appeared in the form of a person who can be seen.

The first three times were calls only, but this time it was accompanied by a divine appearance, as happened to other persons in the Old Testament. When the Lord began His speech, Samuel answered with the words of "Eli": "Speak, for Your servant hears."

God began to speak, declaring to the boy Samuel the first prophecy he received as a prophet from God. The subject of this prophecy was momentous and grave, for God described His work as going to be so severe that people's ears could not bear it, and the expression "both ears will tingle" is a figure for the severity and fear that will strike the people. These events will be like the roar of thunder or the frightening sound that ears dread and fear.

On the day appointed for this matter God will carry out all that He spoke and all that the prophet told "Eli" of punishment (ch. 2:27-33), and when He begins He will not delay or stop until He has fulfilled all His previous words.
Here God explains to the boy Samuel what he had of course not heard in the conversation of the man of God with "Eli." From God's speech here with Samuel we draw more than one spiritual meaning:
1- God wants to speak with every pure and clean heart, and rank does not matter to Him, even if he is a boy.
2- By this speech God wanted to calm Samuel's heart so that he would not stumble at the severity of the coming events, and would understand that all this is God's just judgment.

3- God declares to Samuel and to us that although He is long-suffering, He does not excuse the wicked, licentious one from his guilt, and this makes a person examine himself and take account of his steps.
4- God wanted to declare to Samuel, and afterward to "Eli" the priest, that Samuel is the one chosen as prophet, judge and priest for Israel.

The Lord concludes His speech with Samuel with hard words: that He will not accept from Eli and his family any sacrifices of atonement or any offering to appease Him, because they persist in their faults. Their worship is outward, and God does not accept the worship of the wicked who do not want to leave their sins, but whoever is weak and falls into sin, God accepts him if he repents.

entries.section: (2) Telling Eli, and Samuel's declaration as a prophet of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The vision was at about dawn, after which Samuel settled on his bed for a short time before morning. We do not know whether he slept or remained astonished and meditating on what he had heard and on his first vision. At morning he began his daily work and opened the doors of the tabernacle of meeting in preparation for the morning services. He had made a decision in his heart not to tell "Eli" what he had seen and heard, because of his fear for him on account of the hardness of the news, and this shows the tenderness of his feelings.

entries.section: (2) Telling Eli, and Samuel's declaration as a prophet of the Lord

paragraphs.text: May God do so to you, and more also: may God be angry with you and punish you.

Eli wanted to know what God had said to Samuel, so he summoned him, and when the boy came before him he commanded him to tell him all that had happened and not to leave out a single word, or else God would bring down His wrath.

entries.section: (2) Telling Eli, and Samuel's declaration as a prophet of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Before Eli's insistence and his threat of God's punishment, Samuel confessed everything and hid nothing from him. As for "Eli," he submitted to God's punishment in weakness and defeat, though it would have been more fitting for him to offer repentance with tears before God and to punish his two sons, and then God would have relented of the evil that He was going to do.

entries.section: (2) Telling Eli, and Samuel's declaration as a prophet of the Lord

paragraphs.text: After that Samuel grew in age, mind, wisdom and spirituality, and he was with the Lord, so the Lord was with him and gave him the spirit of prophecy, so that everything he uttered came to pass. All the Israelites in all the land from one end to the other (Dan the farthest north, and Beersheba the farthest south) knew, and it became known among them and they became certain, as time passed, that God had chosen Samuel as a prophet and a man of His.

entries.section: (2) Telling Eli, and Samuel's declaration as a prophet of the Lord

paragraphs.text: This chapter began by affirming the fact that the word of God was precious and rare (v. 1), but at the end of the chapter, with the presence of the spiritual man, Samuel, the chapter ends with the words "the Lord appeared again." The beginning of the Lord's return was by appearing to Samuel when he was a boy, followed afterward by other visions and other works of standing by His people and choosing "David" afterward as their king.

When afflictions come upon you, or you hear the voice of God in the Bible or from the mouth of your father of confession, hasten to repent and change your life, leaving your evils, and you will receive God's mercies, for He is a tender Father who warns you so that you may repent and does not want to punish you.
The defeat of Israel before the Philistines
Aphek: a city in the south of the land of the Jews where the children of Israel fought the Philistines this time and then again in the days of Saul (1 Sam 29:1). Ebenezer: it lies southeast of Aphek.

The first part of this verse is a continuation of the last two verses of the previous chapter. After the people knew that Samuel was a prophet trusted by God, his word came to all Israel, meaning that he became a father, prophet and guide to the people in all their affairs. Despite this, no one consulted him before going out to fight the Philistines, because they did not care to hear the voice of God, so God abandoned them in the battle because of their pride and their sins, as will appear later.

The second part of this verse tells us that Israel went out to fight the Philistines. We do not know the motive or reason behind this war, but it is known that enmity had long been entrenched between the two peoples and they had many wars. The prophet Samuel mentions the place where the Israelite army encamped, whose name is "Ebenezer," a place that Samuel himself gave this name (ch. 7:12), and the Philistines were drawn up before it at a place named "Aphek."
Of the army: of the men drawn up in line, the soldiers. The field: the battleground or the field of combat.

The war broke out between the two sides, and this was the first battle. This round ended in a defeat for the people of the children of Israel, in which about four thousand men died. Although this number is large, it cannot be compared with the greater loss in the second round of the war.
The camp: what is meant here is the army's encampment.

In ancient times war continued throughout the day, and at the end of the day each side returned to its camp until the next day, to resume the war or end it by surrender. At the end of the first day the leaders of the people gathered in their camp and discussed the matter ... why was there defeat, and why did the enemies triumph over them, and what is the secret of God's abandoning them? An idea for victory came to their minds, which was to bring the ark of the covenant, which represented the divine presence in the midst of the people, thinking that the presence of the ark would give them victory, not knowing that their defeat was because of their evil, their lack of repentance and the wickedness of their priests. For the Lord's blessing on a person is connected with his striving and repentance, and not with merely keeping blessed things.

Formal worship without repentance is of no benefit, just as the Jews in the days of Jeremiah relied on the presence of the temple in Jerusalem and their worship in it while immersed in sins, so Babylon attacked them and burned Jerusalem and the temple, and the temple did them no good at all. Likewise today someone wears a golden cross and does not believe in its power, and so he benefits nothing.

In a new haste and error, the people did not consult God about the ark leaving the place He had set apart for it in the Holy of Holies, but carried it and moved it from the tent. Of course the priests accompanied the ark and carried it, among them Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest. When the ark reached the camp of the fighting people, all the men shouted with a great shout, so that the earth shook under their feet from the roar of the shouting and joy, but this shout was from the mouths and not from the heart, so it did them no good.

The Philistines heard the sound of the great shout, and in their astonishment at the roar of the shouting they perhaps sent some of their men to the camp of the Israelites as spies, and learned that this shout was because of the arrival of the "ark of the covenant into the camp of Israel." When the Philistines knew this their hearts melted with fear, and they said to themselves, Woe to us, for nothing awaits us but defeat, since the God of Israel has come to the place of battle. This is something we are not accustomed to from the Israelites in all our wars with them, that they should bring their God with them and show such zeal in fighting.

As fear continued within the ranks of the Philistines, they reviewed the power of the God of Israel, who was always with His people, and how He gave them victory over Egypt, the greatest kingdom in the world in that time, through the ten plagues. They remember well how God drowned the whole army of Egypt in the Red Sea when Israel went out into the wilderness. This fear was of course enough for them to withdraw from the battlefield, but because the Lord's will was something else, and He wanted His just judgment to be carried out, He put something else in the heart of the Philistines. Their fear drove them to take courage and fight bravely with all their strength so as not to be enslaved to the people of Israel, and the expression "as they have been to you" goes back to the fact that the Philistines considered the Hebrews a foreign people whose land this was not, and when they came in the early days from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob they were a small band whom the Philistines looked on with contempt as slaves.

The Philistines fought with strength and intensity, and the Lord did not support Israel, so their defeat was very great, for thirty thousand of the Jews fell and the rest fled. In this place also both Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest, died, and the Lord fulfilled His just judgment and His prophecy concerning them. As for the ark of the covenant, the Israelites left it at the time of their defeat and the Philistines took it with them. The psychological loss of the ark of the Lord was greater than all their slain, for the ark represented their pride and their strength, and its absence was a clear sign of God's anger against them and their loss of spiritual blessing.

Do not rely on your superficial worship of God while excusing some sins, for the only solution is repentance, or else God will abandon you and you will lose every blessing and be defeated before Satan.

Eli the priest was very anxious about the ark of the covenant's leaving the tent and going to the camp of battle, not knowing whether this was right or wrong. He could not wait in his house, but went out and sat by the road waiting for any news that might come to him. A man from the ranks of the army, of the tribe of Benjamin, had come back from the battle to Shiloh, the place of the tabernacle, with dust on his head and his clothes torn, and he told them of the defeat. Then crying and wailing went up over the loss of the war and over the slain men, and the cry of the women rose and covered the whole place.
Eli heard these loud, sorrowful sounds, and was alarmed and asked about the matter, so the Benjamite man came to him and told him all that had happened.
His eyes were set: they had lost sight completely.

"Eli" the priest was nearly a hundred years old and had completely lost his sight when the man told him that he had fled from the battle, that Israel was defeated before the Philistines, that his two sons Hophni and Phinehas were dead, and that they had lost the ark of the covenant.

Eli listened to all this painful news, very sorrowful to his soul, including the report of the death of his two sons, but when he learned that the matter had reached the loss of the ark of the covenant, he lost his balance and his body fell backward, and because of the weight of his body he fell to the ground, so his neck was broken and he died at once, for his old age also hastened the matter. Samuel, the writer of the book, mentions that "Eli" had judged and ruled his people for forty years.
Labor: the contractions, pains and signs of childbirth.

The wife of Phinehas, the son of Eli, was about to give birth, and when she heard the whole set of bad news at once, unexpected contractions came that hastened the birth. At the time of delivery the women around her noticed the paleness of her face and her sharp decline, as if it were the hour of her death. The women wanted to encourage her that she had borne a male son, but because of her intense grief, her sickness and her decline she could not answer, and her heart was not gladdened by anything.
Ichabod: a name meaning where is the glory, or the glory has departed.

The last words spoken by Phinehas's wife, in her intense grief and despair, were that she called her son's name Ichabod, because the glory had departed with the loss of the ark of God's covenant and the death of her father-in-law and her husband. This shows her faith in God, for she grieved over the loss of the ark more than over the loss of her husband and her father-in-law.

The loss of the ark was a discipline for the children of Israel, in that God would not dwell among them because of their evils, and it was a discipline for the Philistines for their cruelty and their many assaults on the people of God, for the ark troubled them and struck them with diseases, as will appear later.

When you hear sorrowful news, do not stand alone, but hasten to God to support you, and speak with your spiritual father and with your loved ones so that your heart may be at rest, then think positively, that is, do what you are able to do to solve the problem. The First Book of Samuel. The ark and its strikes on the Philistines

entries.section: (1) The ark of the covenant in Ashdod

paragraphs.text: Ashdod: one of the important cities of the Philistines, lying north of the city of Gaza.

Dagon: a god worshipped by the Philistines, the Assyrians and the Phoenicians. He is the god of wheat and agricultural crops, and is called the god of fertility. His head, chest and arms were in the form of a man, while the rest of his body was in the form of a fish, because of the great multiplication of fish in the sea.

The Israelites left the ark of the covenant at the place of battle and fled, so the Philistines took it to one of their famous cities, Ashdod. They found no better place to put the ark than the temple devoted to one of their famous gods, the idol Dagon, so the ark was beside the statue of the god. In this they displayed the power of their god Dagon, whom they considered the greatest of their gods, since they brought to him the ark of the covenant of God, the God of Israel, whom they thought weak because they had prevailed over Him and His people. They placed it before Dagon, but Dagon, in whom there was a demon, could not bear to see God, and fell on his face before Him, as we shall see in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) The ark of the covenant in Ashdod

paragraphs.text: On the morning of the first day, after the ark entered the temple of "Dagon," the pagan Philistine priests rose early to stand before their god, and to their surprise they found the statue of Dagon fallen on its face, that is, prostrate! This was a strange thing that had never happened to their statue, so they could do nothing but set it up again in its place. The next day they entered the temple of Dagon to worship, and behold, he was fallen on his face again as the day before, but this time the fall was more severe, for after he fell on his face his head and his hands were severed on the threshold of the temple. This means that the head, which symbolizes the mind, and the hands, which symbolize work, did not belong to this god, that is, he has no mind and is powerless to do anything, and the animal part, the fish, remained to declare the lowliness of this god. In addition, the falling of the head and hands at the threshold, which is trodden by feet, also declares the lowliness of this god and the shame of whoever worships him.
God also declares His power to the pagans. Although He had departed from His people because of their evils, He glorifies His name before those who are far off, that they may believe in Him.
And when God, whom the ark of the covenant signifies, enters the heart, all the powers of the world, of position and money .., are shattered before Him.

entries.section: (1) The ark of the covenant in Ashdod

paragraphs.text: Instead of understanding, realizing and acknowledging that this "Dagon" was nothing but the work of human hands, the priests of "Dagon" went in another strange direction, adding undeserved honor to their stone god. They took a vow upon themselves that their feet would not tread on the threshold of the house, out of respect for the fall of his head and hands on the threshold!! This tradition continued for many years.
The First Book of Samuel

entries.section: (1) The ark of the covenant in Ashdod

paragraphs.text: Tumors: some think it was not the well-known disease of hemorrhoids but the result of the plague, which strikes the lymph glands and the groin. This disease is carried by rats, so the Septuagint declares that rats attacked the land of the Philistines, and it is stated in (v. 11) that they feared death, because of the epidemic of plague.

Since the Philistines did not understand the divine purpose of these blows to their god and their pride, "Dagon," the Lord God made His hand heavy upon them, afflicting them with distress, ruin and lack of blessing in the matters of their material life. Moreover, the Lord added to that by striking them with the very painful disease of tumors, which causes severe distress to the one who has it.

entries.section: (1) The ark of the covenant in Ashdod

paragraphs.text: Finally the people of Ashdod understood and grasped the lesson, and realized that the God of Israel was behind all these blows, and they reached a decision that the ark of the God of Israel could not remain with them. What had befallen them with their god was enough for them on the one hand, and they also feared what was coming upon them.

It took a long time for the people of Ashdod to understand ... Be quick to understand God's purposes, and return at once with repentance and apology and resolve to amend, and you will save yourself from God's disciplines and enjoy a calm, blessed life.
Lords: leaders.
Gath: one of the large cities of the Philistines like Ashdod, lying northeast of Gaza.

The leaders of the Philistine clans gathered after the amazing events at Ashdod, and the purpose of the meeting was one thing: what shall we do with the ark of the covenant and where shall we put it? The opinion was that they should move it to the city of Gath, and in this they proved their lack of understanding, for they thought that the God of Israel did not like Ashdod or Dagon, so they proposed an alternative place.
Broke out: and swelled.

The hand of the Lord was also on the city of "Gath," as it had been on Ashdod, so the same affliction of distress and turmoil struck them, and the tumors broke out and they had the same pain. God allowed these pains and did not destroy them because they had taken the ark of God's covenant in ignorance, not knowing that it was God.
When afflictions recur with you, examine yourself and pray to understand God's purposes, for His aim may be to call you to repent of a certain sin or to correct a certain shortcoming.
Ekron: a famous Philistine city lying south of "Joppa," and its meaning is "barren."

To rid themselves of the ark and its troubles, the people of "Gath" made a decision to send the ark away from them and send it to the city of Ekron, without the permission or knowledge of the Ekronites. For this reason the people of Ekron cried out, murmured and were afraid when the ark reached them, and said, The people of "Gath" have sent the ark to us for our destruction. The First Book of Samuel

As soon as the ark arrived, the people of Ekron sensed God's vengeance and His strong hand, for there was great turmoil because of the rising number of the dead. For this reason they held a meeting of all the leaders of the Philistine clans and asked that the ark return to Israel, to its place and its rest, so that the very severe vengeance of the God of Israel might stop.

Death struck some, while the rest were struck with the disease of tumors, and the pain was severe and the distress great, so that the cry of the people filled the whole city, crying for help to have the ark removed from them.

God may allow His children some discipline, as happened with Israel His people because of laxity and recklessness, but for the sake of the glory of His name God does not allow the enemies to gloat over His children or enjoy victory. He is just and repays with right, and at the same time He is jealous for His name and for His people. So do not wrong anyone and rejoice in what you have gained, for God is able to repay you with many blows if you do not repent. The return of the ark of God

The ark of God's covenant was lost in the war of the children of Israel against the Philistines, at Ebenezer, then it was moved to the Philistine city of "Ashdod," and from there to "Gath," then to "Ekron," and this took a period of seven months. The strange thing is that the people of Israel did not try anything in that time to recover the ark, whether by war or paying money or any kind of negotiation, as if the matter meant nothing. But we understand from this the state of the people, in spiritual heedlessness and strange resignation.
The stay of the ark of God's covenant in the land of the Philistines was long for several reasons:
1- So that the Philistines might understand that the blows that came upon them were not chance but from the God of Israel.
2- So that the Philistines might know that the God of Israel is stronger than their gods, indeed that He is the God of gods.
3- So that the children of Israel might feel their sins that caused God to forsake them, and repent and keep His commandments.
The priests: they are the priests of the gods of the Philistines such as Dagon and Beelzebub.

The diviners: they claim knowledge of the unseen, and Satan may help them in some matters to extend his influence. God is the defender of His glory and of His name, so after He struck the Philistines with all these blows, He moved them to gather their priests and also the diviners to advise the people what to do with the ark of the covenant and how to return it to the Israelites. God does not leave Himself without a witness, and He uses even the pagans and moves them to bear witness to Him.

The first suggestion of the priests and diviners was to send an offering of appeasement to the God of Israel, which they called a "trespass offering," as a kind of apology for what they had committed by their theft of the ark. When sending this offering they expected that the God of Israel would have mercy on them and heal their sickness, so that the Philistines would be sure that all these diseases were because of their wrong against the God of Israel.
Lords: leaders.

The people asked the priests and diviners for their suggestion of the suitable offering, and their answer was that they should make five images in the form of the tumors, which was the disease that afflicted them, and five images in the form of rats, because among God's blows on them mentioned here was the increase in the number of rats that ate most of their crops and made their homes ruins. By this they would appease the Lord God of Israel so that He would lift His anger from the people and from the land. The suggestion of the number five was based on the fact that the main cities of Philistia and the leaders of their clans were five, and so the whole people would share in the offering and the apology.
We notice that the atonement and apology of the Philistines for their sin against the ark of God's covenant shows the following:
1- That it resembles what happened when the children of Israel left Egypt, when they took the gold and silver from the Egyptians.

2- That the pagans' concept of atonement for sin is paying a sum of money, whereas atonement, as the Bible declares, is accomplished only by the blood of Christ, to which the blood of the sacrifices in the Old Testament pointed.
Why do you harden your hearts?!: a question whose purpose is prohibition, that is, do not harden your hearts.

The priests and diviners completed their words by giving advice to the leaders of the Philistines, which was to obey what they said and not make light of their words. They reminded them of the history of the children of Israel and how the great God of Israel struck Pharaoh of Egypt with the ten plagues until he let them go against his will.

God's power appears here in how He moved the pagan priests and diviners to bear witness to Him and to declare their wrong against Him when they stole His ark. So they offered trespass offerings that He might forgive them and heal their diseases, and they believed in His power that struck the Egyptians with the ten plagues. All this is a call to believe in God, that perhaps some of the pious among the people would believe in Him, for God does not leave Himself without a witness in every place, even in places where you do not expect anyone to be found bearing witness to His holy name. For they declared that He is a God stronger than their gods and cannot be resisted, as all the gods of the Egyptians could not resist Him. It is understood of course that the gifts were not a bribe to God but atonement for their sins against Him.

Here appears the virtue of the Philistine priests in learning from the sins of the Egyptians, who opposed the God of Israel so that the ten plagues came upon them, so they decided to submit and apologize to Him. How beautiful it is to learn from the sins of others and be careful not to fall into them.
Cart: a wooden wagon.
Beth Shemesh: the first Jewish city after the borders of the Philistines, lying in the southeast of the tribe of Judah.
The yoke: a rod of wood placed on the necks of two animals to pull agricultural implements or wagons. By chance: by coincidence.

The priests and diviners suggested making a wooden cart with the ark of the covenant placed on it, and another chest carrying the golden tumors and rats. They stipulated that the cart be new, and in this was honor to the ark and the God of Israel, and that the two cows be nursing and their young (the little calves) be left in the pen, and also that they had never pulled any cart or agricultural implement before, "on which a yoke has never come." But why?!
The priests wanted to determine one thing: whether these blows were from the God of Israel or were merely chance!! For this reason they set difficult conditions.

A nursing cow cannot walk while leaving her suckling behind her; this is almost impossible. Likewise a cow on whose back a yoke has never come, and which has not been used before to pull carts, would find it hard to pull the cart toward Israel on a steep, difficult and untrodden road, having no experience in drawing carts without a man to lead her and direct her .. So after all that, if the two cows headed toward the Jewish city of Beth Shemesh, it would mean that the God of Israel was behind all that had befallen them, but if the two cows returned to them and did not go, it would all be chance and the God of Israel had no part in it.

The new cart and the two cows that had not been used in farm work signify that we must worship God with all the heart, and the heart must not be occupied with or rely on the things of the world, nor should a person keep God in his heart while being lax toward sin or the passing preoccupations of the world.

The Philistines did exactly what the priests and diviners had suggested, in choosing the two cows and shutting up their calves, and they placed the ark of the covenant of the Lord on the cart, and beside it the chest of the offering containing the images of the rats and the tumors.
Lowing: crying out in a loud voice.

The two cows went in a straight line to the Jewish city of Beth Shemesh, without turning to the right or the left, and their voice was loud, perhaps because they had left their young. Behind the wooden cart some of the Philistines walked to make sure that the cart reached Beth Shemesh.

If affliction comes upon you, examine yourself and offer repentance, lest your sins be the cause of what has come upon you; and accept the affliction from the hand of God and seek His help, for He is a tender Father ready to forgive you, support you and turn the affliction into a blessing.

entries.section: (2) The arrival of the ark among the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The valley: low land between two high places.

The harvest began at the Feast of Pentecost and lasted about two months (May and June). During this period, while the wheat was being harvested in the fields, the people of the city of Beth Shemesh caught sight of the cart carrying the ark, and their joy was great when they saw it, and they felt God's pleasure with them as He returned to dwell in their midst. Here appears the love of God, who seeks His children in order to dwell among them despite their laziness and their laxity in seeking His dwelling among them.

entries.section: (2) The arrival of the ark among the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The two cows and the cart stopped at the house of a man named "Joshua," and beside his house was a large stone. The Israelites took the cart and cut up its wood to be fuel and kindled it on the stone, then they slaughtered the two cows and offered them up as a burnt offering to the Lord. They broke up the cart and used its wood as fuel because it was not right to use it for anything after it had carried the ark of God's covenant, since it had become holy to Him.

entries.section: (2) The arrival of the ark among the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Since it was forbidden for any of the people to touch the ark, the Levites came and took down the ark, and placed it and the chest that was with it on the large stone. In expression of joy, the people of Beth Shemesh offered other burnt offerings and sacrifices in thanks to the Lord for His great work and how He had returned the ark to them.

entries.section: (2) The arrival of the ark among the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: As for the leaders of the Philistines who followed the cart and the two cows from a distance, after making sure that the ark had reached Beth Shemesh, they returned to the Philistine city of Ekron on the same day.

It is strange that after the leaders of the Philistines were sure that the God of Israel is stronger than their gods and also the gods of the Egyptians, and after they felt the diseases that had fallen on them, and then the ark's return by its own power to its people, all this did not draw them to believe in Him more than in their gods. This still happens even now, a proof of the stubbornness of man's heart and his rejection of the voice of God .. But you, do not be stubborn if God reveals to you any spiritual truth.

It was natural that the Israelites were unable to recover the ark, but what man is unable to do, God completes for him. Be faithful and do what is within your power, and leave the rest of the matters to the Lord Christ, who governs all and who alone is able to complete your human weakness!!

entries.section: (2) The arrival of the ark among the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: A village of the open country: a village without walls.

These two verses speak about the gifts presented by the leaders or rulers of the five great Philistine cities, and here the names of these cities are mentioned: (Gaza, Ashdod, Gath, Ashkelon and Ekron). These gifts consisted of five golden images in the form of tumors, while the golden rats were far more numerous, for five of them were for the five cities, and every village also offered a golden rat besides the five cities, because the rats had spread in the cities and villages. The prophet Samuel adds in his record of these events that the large stone which was used as an altar and on which the ark was afterward placed is still a witness to all these events, standing in its place in the field of "Joshua" the Beth Shemite.

entries.section: (3) The striking of the people of "Beth Shemesh"

paragraphs.text: The ark of the covenant had three coverings (see Num 4:3-6), so that no one would look at it or gaze at its contents. But when the ark reached the town of Beth Shemesh, the people came from every place to gaze at the ark, and perhaps they uncovered its coverings or even opened it to see what was inside. The greatest error was that they did not return the ark to its place in the tabernacle. So the hand of the Lord was heavy upon them, and fifty thousand and seventy men died. Of course this whole number was not from the town of Beth Shemesh, since it is a small town, but from the whole people, because they dared to look at it and did not take care to return it to its place. So there was sorrow and mourning because of this great blow. God punished the lax among the Jews with death because they knew the holiness of the ark and were lax, whereas He did not kill the Philistines who looked at the ark but only struck them with diseases, because they did not believe in the God of Israel and did not know how to treat His ark. In addition, the Philistines had honored the ark by placing it on a new cart drawn by two cows that had not worked before, whereas the lax Jews put it on a stone in the open air and did not return it to the tabernacle of meeting or put it temporarily inside a room set aside for it, covered. This signifies what some Christians do now who approach Communion without repentance or while persisting in their sins, for laxity toward this sacrament angers God greatly.

entries.section: (3) The striking of the people of "Beth Shemesh"

paragraphs.text: Kirjath Jearim: a village 14.5 km west of Jerusalem, lying on a place higher than the village of Beth Shemesh, as shown by his saying "come down" to the inhabitants of Kirjath Jearim.

The people of Beth Shemesh cried out and acknowledged that they were sinners and could not stand before God (and who can?), and asked that the ark of the covenant be moved away from them (taken up), but to where and to whom should it go?! So they sent messengers to the village of Kirjath Jearim, asking them to come and take the ark from their town, and the people of the town responded, as we shall understand from the next chapter. Their thinking was how to be rid of the ark out of fear of it, whereas it would have been more fitting for them to offer repentance to God and be reconciled with Him, seeking to please Him by placing it in the proper place and honoring it as it ought to be.

They sent the ark to the town of Kirjath Jearim and not to Shiloh, where the tabernacle of meeting was, because the Philistines had destroyed it. Samuel afterward set up the tabernacle in the city of Nob and placed in it the vessels and the altar, and the ark remained in Kirjath Jearim until David moved it (1 Chr 15:4-15, 2 Chr 1:4).

The children of Israel dared to look at the ark of God and did not hallow it as the Law prescribed by not looking at it, and this led to their destruction. How much more, then, he who is lax and approaches the Holy Mysteries in the New Testament without repentance deserves a greater punishment. May you prepare with repentance, prayer and purification to receive the power of Communion from the Body and Blood of the Lord.
The settling of the ark, the repentance of the people, and the defeat of the Philistines

entries.section: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

paragraphs.text: The hill: a high place.

The people of the village of Kirjath Jearim responded to the request of the people of Beth Shemesh, and went and took the ark and moved it to their city. With reverence they placed the ark in the house of a Levite man named "Abinadab," whose house was on a high place above the village or city. In honor of the ark, "Eleazar" the son of Abinadab was consecrated and set apart to watch over and serve the ark and to prevent anyone from approaching it. It is noted that the people of Kirjath Jearim were distinguished from the people of Beth Shemesh in the following:
1- They did not lift the coverings and did not look at the ark.
2- They set apart a place for the ark hidden from sight and did not leave it on a rock in a field.

3- They set apart a man to watch and guard it and to keep the people from approaching it, and for all this God did not punish them as He punished the people who dared to look at the ark at Beth Shemesh.

It is noted that "Abinadab" the Levite man cared for the ark and its service, while the priests neglected to honor the ark and move it to the tabernacle of meeting. The ark remained about 100 years in the house of Abinadab, and Samuel did not concern himself with moving the ark because he was occupied with calling the people to repent of their sins and hold fast to God's commandments, for he cared for the essence of worship before its form. This shows how far the people had declined spiritually and their need to repent first and only afterward offer complete worship to God, that is, their worship was incomplete because the ark was not in the tabernacle.

entries.section: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

paragraphs.text: Lamented: grieved and wept.

Twenty years passed with the ark settled in Kirjath Jearim, and they were hard years for Israel, in which the Philistines humiliated and oppressed them. So Israel returned to the Lord with weeping and mourning over their sins that had brought them into all this, and thus Samuel's ministry bore fruit in the collective repentance of the people. The ark continued in Kirjath Jearim after that for more than 50 years until King David moved it to Jerusalem (1 Chr 13:3, ch. 15).

entries.section: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

paragraphs.text: The Ashtoreths: female pagan goddesses, the plural of Ashtoreth. Ashtoreth was the wife of the god Baal, and adultery was among the rites of her worship.

Samuel, the spiritual servant, seized the opportunity of the people's state, their mourning and their desire to return to God, and spoke to all the people, saying: If you truly want to return to God with all your hearts, you must first cleanse your hearts and your houses of the strange gods that crept in among you, which you took from the nations and worshipped with the God of Israel, and you must also prepare your hearts with repentance for the one God, the Holy One of Israel. Then God will look upon you with an eye of mercy and accept you and help you and give you victory over the Philistines, for the worship of God cannot be mixed with the worship of idols, and we cannot keep sin together with the worship of God, but we must cut ourselves off from sin and keep away from it, or else our worship will become formal and without value.

entries.section: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

paragraphs.text: Baal: a word meaning "master or lord," applied to the pagan gods, to the male god, and its plural is Baalim.

The people responded to Samuel's words, and indeed they removed all the pagan gods from among them, whether the statues of Baal or the Ashtoreths, and returned with all their hearts to the God of Israel.

entries.section: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

paragraphs.text: Mizpah: a city lying in the middle of the lands of the tribes, which everyone could easily reach, and lying eight miles north of Jerusalem.

Samuel also asked the people to gather in the town of Mizpah, which lies in the land of the tribe of Benjamin, in order to stand with them before God and pray for them, so that God might forgive them their sins.

How beautiful is this scene in which Samuel stands between God and His people, praying with them to bring them near to God .. Is this not the very scene of the Divine Liturgy, in which the priest stands between the people and God to present them to Him and to present the Holy God to them, that is, His most holy Body and Blood? Beloved, how can you miss attending the Divine Liturgy from its beginning, so that your heart may be lifted to God and you may be worthy in the end to receive the greatest thing in the world, the sacrament of Communion?..!

entries.section: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

paragraphs.text: They drew water: they filled their jars with water.

The people of Israel gathered at Mizpah as Samuel had asked. They filled their vessels with water and poured it out before the Lord, as an offering pointing to the pouring out of the heart before God and submission to Him. They also offered an ascetic fast as an expression of their repentance, and acknowledged to Samuel their faults against the Holy One of Israel.
After that Samuel stayed for a time at Mizpah, ruling, judging and guiding the people in their questions, their complaints and their various affairs.
From this appears the role of Samuel, which was:
1- A spiritual leader leading the people to repentance.
2- A priest who accepts their repentance.
3- A judge who decides their problems according to God's Law.
4- His strength depended on God, therefore he constantly lifted up prayer for his people, for God is the one who protects His people and their true leader.

The Philistines heard the news of the gathering of the children of Israel with Samuel at Mizpah, perhaps through spies or through some commercial dealings, since the enmity between the two peoples did not prevent their dealings in buying and selling. Because the Philistines were anxious about this gathering, they sent some of their leaders to Israel to verify the matter, and when the Israelites saw these Philistines they were very afraid and went quickly to their judge Samuel, asking him to pray earnestly to God that He would grant them salvation and victory over the Philistines.
Here appears the virtue of the people in the following:
1- Their turning to God, their Savior and Deliverer from the enemies.
2- Their faith in the intercession of Samuel, their spiritual leader.
This did not happen the first time at Aphek, therefore they were defeated before the Philistines.

Samuel responded to the people's cry and approached God, taking with him a lamb to offer as a burnt offering, that is, to burn it entirely on the altar (Lev 1). After he offered the sacrifice he prayed a fervent prayer, which the inspired text describes as a crying out, and the Lord heard and accepted the sacrifice and prayer of Samuel. The burnt offering is offered entirely to God as a symbol of the consecration of the whole person to God and the obtaining of His favor, just as Christ offered His life on the Cross to please the Father so that He might be pleased with our race.

Samuel offered a sacrifice although he was a Levite and not a priest. This was with God's permission because of the special circumstances through which His people were passing, of spiritual decline and the priests' neglect of their office.

Prayer is the best spiritual work a person does, and crying out means that the prayer is from the depth of the heart. The people prayed and also asked for the prayer of the man of God on their behalf; you too do likewise. Cry out to God in your affliction and ask those around you in the Church to cry out with you, especially your father the priest, and God will hear and answer.

While Samuel was offering his sacrifice, the Philistines gathered to fight the people of God, but God "thundered" upon them. The word thundered may mean one of two things: the first, a figure for God's intervention, who struck terror into the hearts of the Philistines, and the second, that God in reality commanded nature, so that real thunder occurred, very severe and resounding, which unsettled the hearts of the Philistines and made them flee and retreat before Israel. The divine thunder represents the work of grace that supported the men of Israel in their war with the Philistines, which represents spiritual striving, and by the two they triumphed over the Philistines, who fled before them.

Beth Car: a Hebrew word meaning house of lambs, and it is a village lying near Mizpah. The Philistines were thrown into confusion and began to withdraw, and the children of Israel followed them to a village called "Beth Car" and beyond, until the Philistines fled completely.

As for Samuel, the faithful servant, he did not forget what God had done with the people, and for this reason he wanted to make a memorial that would always be before the people.
