So he took a stone and set it up between the city of Mizpah and a village called "Shen," and he called this memorial "Ebenezer" (the stone of help), making clear the reason for this name, which was God's help to the people that ended in the defeat of the Philistines before them.

Whereas the Philistines had been going in and out of all the lands of the children of Israel in all their arrogance, the hand of the Lord was now against them, and He allowed their humiliation after their haughtiness and pride. This state continued all the days of the prophet Samuel, the man of prayer, who cared for the shepherding of his people, so they lived in the fear of God.

The Amorites: among the strongest of the Canaanite peoples, and they dwelt here west of the Jordan, while in the days of Moses they also dwelt east of the Jordan, and he triumphed over them and over their two kings Sihon and Og (Num 21:

21-25.) Israel was able to recover all the small cities lying between the large Philistine cities (Ekron and Gath) which the Philistines had previously occupied, and when the Amorites saw Israel's victory over the Philistines, they sought a peace treaty with Israel, so the days of Samuel were also full of peace with all the neighbors.
Bethel: it lies east of Jerusalem and west of Nablus, and it is the first place where Abraham, the father of the fathers, stayed when he entered Canaan.
Gilgal: near Jericho, and it was a political and military center in the days of Joshua.
Mizpah: in the land of the tribe of Benjamin, lying in a central place of the land of Israel.

Samuel was the last of the judges of the people of Israel before they afterward had kings like the rest of the nations. The days of Samuel's service as a judge were blessed days for the people, in which he spared no effort, visiting all the people and going from place to place to judge for them, solve their problems and guide them. The text mentions here the most important stations and centers to which he went every year so that the people could find him.

The permanent residence that Samuel took for himself was Ramah (ch. 1:1), where he built an altar after God had established him as priest and accepted his sacrifices ... As for the tabernacle, the morning and evening offerings were offered in it as usual in the city of Shiloh, but the people turned away from it, especially after the ark remained in the town of Kirjath Jearim, and they regarded Samuel as the true priest and leader. Although there was a high priest, most likely Ahitub (ch. 14:3), who followed Eli the priest, all the eyes of the people were toward Samuel the priest and their true leader.

It is noted here that there are some exceptions to the rule, which is offering sacrifices only before the house of the Lord, for Samuel offered them in Ramah as he offered a burnt offering at Mizpah (v. 9). For the people were passing through unusual circumstances: they had neglected to return the ark to the house of the Lord at Shiloh and left it in the village of Kirjath Jearim, and thus the tabernacle of meeting at Shiloh was without the ark.

In proportion to your prayers and your care for those around you, God intervenes and keeps you and those with you and shepherds you with His fatherhood. So do not neglect prayer and concern for the salvation of the souls of those around you, whether you are small or great, for God works through all.

The demand for a king (1) The corruption of Samuel's sons (vv. 1-5:) 1 And it came to pass, when Samuel was old, that he made his sons judges over Israel. 2 Now the name of his firstborn was Joel; and the name of his second, Abiah: they were judges in Beersheba. 3 And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment. 4 Then all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together, and came to Samuel unto Ramah, 5 And said unto him, Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.

Samuel used to go about the land of the Jews and judge for them, and when he advanced in days he appointed his two sons Joel and Abiah at Beersheba in the south of Judea to help him in judging the people. It seems that they were distinguished in their character, so the people chose them and Samuel appointed them, and they did not receive this office by inheritance. Samuel had reached the age of about seventy years, that is, about twenty years passed between the previous chapter and this chapter. Samuel judged at Ramah, which lies in the north, while his sons were at Beersheba, which lies in the south, and this shows that there were no wars with the Philistines and consequently there was calm and stability among the tribes of Israel.

Near the end of Samuel's life and his judging of the people, we come to the end of the age of the judges, and we shall find that the people will ask for a king, that is, they will enter a new age, the age of the monarchy.

But his sons did not walk as their father walked and did not put the fear of God in their hearts, so they turned aside after the desire of the love of money and accepted bribes, and their judgments for the people became unjust, since they looked to their own interests and not the interest of the people. Perhaps this teaches us the necessity of spiritual follow-up with our children, and perhaps this is the only error into which Samuel fell, that he did not follow his sons in their course and their work. For recognizing the fault at its beginning and warning against it is better than slackness and waiting, which makes it a disease that is hard to cure.

It may seem strange that Samuel did not profit from the error of Eli the priest, so that corruption also appeared in the two sons of Samuel. But we notice that there are differences between the sin of Eli and that of Samuel in the raising of their sons, so God allowed the death of Eli and his two sons and did not allow it in the case of Samuel and his two sons, for the following reasons:

1- The two sons of Eli the priest were priests and were doing evil in the temple in front of their father, whereas the two sons of Samuel were judging in another place, Beersheba, far from the place where their father lived, which was Ramah.
2- The sin of the two sons of Eli was violent, namely adultery and theft by compulsion.

3- The two sons of Samuel were good and the people chose them, then they erred, and Samuel agreed to their submission to the king and their being tried for any errors into which they fell (1 Sam 12:2).

The matter greatly displeased the people, so the leaders of the people gathered and went to Ramah, the permanent residence of the prophet Samuel, and confronted him with the actions of his sons, and how they had turned aside and not walked like him. The surprise that Samuel had not expected at all was that the elders of the people demanded that he appoint a king for them to rule and judge like the rest of the peoples and nations around them.
The evident sin of Eli the priest was his laxity with his two sons, who were committing adultery and robbing the people.

The strange thing is that despite the holiness of the prophet Samuel, he was lax in the raising of his two sons, so they took bribes when they became judges, which drove the people to an error, namely demanding a king, forgetting God their King.

May you learn from the errors of others lest you fall into the same sin, and do not judge them lest you be judged; but hold yourself to account and examine your life carefully and seek God's help, and He will help you to correct your faults and you will enjoy His mercies.

(2) God's agreement to their request for a king (vv. 6-9:) 6 But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, Give us a king to judge us. And Samuel prayed unto the LORD. 7 And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them. 8 According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even unto this day, wherewith they have forsaken me, and served other gods, so do they also unto thee. 9 Now therefore hearken unto their voice: howbeit yet protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them.

The request of the leaders of the people seemed very ugly in Samuel's eyes .. Perhaps he felt an unexpected boldness from them, or that they were rejecting him after all these years of service, but because he was a spiritual man he found no way out for his bitter inner pains except prayer .. There is no rest except by opening the heart before God.

The Lord answered Samuel's prayer, and wanted to comfort him and soothe his heart, so He told him to grant the people their request to appoint an earthly king for them, and not to grieve himself, for this people had not rejected him but had rejected God, their true King. In real fatherhood, simplicity and humility from God, God likens Samuel to Himself and says to him that this people is difficult: after all that I did with them of great works, bringing them out of the land of Egypt, sustaining them and bringing them into the land of Canaan, they forsook Me and served Baal and the Ashtoreths, and as they have done to Me so they do to you also .. that is, you are like Me, O Samuel ..

Every priest, servant, father or mother learns from Samuel that the insult directed at him is directed at God, so he bears with those he shepherds in their faults, and that every honor directed to him is God's, so he gives thanks to Him.

And now, Samuel, respond to the people in their request to appoint a king for them, but before that you must tell them what will happen when a king is chosen, and what the results and consequences are that they did not study when they made that request, so that you will be innocent afterward of the results of their choice.

Here God allows them to appoint a king, and in His foreknowledge He knew that they would reject Him and ask for a king over them, so He declared this in the Law to Moses, and out of fatherly love He set conditions for this king so that he would not lead them away from God (Deut 17:14, 15). The conditions for this king are:
1- God is the one who chooses him.
2- He must be from the children of Israel and not a foreigner, lest he lead them astray to the worship of idols.

3- He must not multiply horses, lest he become proud and enter into many wars that take him away from God and from care for his people, or return to Egypt to buy horses from it and so be tied to the worship of the Egyptian idols.
4- He must not multiply wives, lest they turn his heart away from God.
5- He must not greatly multiply silver and gold, lest he be proud of his wealth and be occupied with material things instead of God.
6- He must write for himself a copy of the Law to read it always and act by it.
7- The priest, as God's representative, anoints him.
8- He has no right to perform the priestly service.
9- God punishes him if he sins.
He is subject to God and has no absolute authority. As will appear in God's punishment of David at the numbering of the people...
In His foreknowledge God knew that they would ask for a king, so He laid down rules in His Law for the king to follow (Deut 17:

14-20.) It is noted that the people asked for a king with the appearance of material power and not one who follows his heart after God, for they asked for a king to lead them in war and forgot that the true Leader who gives them victory is God, and that they had prevailed through the prayers of Samuel. The people forgot that God used to choose the judge in the age of the judges, whereas in the age of the monarchy the kingship is inherited by the son even if he is not suited to this office.

(3) The consequences of appointing a king (vv. 10-18:) 10 And Samuel told all the words of the LORD unto the people that asked of him a king. 11 And he said, This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and some shall run before his chariots. 12 And he will appoint him captains over thousands, and captains over fifties; and will set them to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and instruments of his chariots. 13 And he will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers. 14 And he will take your fields, and your vineyards, and your oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants. 15 And he will take the tenth of your seed, and of your vineyards, and give to his officers, and to his servants. 16 And he will take your menservants, and your maidservants, and your goodliest young men, and your asses, and put them to his work. 17 He will take the tenth of your sheep: and ye shall be his servants. 18 And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the LORD will not hear you in that day.

Samuel gathered the leaders of the people and told them the word of God that He had spoken to him, which was that the people had rejected God, their King and Savior, and then he began to explain to them how it would be if an earthly king were chosen for them. The first thing is that this king will choose the best of their young men and make of them horsemen and slaves devoted to guarding him and driving his royal chariots, and some of them will have the task of running before the procession of his chariots in order to clear the way for him.

Likewise this king will appoint others whom he will make captains over fifties, hundreds and thousands to organize his service, that is, he will give them regular ranks as is customary in armies, and the task of these captains will be to oversee the plowing of his land and the harvesting of his crop, as well as the making of the instruments of war and the making of his own chariots.

Likewise also, he will take many of your daughters, and some of them will make perfumes and spices for his wives, and some will work in the royal kitchen as cooks, and the last as bakers. That is, whereas your daughters were free and honored in their parents' houses, they will become maidservants to the king.
Likewise he will take the best of your lands, and who will oppose a request of the king?

Or at least he may demand their produce to spend on his servants and soldiers who serve him, and whereas the tithes of the crops were given to the Levites, he will impose new tithes upon you (as a tax) to spend on his servants to ensure their loyalty and service to him.

And if he has need after that, he will dare more and more and will press your servants and animals into his service and the service of his house, his wives and his requirements, and no one will be able to say no to the king, even if he asks for your best and goodliest sons.

The taxes he imposes in the form of new tithes will not include only the agricultural crops, but will also include tithes of the sheep, as if the people were forced to pay two tenths of everything, one to God and the other to the new king. Besides this, the whole people will become slaves to him .. he commands and is obeyed, and presses them into all he wants, and no one can object; he permits whom he wishes and forbids whom he wills.

As a result of all the above, and with the increasing might of the king, you will murmur and then cry out because of what he inflicts on you, and your crying will increase and God will hear, but He will not answer, because you are the ones who chose this king in place of God.

Know that sin, however dazzling and pleasant it may seem, has its many troubles. So do not rush after your desires and personal opinions, but seek God and obey His commandments and you will live in security.

(4) The insistence on appointing a king (vv. 19-22:) 19 Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us; 20 That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles. 21 And Samuel heard all the words of the people, and he rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD. 22 And the LORD said to Samuel, Hearken unto their voice, and make them a king. And Samuel said unto the men of Israel, Go ye every man unto his city.

Despite God's clear warning that Samuel spoke, the people refused to listen to the voice of wisdom, but increased in their demand and said with insistence: We must have a king and become a kingdom like the rest of the peoples around us who have kings .. and this king will have the awe of going out and coming in and leading the wars, and will also be the ruler and judge of all our problems and needs.

God, in His love and long-suffering, did not reject the people's request and gave them their freedom of choice, but He warned them of the results of appointing a king for them and they did not listen, so He allowed the appointment of the king as a kind of discipline for them for their insistence on their wrong request. God respects the freedom of your will, but may you seek His will, and so protect yourself. They chose a king with earthly, material qualifications and he wearied them, whereas Christ, the heavenly King, who reigns over the hearts of His children, gives them endless blessings and exploits them in nothing.

My God, You were the One who went out in the wars and led Your people, and You guided them through the judges, the prophets and the priests, but they rejected all that and asked for a king created from dust... How strange!!.. But I fear, my God, for myself... I fear that I may be like Your people and replace You with a king who reigns over my heart, a king whose name may be money, or another whose name is my mind and my thoughts... Do not allow it, my God, do not allow it, for I am afraid of myself.

Samuel heard from the people and returned to his prayer with God, and of course God was knowing and hearing, but this is the way of the faithful servants of God, who lift everything to God in their prayer. The Lord's answer to Samuel came clearly because He respects the will and freedom of man even in his betrayal of Him and departure from Him, and His answer was to appoint for them the king they asked for. With words like these Samuel spoke with the men and sent them away, each to his city.
God chooses Saul as king

These two verses are an introduction and presentation of the person of Saul the son of Kish. Since Saul was to become the first king of the children of Israel, it was fitting and proper to mention his lineage. Samuel tells us that he was the son of a Benjamite man named Kish the son of Abiel, and this man was known to be a mighty man of valor, that is, a man of influence and standing, in whom all the qualities of manhood were complete. As for Saul himself, he was a handsome young man, of splendid appearance, and there was none taller than he among all the people, that is, by physical standards he was the pride of all the youth of Israel. This is what the people asked for, physical standards and not spiritual standards, for they wanted a great appearance for the king in form and strength, and not his relationship with God and his piety.
Donkeys: the plural of she-donkey, the female of the donkey.

Kish, Saul's father, lost a group of donkeys that had perhaps been left grazing in the fields, and when he did not find them it was natural for him to assign his son, with one of the servants or workers of the house, to go and look for them.
Shalisha: it means three, and it is three small peaks of a mountain west of Ephraim, lying southwest of Shechem.

Saul was a young man equal to responsibility, for he covered a great distance in searching for the lost donkeys. He went north toward Ephraim, then west to the region of Shalisha, and he did not despair but went to another district called Shaalim.

The search for the donkeys continued, so they left Shaalim and headed to the land of "Zuph," near Ramah, where Samuel lived, and yet they found nothing. So Saul suggested returning to his father's house, for fear that the father's anxiety about the donkeys would turn to his son and he would send another to look for his son. A good quality in Saul appears here, namely his bearing of responsibility and his concern not to worry his parents, and this makes him worthy of kingship, though his pride corrupted his life and made him rejected by God.

We see here how God turns small events to carry out His will, for the loss of the donkeys was the means by which Saul met Samuel and Samuel anointed him king. So be confident that everything that passes in your life God uses for your good if you love Him.

The servant spoke with his master Saul and said to him: We are now beside the city of Ramah, where Samuel the man of God lives, and he is a man known to all the people as a prophet, and everything he says is from the Lord. So why do we not go to him and ask him, and he will guide us to the way and the place where we shall find the donkeys? The prophet is called "a man of God" because he leads his people in the way of God and prays for them before God. We should not wonder that Saul did not know the name of the prophet Samuel, for he lived in one of the villages and did not concern himself with general political affairs.

Saul did not object but accepted the servant's suggestion, but he wanted to honor the man of God and to give him a gift, yet he found no bread or anything that could be offered to him. The servant answered him that he had a fourth of a shekel of silver (equal to 3 grams of silver), and suggested offering it to the man of God, who would tell them about the way.
This verse is a parenthesis that interrupts the story of Saul and the donkeys, and the prophet Samuel mentioned it in his writing of this book to make clear two things:

The first: that people were accustomed to ask God through the man of God about everything that concerned them or was lost to them. The second: that the title prophet is a newer title that came into use in the last days of Samuel, in place of the common title for the prophet, which was "seer," that is, the one who sees the visions of God.
Saul approved of the servant's words and was reassured by the presence of the fourth of a shekel that he would offer to the prophet Samuel, and they went to Ramah to meet him.

Wells and watercourses were usually outside the cities, so while Saul and the servant were making their way up to the city of Ramah, they met the young women carrying jars to fill with water as they were coming down from high Ramah to the valley where the wells were. They asked them whether the seer was in the city.

The young women answered yes and asked Saul and the servant to hurry, because he had come today to Ramah and was also about to offer a sacrifice at the high place, that is, the altar that Samuel built in Ramah, his permanent residence (ch. 7:17).

The young women added that the people were gathered at the high place to offer the sacrifice and were waiting for Samuel to bless the sacrifice and then eat of it, so they could meet him on his way from his house to the high place.

Indeed they went up to the city, and as they headed toward its middle, they met Samuel coming out of his house on his way to the place of the sacrifice at the high place. Thus the loss of the donkeys made Saul seek Samuel to meet him, and from him he learned that God had chosen him as king, as you will see (vv. 15, 16). God allows everything to lead to our salvation if we love Him and submit to Him.

Take care to hear the voice of God in all the matters of your life through prayer and the guidance of the father of confession and spiritual guides, and your heart will be at ease and you will be strong in your steps, relying on God who supports you.
Had told Samuel in his ear: had revealed to Samuel.

In God's ordering and guiding of matters, just as He moved Saul because of the donkeys to meet Samuel, He also here prepares Samuel to receive Saul. The Lord revealed to Samuel, a day before Saul came to him, that tomorrow He would send him a Benjamite man to anoint as leader and king over Israel, and that He would enable him to save His people Israel from the humiliation of the Philistines, because He had heard the cry of His people and the time for deliverance had come. This does not contradict what is stated in (ch. 7:13), that the Philistines were defeated before the children of Israel and no longer attacked them, for the enmity was still present, as shown by their rising afterward and attacking the children of Israel. The people were crying out to God to give them a king who would always protect them from any Philistine attack or any enemies.

When Samuel went out on his way to the high place and saw Saul, the Lord spoke to him again and said to him: This is the man of whom I spoke to you, who will lead and restrain the people, that is, become king over them. At that moment Saul approached Samuel, not knowing who he was, and asked him where he could find the seer's house. We understand from this that Samuel was wearing ordinary clothes and had no large retinue around him, but was humble, walking quietly like the rest of the people. The expression "in the midst of the gate" means in the middle of the city gate, since all the ancient cities had gates that were closed at night to protect them.

Samuel answered Saul that he was the man Saul was seeking and looking for, and Samuel invited Saul and the servant accompanying him to go up with him to the high place, where Samuel would offer the sacrifice and then all would eat together. He also invited him to stay overnight until the morning of the next day, and he would tell him all that was on his mind. Of course God had already revealed all this to Samuel.

Samuel surprised Saul by telling him about the lost donkeys that they had been found. No one knew the story of the donkeys except Saul and the servant, so how did the man know this? Of course Samuel intended this to confirm to Saul that he was truly a man of God and knew his affairs, and this would be a greater motive for believing him in the important words he would say to him afterward. He let Saul know that he would obtain the greatest and finest thing in Israel, because he was to be king over it.

Saul did not understand Samuel's words or his hint, but was amazed at his speech and astonished at Samuel's knowledge of the story of the donkeys. At the same time he found the second part of his words incredible: how could all the wealth of Israel be his when he was a Benjamite, that is, of the tribe smallest in number and importance of all the tribes, and he and his family and his clan were also the least of the families in the tribe itself... With this Saul answered Samuel.
The parlor: a place like a hall beside the high place, set apart for eating the sacrifice.

After offering the sacrifice, Samuel took Saul and his servant and seated them with those invited in a special place called the parlor. The number of those invited as Samuel's guests was thirty men, and as a kind of honor Samuel seated Saul and his servant in the place of precedence before everyone.

It is understood implicitly from this verse that when Samuel slaughtered the sacrifice he took a part of it and gave it to the cook and charged him not to bring it out until he asked him for it, and here Samuel asked for it, so the cook brought the front leg with what was on it of meat and set it before Saul according to Samuel's command. It is known that the front leg was the priest's portion, and this means that Samuel gave his own portion to Saul and they ate together from it, which was a great honor from Samuel to Saul ... Samuel continued his speech saying that this was what was left of the whole sacrifice and that he had kept it for him as a portion, besides what was offered to all the people.

After the sacrifice and the feast were over, Samuel came down from the high place, taking Saul and the servant with him to his house, and went up with Saul to the roof of his house to speak with him. It is expected that he was preparing the matter for him, that he was to become king of Israel.

Saul spent the night on the roof of Samuel's house, and very early in the morning Samuel woke Saul to bid him farewell and send him to his father's house. After Saul woke up and he and Samuel came down and left the house, before reaching the city gate Samuel asked Saul to tell his accompanying servant to go ahead of them. Samuel's purpose in this was to be alone with Saul in order to let him hear the rest of God's decrees about his choice, and after this to anoint him king over Israel.

It is noted in the preceding verses that Samuel was preparing Saul to receive the news of his appointment as king from the time he met him at the gate until this verse, and then he will declare to him that he is the king at the beginning of the next chapter when he anoints him with oil. God in His love prepares a person for any great news, for He is considerate of the feelings of His children. May you take care of this in conveying news to others.

God honored Saul through Samuel and then made him king, but sadly he ruined his life by pride. May you thank God for His gifts and submit to His commandments with humility, and not forget your first weakness and helplessness and attribute God's gifts to yourself, thinking that you are great in yourself, so that God leaves you and you perish like Saul.
The anointing of Saul and his choice as king by lot

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Flask: a small vessel in which oils or precious perfumes are placed.

The holy oil: it was oil that the priests used to anoint persons and holy things and consecrate them to God, and it was of pure olive oil with some perfumes added (Ex 30:22-25). Anointed you: anointing with oil was among the functions of the priest, and God appointed Samuel as priest in an exceptional manner because He refused that Eli and his offspring should be priests on account of their evils, and we find Samuel offering sacrifices in more than one place (ch. 9:12). Samuel, as prophet and priest, appointed by God in an exceptional manner, carried the flask of the anointing oil, and Saul, after Samuel's talks with him, was prepared for what was coming, so he lowered his head before Samuel, who in turn took from the oil of the flask and poured it on Saul's head as a sign of his anointing as king of Israel. Samuel added, saying that God is the One who anointed you over Israel (His inheritance) as king and leader, and then he kissed him as a sign of love from Samuel to the man chosen by God. Here appears Samuel's submission to the will of God in establishing the king, although the request from the people was wrong, for we find him welcoming the king and kissing him.

Beloved, in the grace and wealth of the New Testament, all of us were anointed with the anointing of the Holy Myron, so all of us became children of the King of heaven and earth, and we have a name in the book of life, and we have authority as kings over our senses and over all the power of the evil one; so do not forget what you received freely, and take care not to lose it, by submitting to the voice of God and keeping His commandments.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Rachel's tomb: it lies a mile north of Bethlehem and four miles from the southern border of Benjamin. Border: boundary.
Zelzah: it lies between Rachel's tomb and the southern border of Benjamin.

After Samuel anointed Saul king with the holy anointing oil, he began a prophetic discourse with him in which he told him of events that would happen, which God had revealed to Samuel. God's purpose in this was that Saul might be sure that his installation as king was from God directly, and that Samuel was truly the man of God. The first of these signs was that Saul, after Samuel left him, and before Saul left the border of the tribe of Benjamin, near Rachel's tomb at a place called Zelzah, would meet two men looking for him, who would tell him that his father had found the lost donkeys and that his father was concerned about nothing now except finding him.

By Samuel's words to Saul, Saul is assured that God, to whom he is consecrated and whose service he is to perform as king, will arrange all his affairs for him, however small they seem, like the loss of the donkeys, and that he must concentrate on the service of God.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Another prophetic sign Samuel gave Saul was that after that, at a place known to the Israelites having a large oak tree and called the "terebinth of Tabor," he would meet three men going up to "Bethel," which is a holy place to all the Israelites, since Jacob met God there and consecrated it, and this place afterward became a holy shrine for the Jews, who come and offer sacrifices in it. Of the three men, one is carrying three kids (young male goats), another three loaves of bread, and the third a skin of wine to pour out on the sacrifices that will be offered on the altar of "Bethel," and the men will give you two loaves for you and your servant to eat, so accept from them what they offered.

It is as if God also wanted to prove to Saul, the one chosen as king, that God is the One who provides for him and arranges his needs and feeds him in his hunger. This is a useful lesson he must not forget when he becomes king and receives the people's offerings in his honor, for it is God who gives to him through the people, so he will always know that God is the Giver and Provider.

The men did not give him a kid, because he is not a priest who offers sacrifices, nor to slaughter it and eat, lest he be occupied with the pleasures of food. For the same reason they did not give him wine, because it represents worldly joy, but gave him bread, which is the necessary sustenance with which he should be content, and not be occupied with the pleasures of the body but devote himself to the service of God and His people.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Gibeah: it means a high place or a hill, and there are several cities bearing the same name, and the Gibeah mentioned here is most likely Gibeah of Benjamin, lying about 6.5 km north of Jerusalem. The garrison of the Philistines: places where the camps and tents of the Philistines were pitched.
Prophesying: praising.

As for the third sign, you will continue on your way to the high place "Gibeah of God," which is so called because it is a place that some prophets chose to be in, and this place was also near the border of the Philistines, who had pitched their tents and camps there. At "Gibeah of God" you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with their instruments of praise: a psaltery (the plural of lyre), a tabret (like a flute), a pipe and a harp. You will meet them as they praise God using their instruments.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: And the Lord will give you a special gift, in that you will share with this company although you have no experience of what they do, and this will be a sign to you that God has given you a new heart and mind that were not yours, and you will become another man, different from what you knew in yourself.

Here appears the work of the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament, who would come temporarily upon the children of God to accomplish works. In the New Testament, however, He dwells permanently in the children of God after their Baptism through the sacrament of the Holy Myron.

Note: who are the prophets and the sons of the prophets: a spiritual group appeared from the days of the prophet Samuel and throughout the age of the monarchy of the people of the children of Israel. This group were disciples of a great prophet such as Samuel or Elijah or Elisha, and they had places where they gathered for the praise and glorification of the God of Israel. If their master, the great prophet, died, they followed the one after him or elected a leader for themselves from among themselves. They were not necessarily prophesying but praising, but this does not prevent some of them from being sent by God with certain prophecies to certain people, and the one of them who carried a prophecy and whose name was not declared was called "a man of God," as was said of the man who went and informed Eli the priest of his end.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Samuel continues his discourse with Saul and says: When these three signs that God gave you are fulfilled, you must be sure that God is with you and supports you in all your steps, so go and do what you see fit for the good of your people as their king.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Gilgal: a region beside Jericho, and it was a religious center in the days of Joshua.

Burnt offerings: sacrifices burned entirely to please God, and they are a symbol of the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which pleased God (Lev 1). Peace offerings: sacrifices offered to God of which the one offering eats with the priest, and they signify partaking of the Holy Mysteries (Lev 3). Before leaving him, Samuel asked Saul to go ahead of him to the region of Gilgal and wait for him there for a week, after which Samuel would come to him to offer to God burnt offerings and peace offerings in thanks to God for all that He had permitted and arranged for His people Israel and for the consecration of His servant Saul as their first king. There was another purpose in going to Gilgal, namely that Saul might spend a period of discipleship in which he would learn from Samuel. The importance of discipleship to spiritual fathers appears here.

It is noted that the Bible does not mention when Saul went to Gilgal, and most likely this took place after his victory over the Ammonites (ch. 11). Samuel's call to Saul to go to Gilgal was repeated afterward, as stated in (ch. 13:8).

Gilgal here reminds us of the monastery in which the priest spends a period of contemplation and learning before beginning service, which is a very important period in his life, and all of us are called to have periods of retreat to thank God, examine ourselves and review our goals and the way.

entries.section: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

paragraphs.text: As soon as Samuel finished speaking with Saul and Saul turned to go on his way, we find that God gave him another heart and spirit. What is meant by the other heart is the resolve, seriousness and zeal that any person needs to accomplish his purposes. As for the signs that Samuel spoke of to Saul, they were all fulfilled as he prophesied and on the same day, and of course all this was to establish God's word in Saul's heart.
Prophesied: it does not necessarily mean that he spoke of future things, but prophesying also means prayer and praising God.

Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, as Samuel had said (v. 5), and indeed he met the prophets, and as another sign by which God wanted to distinguish Saul, the Holy Spirit came upon him, so he began to praise and glorify God exactly like the prophets, so that all the people who had known him for no short time and saw him prophesying were very amazed and said: What has happened to Saul the son of Kish? Has he also become a prophet from the company of the prophets?.!

And another said: Is not his father Kish, who is known to us, and they are all ordinary people, we have not heard that any of them prophesies ...!! Because of the strangeness of the matter it became a proverb in all Israel, which they say when something strange happens, for Saul was one of the young men far from God, and it was not expected of him that he would be among the prophets, and this was the proverb that came to be: "... Is Saul also among the prophets?"

There is another opinion about the phrase "who is their father": that what is meant is God, who is able to give the spirit of prophecy to any person He chooses. The third opinion is that what is meant is Samuel, the father of the school of the prophets, and he is a great prophet able to teach many, even those far away like Saul.

After Saul finished prophesying with the prophets, he came to the high place near Gibeah and met his uncle, who was anxious about him, he and the whole family, because of his absence for all this unexpected time in searching for the donkeys. The uncle asked him where he had been all this time, and he explained to him that the reason for his delay was his visit to Samuel to ask him about the place of the donkeys.

This aroused the curiosity of Saul's uncle, so he asked him what Samuel the man of God might have said, knowing of course this man's spirituality. But Saul did not tell all that Samuel had said, and cut his words very short, and mentioned only that Samuel told him that the donkeys had been found, while the rest of the matter he kept in his heart as his own secret.
In Saul's reply to his uncle many virtues are noticed, the most important of which are:
1- His humility, for he did not show that he was the king.
2- His wisdom, for he left the announcement of the matter of the kingdom to Samuel.

If the Holy Spirit came upon Saul and changed him and made him prophesy, He is also able to work in you, whatever your sins, to bring you to repentance, and even to bring you near to God so that you worship Him faithfully and praise Him, and then afterward you become one of His servants.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Samuel called the people together: this means the males over twenty years of age and not all the people, because these men represent all the families.
Mizpah: it lies about 13 km north of Jerusalem.

Samuel anointed Saul but did not declare anything to the people, so Samuel called the people and their leaders for this purpose, which was to announce Saul, the new king, to the people. Mizpah was the suitable place, as we pointed out before, because it is in a middle place among the lands of the tribes.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Samuel began his speech to the people by making clear that what he says is the word of the Lord and not his personal words. The Lord began His message to His people by reminding them of His great work of salvation and how He rescued them from the bondage of the Egyptians and from the kingdoms that stood in their way until they possessed the land.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Samuel pointed to the strange reaction of the people toward God: they rejected Him as king over them, though He is the only Savior who turned back their oppressors from them, and now they ask in place of Him for a king over them, and God agreed to that. Samuel made them stand before him according to the order of their tribes and the heads of their thousands (each tribe had a head over the thousand and a head over every fifty to judge and settle small disputes).

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Samuel caused all the tribes to come near: this means that they all stood before God so that God might choose a tribe from them, and the most common method was casting lots with the names of all the tribes and choosing one name from them, and this is what was done, and the result of the divine lot fell to the tribe of Benjamin.
Although God had already chosen Saul and told Samuel so, Samuel did not announce this to the people for two reasons:
1- Because some might doubt Samuel's word if he did not cast the lot.
2- One of the tribes might be angry, especially those large in number or strength, if the king did not come from them.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: After the tribe of Benjamin was chosen, all its clans came near, and from among the clans of the tribe the lot fell on the clan of Matri, in which was Saul, who was also chosen by lot from it. When the lot was declared and his name called, he did not appear, for he was hiding.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Those gathered were bewildered by Saul's disappearance, so they asked God through Samuel whether they would find him or not, and God answered them that Saul was there but was hidden among the baggage of the people who had come from their cities to Mizpah. Saul's hiding in this way was perhaps because of his sense of unworthiness, or fear of responsibility, or shyness at facing the people.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: After God declared to them the place of Saul, some of the people ran to the baggage and brought him to the place of their gathering, and when he stood among them he was taller than all of them, so that the tallest man among the people did not reach above Saul's shoulder. Saul's distinction in physical terms appears here, and this is what the people asked for, but he was not distinguished spiritually, and it would have been more fitting for the people to ask for the wise, spiritual leader to lead them in the way of God.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Samuel presented Saul to the people, making clear that he was the Lord's choice for them, and that God had chosen the best of those who find approval with the people, and that it was not one in his appearance or the height of his stature. The people shouted, hailing Saul and expressing their joy that he had become king to them .. and "Long live the king" is the traditional cry among peoples for their kings, and its meaning is may God prolong the life of our king over us.

Of course God's choice of Saul was not His first divine desire, but He condescended and accepted the desire of His people, so He chose the best in the eyes of this people who rejected their heavenly King, so that the people might know the result of their choice according to material standards and not spiritual ones. The strange thing is that the people did not thank God for the new king, but were occupied with the gift rather than the Giver, that is, they were occupied with the king and forgot God.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: After this Samuel began his speech with the people, explaining to them what the new monarchical system requires of rights and duties for the king, as well as the king's rights of the people's submission to him. We do not know the details of the speech of course, but he thought it good to write all that he said and put it in a book, which is considered the first civil constitution known to the people of Israel, defining the relationship between the king and the subjects. After Samuel finished his mission he sent the people and their leaders away, each to his house.

entries.section: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

paragraphs.text: Saul also went away to his house, and many of his supporters followed him, whose hearts God had touched by His grace so that they loved Saul and followed him. But there were other people who despised Saul and belittled him and spoke against him with mocking words and did not bring him any gift, but Saul stopped his ears and did not hear their words. God and the holy inspired text described them as sons of Belial, an expression used for followers of Satan, or doers of evil, or those who worshipped idols.

Do not be disturbed if someone attacks you or directs criticism at you, but listen to him with humility, for it may be a message from God to you, and if you feel that the words are wrong and are enmity from the one speaking to you, then pray for him and do not enter into an unprofitable discussion with him.
The war against the Ammonites

Nahash the Ammonite: The Ammonites and the Moabites were descendants of Lot and lived east of the Jordan River, and their land became the portion of the tribe of Gad together with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh. They had wars with the people of Israel, such as what happened in the time of the Judges (Judg 11:5), when Jephthah the Gileadite defeated them. Their king was called Nahash, and the meaning of his name is “serpent,” that is, a snake.

Jabesh-gilead: One of the cities of the tribe of Gad, located on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan River. It seems that it had a relationship with the tribe of Benjamin, so that its people did not join the rest of the tribes in disciplining the tribe of Benjamin when it sinned. For this reason the tribes attacked the city of Jabesh, killed many of its people and destroyed the city (Judg 21:10). Jabesh-gilead: it is a city on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan River.

Shortly after Saul began to reign (and the Septuagint mentions that it was after a month), Nahash king of the Ammonites made a raid in which he prevailed over the people of the cities of Jabesh-gilead. When the people of the city feared that he would kill them, they asked him for a covenant and a promise that he would let them go their way, and they were ready to become his servants all the days of their lives.

There is another opinion, mentioned in (ch. 12:12), that the people of Jabesh asked for a king to repel Nahash from them, so God chose Saul as king for them by the hand of Samuel. This does not contradict what is said in this verse, because Nahash may have made earlier raids on Jabesh months before, on account of which they asked for a king; and after Saul was anointed, Nahash rose up to seize the city and kill those in it, so here they called for help upon Saul, who had been anointed about a month before.

In the pride and arrogance of the conqueror, Nahash king of Ammon answered that he was ready to make a covenant with them not to kill them, namely that he would put out the right eye of all the people of the city, so that this would be a disgrace and a reproach not only to the people of Jabesh-gilead but to all the people of Israel.

Putting out the eyes was a well-known humiliation among the pagans in ancient times, as the Philistines did to Samson (Judg 16:21) and as Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon later did to Zedekiah king of Judah (2 Kgs 25:7). For putting out the right eye made men unable to fight, because the warrior carried the shield in his left hand to protect his face and body with it, yet he could at least see with his right eye; but if that eye was put out, it became very difficult for him to fight, because if he protected himself with the shield he could not see his enemy, and if he did not protect himself with the shield he became exposed to the enemy’s arrows.
Putting out the eyes is a symbol of a person losing his spiritual sight, and this is what Satan tries to do to the children of God.

Faced with this ordeal and this hard demand, the inhabitants of Jabesh did not know what to do, so their elders came out with a proposal to Nahash king of the Ammonites: that he give them a respite of one week to seek help from all the tribes, and if no one responded to rescue them, they would come out to him, meaning they would surrender themselves to him to do with them what he wished. Nahash agreed, being certain that no one would dare to support them for fear of him, for his arrogance made him sure of his strength. And so, in the end, because of the threats and cruelty of Nahash, they asked for a respite in order to take refuge in God and to seek the help of Saul their king. It would have been better for them not to accept slavery to Nahash, even if he were not going to put out their eyes, but to pray to God and ask the help of their king.

Indeed, the people of the city sent their messengers to the place where Saul lived and told what had happened to them, and everyone was moved and wept for their brothers. As for Saul, who was not yet a king in the accepted sense and had no retinue or the like, he was carrying out his daily work of plowing the land to sow it or tending the cattle by feeding them the grass of the field. On his return he heard the cries and weeping of the people, and when he asked them the reason, they told him what they had heard about the story of the people of Jabesh.
We notice that Saul was still afraid of his new position as king and still carried on his ordinary work of tending the cattle.

Saul became very angry when he heard this story, and the expression “the Spirit of God came upon him” is so that we may know that it was a holy anger, according to God’s purpose, and not merely a human emotion.
A yoke of oxen: a pair of oxen.

Saul took a pair of oxen, slaughtered them and cut them into pieces, and sent the messengers to all the tribes carrying these cut-up oxen. There was a clear and decisive message directed to all, which was that whoever held back from answering the call and going out to war behind Saul and Samuel would have as his punishment that Saul would tear his oxen apart as he had slaughtered and torn apart these oxen. This message, together with the sight of the torn oxen, had a fearful effect on the people in every direction, so all the Jews went out behind Saul as one man.
His mention of “after Saul and after Samuel” shows his faith that the war belonged to God, whom His prophet Samuel represented. It shows his submission to God and to Samuel.

Perhaps Saul cut up the oxen in this way in imitation of what the Levite did with his concubine (Judg 20:6). Saul was gentle at the beginning of his reign, for he did not declare that he would kill every person who did not go out with him to war, but only that he would slaughter his oxen.
Bezek: a city located in the portion of the tribe of Judah.

The men of the children of Israel gathered for war, from twenty years old and upward, in the town of “Bezek,” and Saul numbered them as the commander of the war; and three hundred thousand men came out from the eleven tribes. The number of the tribe of Judah is given as thirty thousand because it is smaller than would be expected of the tribe of Judah, which was one of the largest tribes in number at that time. Perhaps this was because of the pride of the tribe of Judah and their distress that the king was not taken from their tribe but from the tribe of Benjamin.

We understand from this verse that the messengers whom the people of “Jabesh-gilead” had sent did not leave Gibeah of Saul, awaiting his reply. When this vast number of Israel had gathered, Saul gave a reassuring reply to the people of “Jabesh,” saying to them that by the time the day grew hot they would have deliverance and victory over the Ammonites and over their king. When this good news reached the people of Jabesh, they rejoiced greatly that Israel had responded to their cry for help. After this they sent messengers to Nahash king of the Ammonites, who had given them a respite of a week, and said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us all that seems good to you.” This was a kind of camouflage and deception in war, for the children of Israel attacked him before that time while he was not prepared for battle.

God gave Saul the opportunity to establish his kingdom and lead the people in war. So do not be careless when God gives you an opportunity to prove your love for Him; that is, seize every spiritual opportunity to draw near to Him, and when distress meets you, hasten to Him to declare your repentance to Him and receive His strength and His blessings.

entries.section: (2) Saul’s victory and the establishment of his kingdom

paragraphs.text: The morning watch: very early morning.
The heat of the day: the intensifying of the sun, which is the time from noon until three in the afternoon.

Although Saul was a farmer who knew nothing of the affairs of war, yet because God was with him we find him thinking like a seasoned commander and dividing the number of men into three companies. He surprised the camp of the Ammonites before dawn, and they kept striking and fighting the Ammonites with strength until the sun grew hot. The victory of Israel was great, for the Ammonites fled and were scattered, each in a different direction to save himself. The people of Jabesh-gilead rejoiced more than all the children of Israel because God delivered them by the hand of Saul, and they kept this kindness for Saul even after his death: they took down his body and the bodies of his sons when the Philistines hung them up to put them to shame, and they buried them, and David praised their deed (ch. 31:11-13, 2 Sam 2:4-7). Thus this ordeal showed the strength and wisdom of Saul which God had given him, and he became king officially and won the confidence of the people after his victory over the Ammonites. So do not fear temptation, for it may be your road to glory by the ordering of God.

entries.section: (2) Saul’s victory and the establishment of his kingdom

paragraphs.text: The victorious people gathered, greatly rejoicing in their king Saul, the leader of the war. In the exhilaration of this victory, and either to flatter Saul or out of sincere feelings of love for him, they asked Samuel, who was still regarded as the spiritual leader of the people, to bring the men who had rejected Saul as king over the people, and who had earlier been described as “sons of Belial” (ch. 10:27), in order to put them to death, since they regarded them as traitors to the new king who had disobeyed God’s command in appointing Saul king.

entries.section: (2) Saul’s victory and the establishment of his kingdom

paragraphs.text: But Saul showed wisdom, love and forbearance when he did not listen to them, and his answer was sober. He directed the people’s attention to the fact that this day was a day of rejoicing in God’s victory for them over the enemies, so it was more fitting that they offer in it thanksgiving, praise and glorification to the name of God rather than that blood be shed in it and it become a sorrow in Israel, at least to the families of those men.

It is good for a leader, a priest or a servant to be merciful to those who oppose him or are hostile to him, however wrong they may be, and to be long-suffering toward them, so that perhaps he may bring them back to God by love and persuasion instead of taking vengeance for himself by exploiting his authority.

entries.section: (2) Saul’s victory and the establishment of his kingdom

paragraphs.text: Gilgal: a city near Jericho which Joshua took as his center for leading the people.

We have said before that Gilgal was a spiritual and political center for the people. When Samuel saw that the people were gathered around Saul and rejoiced in him, he too rejoiced and took advantage of this opportunity and called the people to go to Gilgal to renew the kingdom. The meaning is that he used this victory to establish Saul in the kingdom, or, as we say in political language these days, “we pledge allegiance to so-and-so” ... that is, the pledging of allegiance to Saul as king over all the tribes.

entries.section: (2) Saul’s victory and the establishment of his kingdom

paragraphs.text: Peace offerings: sacrifices of thanksgiving to God in which those who offer them share in eating of them.

The people’s celebration of Saul at Gilgal is considered his real coronation and the beginning of the establishment of his kingdom after his victory and the rallying of the men around him. Among the features of that celebration were the offering of sacrifices to thank the Lord for His deed and His deliverance, and other festivities that were a cause of gladness to the heart of Saul and all the people of Israel. A long address by Samuel to the people

Samuel begins his address to the people by explaining to them that he had responded to what they asked, setting a king over them, even though this involved a rejection of God and of Samuel’s leadership.

“And now you have this king who goes before you and leads you; as for me, my task as the last judge of Israel comes to an end. I was a spiritual leader and a judge to you from the years of my early youth until now, and I have grown old and my hair is gray, and my sons will be with you.” His words “behold, my sons are with you” have two interpretations:
1- Either Samuel had removed them because of their bad conduct, so “with you” means that they had become like the rest of the people, and the king alone has the authority of ruling and judging.

2- Samuel did not remove them but rebuked them and left them with the people under the rule of the new king, who has the right to supervise them and confirm them if they judge rightly or remove them if they err, for the king has authority over them like his authority over the rest of the people.
Bribe: given to pervert justice.
Hide my eyes: not look; the meaning is being lenient with the wicked and leaving them to do evil in return for a material reward.

Samuel declared his innocence of seizing the livestock or possessions of anyone among the people, or of taking a bribe to be lenient with the wicked, or of wronging anyone. He said this before the people and in the presence of the anointed king Saul.

The answer of the people came as Samuel expected, for they testified to his justice and integrity, and that he had not wronged anyone in anything, had not oppressed anyone in anything, and had taken nothing from anyone’s hand.

Despite the people’s acknowledgment of his integrity, Samuel was not content with this but wanted God also to enter as a witness, and Saul as well. So he repeated to them that God is witness to what they had said, and Saul is also witness to what he had heard from them, and they answered, confirming: “Yes, God is witness to what we have said.”

By this Samuel declared his innocence in his shepherding of the people, as Christ did when He said to the people, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Jn 8:46). By this he is an example to the king, the leaders and all the people in their conduct with others. And as the Apostle Paul said, “Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor 11:1). By this Samuel declares three things:
1- The end of his political work and his work as a judge, so as to devote himself to spiritual guidance and leave the ruling to the king.
2- The declaration of his integrity, to be an example to the new king.
3- The declaration of his integrity helps him in warning the people as a spiritual guide who is responsible for them before God, and a warning is accepted only from an upright person.
He will declare this warning in the following verses.

Be pure in carrying out your responsibilities for the sake of God, who sees everything and will reward you and bless you. Do not cause anyone to stumble for the sake of passing things, and do not flatter anyone at the expense of the truth, or out of fear of him or out of shyness.

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: One of the beautiful and recurring pictures is that when a man of God wants to speak to the people, he begins first by reviewing God’s work with the people before addressing his personal words to them. So did Moses and Joshua, and also Peter and Stephen (the Book of Acts). Here we see Samuel reviewing with the people God’s power and His care for them: when the humiliation increased in the land of Egypt, He raised up for them Moses and Aaron, who led the people and brought them out of the land of Egypt.

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: The righteous acts of the Lord: His care and His works with His people.

“Now therefore, O people, come forward and stand before God, that you may be reckoned with before Him and before all His mighty works with you and with your fathers of old. When Jacob and his sons went down to the land of Egypt and stayed there many years, they multiplied in it, and Pharaoh made them slaves to him and humiliated them. Did not God bring out for you Moses and Aaron, who led the people in the wilderness for forty years, and afterward God settled you in this land which you have possessed?”

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: Hazor: the name of a Canaanite city.

“But your fathers disobeyed God and did not keep His covenant and served other gods, so the Lord left them to the hand of Sisera the Canaanite to humble them, and likewise He left them to the hand of the Philistines to weary and oppress them in the land, and likewise He let the Moabites loose on them, and they fought them, and there were no days of rest for our people!”

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: Jerubbaal: Gideon (Judg 7:1). Bedan: he is Barak, or Samson, or another judge who is not mentioned in the Book of Judges.

Whenever they were defeated before the enemies of the land, they cried out to God, asking forgiveness for having forsaken Him and worshiped Baal and his wife Ashtoreth (from the gods of the pagan nations). Each time God had compassion on His people and sent them judges such as Gideon and Bedan, and likewise He sent them Jephthah and Samuel, who delivered them from their enemies who had oppressed them.

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: And after all of God’s previous work with them, when Nahash king of the children of Ammon came upon them and besieged them and prevailed over them, instead of crying out to God to deliver them, they asked for a king from among men, like the rest of the peoples, to deliver them, and they replaced God with him.

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: “And here now God has responded to you and given you a king according to your choice. If you walk in the fear of God and serve Him, and do not take gods from the nations to worship them, and listen to His voice and His commandments and do not disobey any command of His, but you and the chosen king follow Him with all your hearts, then of course God will be with you and will bless the people and their king.

entries.section: (2) God’s care and warning them against opposing Him

paragraphs.text: But if you do not listen to the voice of the Lord, and go after what angers Him and disobey His command, the hand of the Lord will be against you, and He will avenge Himself for your evil and allow your enemies to rule over you and humble you, exactly as it was with your fathers when they turned aside from God.”

God stretches out His hand to you in love and is ready to keep you and care for you, on condition that you hold fast to your sonship to Him and keep His commandments. But if you become preoccupied with the world and attached to its material things, God will forsake you, and the evils and troubles of the world will crush you.

After Samuel finished part of his address, he asked all the people to stand attentively before God, because he was about to ask the Lord for a sign before the eyes of the people, to confirm to them their error when they chose for themselves an earthly king instead of God, their true King.

Samuel asked God to show His glory by working a miracle, which was the coming forth of thunder and the falling of rain at the time of the wheat harvest, which is the month of May, when the hot weather begins and the rains end in this region. This was so that the people would know their evil in asking for an earthly king instead of God their true King, and so that they would fear God, their true King, who is able to do all things, before they feared the earthly king Saul, who is an instrument in God’s hand. Thus they would realize their evil in replacing God, who is almighty, with a man limited in his abilities, and would understand that if they and the king submit to God, He will not forsake them but will bless them.

When Samuel asked God to show His glory, the people heard mighty thunder and the rain fell at once, so the people feared God and felt the greatness of their sin. They also feared Samuel, for they felt that he was the mighty man of God whose word the heavens carry out at once, so the thunder comes forth and the rains fall. On the other hand, they became aware that God is their true King and not this anointed king.

Beloved brother, this lesson is for all of us, for we often replace God and rely on people and acquaintances to help us in managing our affairs ... Turn to God first, and He will guide you to whom you should go and how the matter will be settled for you, and do not forget that God cursed the one who trusts in the arm of man.

In front of this miracle and this wonderful event, the people stood before Samuel the prophet, asking him for intercession and prayer for their sin which they had committed, so that God would not destroy them from before Him, and they confessed their pride when they asked a king for themselves.

Samuel reassured his frightened people that God would not destroy them, since He is long-suffering, but on condition that they hold fast to His commandments and not imitate the nations by worshiping idols, which profit nothing, for they had asked for a king to be like the pagan nations around them.

Samuel explained the reason God does not destroy them, which is that He wants them to be His people, and for the sake of His holy name He will keep them, not because of their goodness, giving them an opportunity to repent. For He wants to make His name known among the nations through His people, therefore He is long-suffering toward them despite their sins.

“As for me, Samuel, far be it from me that I should neglect to pray for you.” The meaning of this is that he will not cease praying for his people, and he considered not praying for them a sin before God, and for this reason he used the expression “far be it.” “And I will not stop at praying for you only, but I will also not cease teaching and directing you to everything that is good and right before God.”

“And you must set God before your eyes, and serve Him with all faithfulness and care and with pure hearts, and not with the worship of the tongue, and meditate on all His works, past and present, by which He has repeatedly raised you from your humiliation before your enemies.”
Samuel warned them not to return to their evils, lest God destroy them and their king.

Take care to pray for those around you, especially when you see some committing obvious sins. Do not condemn them, but know that God has allowed you to see these sins so that you may pray much for them, and God will rejoice in your love for them and lift their sins from them, and you will grow in the love of God and receive His blessings.

Preparation for fighting the Philistines (1) Saul prepares an army and offers a burnt offering to the Lord (vv. 1-9): 1 Saul was one year old in his kingdom, and he reigned two years over Israel. 2 And Saul chose for himself three thousand men of Israel, of which two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and in mount Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin: and the rest of the people he sent every man to his tent. 3 And Jonathan smote the garrison of the Philistines that was in Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, Let the Hebrews hear. 4 And all Israel heard say that Saul had smitten a garrison of the Philistines, and that Israel also was had in abomination with the Philistines. And the people were called together after Saul to Gilgal. 5 And the Philistines gathered themselves together to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots, and six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the sea shore in multitude: and they came up, and pitched in Michmash, eastward from Beth-aven. 6 When the men of Israel saw that they were in a strait, the people hid themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits. 7 And some of the Hebrews went over Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. As for Saul, he was yet in Gilgal, and all the people trembled after him. 8 And he tarried seven days, according to the set time that Samuel had appointed: but Samuel came not to Gilgal; and the people were scattered from him. 9 And Saul said, Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and peace offerings. And he offered the burnt offering.

Samuel wrote this verse three years after the anointing of Saul as king, and he makes clear to us in this verse that Saul was anointed king and remained for a year until he was crowned and declared king to the people at Mizpah (ch. 10:24). During the two years after the first year his kingdom was established, especially after his victory over the Ammonites and his being declared king at Gilgal (ch. 11:14). There is another opinion that during the first year he was crowned and was victorious over the Ammonites and all the people submitted to him, and then in the following two years he organized the kingdom and began to prepare the army.
Michmash: located about 8 km north of Jerusalem, and it has the same name today.
Mount Bethel: the hill country at Bethel, which lies east of Jerusalem, midway between it and Nablus.
Gibeah of Benjamin: north of Jerusalem and about 1.5 km south of Michmash; the meaning of Gibeah is “hill.”

About twenty years passed between this verse and the previous verse, in which Saul, who was a young man when he was anointed (1 Sam 9:2), grew older and had a young son, Jonathan. It seems that he organized the kingdom during the twenty years, and perhaps a weakness occurred in the army, so he organized his army anew, placing two thousand soldiers with him at Michmash and the other company, numbering a thousand, with his son Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin.
The garrison of the Philistines: the camp of the Philistines.
Geba: located about 9.5 km east of Jerusalem. The meaning of Geba is “hill.”

The Philistines often occupied some Israelite villages or hillsides and would set up a camp in the middle of the land to establish their presence. Their camping at Geba, which is in the tribe of Benjamin, and Saul’s slackness in driving them out from there, was due to his preoccupation with kingship, his personal glories and his comfort, so he neglected their presence inside his own tribe. This is a symbol of a person’s neglecting the presence of sin within him and being occupied with his many interests, so that it can corrupt him and destroy him.

Jonathan, who had become a young man, took notice, and he rose with the thousand men and made a raid on one of the camps of the Philistines and prevailed over them. The matter naturally reached the rest of the Philistines and also Saul, and for this reason Saul expected a retaliatory attack from the Philistines, so he blew the trumpet, proclaiming in all the tribes the necessity of the people gathering around him.
Israel had become a stench: Israel had become hated by the Philistines.

The news reached all the people that Saul had smitten the camp of the Philistines (the one meant here, of course, is his son Jonathan), and it also became known to all that the Philistines were enraged because of what had befallen them and were preparing for war. So the men of the people gathered with King Saul at Gilgal for war, to support Jonathan in the face of the many armies of the Philistines.
Beth-aven: located between Bethel to the west and Michmash to the east, and it means “house of idols.”

In a way not seen before, the Philistines gathered with a great army from all their cities. The army consisted of thirty thousand chariots, some of them war chariots used in fighting, some carrying supplies, and others used for the lodging and sleeping of the commanders, as well as six thousand horsemen skilled in fighting and a countless number of men. They drew near and encamped before Michmash, which was the town Saul had taken as a base for his men (v. 2), and by this the Philistines separated the army that was with Saul from the army that was with Jonathan, so that Jonathan could not come to his father’s aid.
A strait: severe distress.
Caves: plural of cave, a hollow like a cavern in the belly of a mountain, suitable for hiding.
Thickets: a place like a marsh, with water that is not deep, containing some trees and tall grasses.
High places: plural of a high place, a large, strong building suitable for taking shelter in.

Before these huge numbers of the Philistines, the people gathered around Saul were terrified, so they fled and hid in the caves and among the trees growing in the thickets, and others in the high places, and some went down into deep, dry pits, because of the weakness of their faith. It would have been better for them to pray to God to rescue them.

Many of the men of Israel also slipped away to the eastern side of the Jordan River, where the lands of the tribe of Gad and some of the Gileadites are. As for Saul, he felt all this and saw that the frightened people were dispersing and going away from around him.

We understand from this verse that when Samuel learned of the people’s gathering behind Saul at Gilgal, he had given him an appointment to come after seven days to offer his sacrifices and bless the people before the battle, but it seems that he was late for his appointment, and the people had begun to slip away from behind Saul.

With Samuel’s delay and Saul’s fear that the rest of the men would leave him, his soul was distressed and he lost his wisdom, and he decided to do a work that was not his to do, which was to offer by himself the sacrifices and the burnt offering to God ... the work that God assigned only to the priests.

There are two important lessons, beloved. The first lesson we learn from the frightened people who slipped away in flight, for they looked at the strength of the enemy (Satan) and forgot God’s former works with them, which never depended on number or equipment ... This is what happens to us often, and it makes us look for human methods in facing evil and forget our God who is able to do all things.

The second lesson is Saul’s mistake: however great the distress or anxiety, you must not, in your tension, transgress against God in one of His important commands, as Saul did by offering the sacrifice.

(2) Samuel rebukes Saul (vv. 10-15): 10 And it came to pass, that as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came; and Saul went out to meet him, that he might bless him. 11 And Samuel said, What hast thou done? And Saul said, Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash; 12 Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the LORD: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering. 13 And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the LORD have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever. 14 But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the LORD hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the LORD hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee. 15 And Samuel arose, and gat him up from Gilgal unto Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people that were present with him, about six hundred men.
Samuel came to Gilgal, but Saul had finished slaughtering and offering the burnt offering, and when Saul saw him he went out to meet him and welcome him and to receive the blessing from him.
