Samuel knew that Saul had offered a burnt offering, whether from its traces, or because the people told him, or because he knew it by the Spirit of God who was in him, so he took the initiative with a direct question to Saul about what he had done. Because the question was stern, Saul began to justify his act, offering excuses first before answering Samuel about what he had done. His arguments were that Samuel was late for his appointment, that the people had slipped away and dispersed from around him, and that the Philistines were encamped at Michmash, and he feared that the Philistines would attack him at Gilgal before he prayed to God and offered the sacrifices, and for this reason he took courage and offered the burnt offering. This shows Saul’s pride, which made him presume and do the works of the priesthood; and when Samuel confronted him with what he had done, he did not repent and grieve but justified his error. We notice here a group of mistakes that Saul committed, which are:
1- His neglect to receive Samuel’s blessing, contrary to what he did at the beginning of his wars when he was victorious over the Ammonites (ch. 11:7).

2- In pride and slackness he usurped the right of the priesthood and offered the sacrifice, although he was not a priest, since he considered the offering of the sacrifice a formality, and, being king, why should he not do it, for the position of king is very great.

3- His neglect of the continual preparation of the army in the previous years, so that the Philistines moved and seized some of the lands and set up camps for themselves while he was heedless, preoccupied with himself as king.
4- In pride he rebuked Samuel for his delay, in order to cover his error and justify himself.
5- When Samuel rebuked him, he did not repent from his heart because he did not feel all his former errors.

All these excuses were not sufficient or a justification for the great error Saul committed by offering the burnt offering when he was not a priest, and for this reason the words of Samuel (which were from God) to Saul were stern and harsh. He first described him as foolish and rash, and said that he had broken the commandments and laws of the Lord concerning the person who offers the sacrifice, for he must be a priest, and that by this he had exposed himself to God’s rejection of him. God had promised to establish Saul’s kingdom, and that the kingdom and its kings from his seed would endure for ever, but because of this grave error, God would take the kingdom and the rule away from his seed. Moreover, God would raise up another man from the people, according to His own choice, whose deeds would be pleasing before God, and he would reign over the people in place of Saul, who did not keep God’s commandments. The reference here was of course to David the prophet, the coming king of Israel, and Samuel knew this by the spirit of prophecy and spoke of the events in the past tense because what God has decided must come to pass.

Samuel’s words are the carrying out of the prophecy of Jacob, who declared in his prophecy to his sons that the kingship would belong to the tribe of Judah, from which David came (Gen 49). Therefore Saul’s kingship was temporary and a preparation for the true king, who is David, and from whose seed Christ would come. Saul is considered a king in form, but a preparation for the true king. The same meaning was repeated at the birth of Christ among the Jews: His descent from them according to the flesh is the beginning, but the truth is that those who believed in Him most were the Gentiles. He is King over the children of Israel according to the flesh, but He reigns spiritually over the Gentiles more than over the Jews, because few of the Jews believed and the rest persecuted Christianity.

After this severe rebuking speech from Samuel to King Saul, Samuel left Gilgal for Gibeah of Benjamin, angry and sorrowful at and for Saul, who by his foolishness lost everything. As for Saul, he numbered the people who remained with him and found them very few, six hundred men, who were of course unable to face the Philistines.
Do not rush in speech or action without asking God and thinking calmly, lest you break His commandments, wrong others and lose many blessings.

(3) The movement of the Philistine army (vv. 16-23): 16 And Saul, and Jonathan his son, and the people that were present with them, abode in Gibeah of Benjamin: but the Philistines encamped in Michmash. 17 And the spoilers came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies: one company turned unto the way that leadeth to Ophrah, unto the land of Shual: 18 And another company turned the way to Beth-horon: and another company turned to the way of the border that looketh to the valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness. 19 Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears: 20 But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his plowshare, and his sickle, and his axe, and his mattock, 21 when the edges of the plowshares and the sickles and the three-toothed forks and the axes had become dull, and to set the goads. 22 So it came to pass in the day of battle, that there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people that were with Saul and Jonathan: but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found. 23 And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the passage of Michmash.

After the new circumstances, Saul was compelled to join his son Jonathan in an attempt to unite efforts. We understand from this that he left “Michmash,” which had been his base before (v. 2) and was now a high base for the Philistines, and Gibeah of Benjamin was also a high base for Saul, his son and their men, and between the two places was a low, deep valley.
The spoilers: the plunderers.
Shual: about 6 km east of Bethel.
Beth-horon: about 19 km north of Jerusalem.

There were three roads going out from Michmash: the first to the north, heading toward the land of Shual, which was in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin; the second road to the west, heading to the town of Beth-horon, which was in the portion of Benjamin and Ephraim; and the last road to the east, heading toward the wilderness of the Jordan. So the Philistines divided themselves into three groups like highwaymen, ruling and plundering all the Israelite villages along the three roads going out from Michmash. They would seize the crops and impose tolls for passing along these roads, so the children of Israel were in great distress. Also, the Philistines’ movement and their control of the northern and central region isolated Saul in the southern region, and a narrow, deep valley separated him from them. Despite this devastation and the severe distress that befell the children of Israel, God’s mercy appears in that He allowed the Philistines to carry out this devastation so that the people would repent and return to God, because if the Philistines had fought Saul and those with him and prevailed over them at Gilgal, they would have occupied the lands of all the tribes of the children of Israel. This shows that God let the Philistines stray from destroying His people and be occupied with the idea of blocking the road to Saul and not strike him directly, although this would have been easy for them. For God leads your enemies astray until you repent and return to Him, and then you prevail over them, as happened with Jonathan and Saul (ch. 14).

The Philistines were able to close all the blacksmith workshops and forbade every craftsman in Israel from practicing his trade, so that the Israelites would not be able to make the weapons their army needed, swords or spears.
To sharpen: to whet the iron.
His plowshare: the iron of the plow that cuts the earth.
The mattock: like the axe but with a larger head, and used with rocks.

The misery and humiliation of the people reached their height, for they resorted to the Philistines’ blacksmith workshops in order to be able to sharpen the farming tools, the sickle, the plow, the axe and the mattock, after the Philistines had closed all the workshops of the children of Israel.
Dull: wearied, and it comes here in the sense of having lost its sharpness.
Plowshares: plural of plowshare, the iron of the plow.

Three-toothed forks: three metal teeth with a long handle, like a fork (the pitchfork). To set the goads: that is, fixing the metal pieces onto the wooden handles in all the farming tools mentioned above.

This verse is entirely connected with the preceding one, for it completes the meaning that the Israelites were not permitted to sharpen their farming tools when they became worn with age and needed sharpening.

To show the bad condition of the men gathered with Saul and his son Jonathan, it explains that none of them carried a weapon except Saul and his son, because of the people’s distance from God and Saul’s pride. This is a symbol that when a person moves away from God he loses the spiritual weapons with which he overcomes Satan.
The garrison: they are the vanguard of the army, or what are called reconnaissance units.

The Philistines became still bolder and sent men from among them to the passage of Michmash, which is a narrow pass governed and bounded by two great rocks, and whoever controls this pass tightens his grip on Michmash and is able to set out from it to other places. That is, the Philistines took control of the road to the city of Michmash and beyond it.

Satan tries to strip you of your spiritual weapons and make you depend on the desires of the world, just as the Philistines made the children of Israel depend on them for sharpening their weapons and farming tools. But you, as a spiritual person, rely on God and do not indulge in material desires; rather, use everything in measure, and depend for your strength on God and not on passing material things, and the devil will not be able to humble you. The victory over the Philistines

Despair surrounded the Israelite people because of the strength of the Philistines and the small number of the army with Saul, but Jonathan was filled with hope and thought courageously of crossing the valley separating Michmash, where the Philistines were, from Gibeah of Benjamin. He asked the man who carried his weapons and accompanied him to go with him, and he deliberately did not tell his father, because he knew that he would prevent him from doing so.

As for Saul and the six hundred men with him, they hid and took shelter under the shade of a pomegranate tree to watch the Philistines from one edge of Gibeah. This pomegranate orchard was located in a region called Migron, which means “the slope.”

This verse is a parenthesis and has no bearing on the events, for it takes us to “Shiloh,” where the Tabernacle of Meeting is, and teaches us that the present priest, or the present high priest, who wears the ephod (one of the priestly garments), is “Ahiah,” whose uncle was “Ichabod” the son of Phinehas the son of Eli; and this Ichabod is the one whose mother died after bearing him (ch. 4:21). Perhaps Ahiah is Ahimelech, to whom David went in the city of Nob (ch. 22:9). Ahiah is mentioned here because King Saul will consult him in matters of war, as will come later (vv. 18, 19). After this we return to follow the events, and we learn that Jonathan went to the place of the Philistines without the knowledge of anyone of the people.
Bozez: shining.
Seneh: a name given to the acacia tree.

To reach the Philistines, Jonathan had to cross a narrow pass in the valley, and on either side of this pass were two rocks facing each other, both sharp-pointed. The name of the first was Bozez and of the second Seneh; the top of the first rock was pointed toward the north in the direction of Michmash, and the other toward the south in the direction of Gibeah of Benjamin.
The uncircumcised: they are those who are not circumcised, and the Philistines are meant.

After the idea had matured in Jonathan’s mind, he opened to his armor-bearer what was in his heart to encourage him to go on with him, and he invited him to cross over to the camp of the Philistines, explaining the power of God, who is able to save at all times regardless of the number of the enemies.

The man’s answer was strong and spontaneous, and he said to Jonathan, do all that pleases you and that you see to be right, for I am with you and follow you in all that you do and in all that your heart and mind urge you to do.

The man’s answer to Jonathan carried more than one beautiful meaning; for despite the great danger, we find ourselves before a following, obedience, loyalty and manliness without equal. Would that we learn to obey the Church and our spiritual fathers, who will not expose us to dangers but protect us from them.

After Jonathan prayed, he spoke with his armor-bearer, saying, we will ask God to give us a sign, which is that we first show ourselves to the Philistines in a place midway between Gibeah and Michmash. If they say to us, “Stand still until we come to you,” we will know that God does not want us to go up to them, and we will return to Gibeah; but if the Philistines ask us to come up to them, we will know that God will give us strength and victory so that we go up and prevail over them.

Indeed the two crossed the narrow pass and showed themselves to the Philistines. The Philistines, with the utmost mockery and sarcasm, and in a figurative expression, described the two men as being like mice that come out of holes dug in the mountains; and of course what is meant is not Jonathan and his companion but all the Hebrews.

The men of the Philistines asked Jonathan and his servant to come up, and said to them, “Come up to us, and we will show you a thing,” the meaning being that they would defeat them so that they would know their weakness before the strength of the Philistines.

But Jonathan considered what the Philistines said to them about coming up to be the very sign awaited from God, and for this reason he encouraged his armor-bearer, saying that the Lord had delivered the Philistines into the hand of Israel, that is, that God would give us victory over them.

The hill on which the camp of the Philistines stood was steeply sloped, so Jonathan and his armor-bearer were compelled to go up on their hands and feet, climbing, and the Philistines were looking at them with scorn, since they were merely two going up to fight a great host of Philistines. This was an arrogance on the part of the Philistines which God allowed in order to make His power known to them with the humble, even if they were very few, that is, only two soldiers. So the Lord gave victory to Jonathan and his armor-bearer: Jonathan would kill those in front, and his armor-bearer would kill everyone who came from behind. To picture the situation, Jonathan and his armor-bearer placed their backs against each other so that each protected the other’s back.
Half a furrow of an acre: an expression and idiom meaning half the area that a plow plows in one day, which is a small area.

Jonathan and the man with him were able to kill twenty men of the Philistines in a very narrow area, in which the scouts of the Philistine camp were waiting; that is, they did not penetrate inward into Michmash, where the rest of the Philistine army was.
The host: the men drawn up in ranks and ready for war.

Fear and trembling fell on the hearts of the Philistines of every class, the scouts and those prepared in the camp, those in the fields, and the spoilers (highwaymen) among them. Perhaps they felt that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were the advance of large numbers of the children of Israel who had begun to attack them, in addition to the work of God, who cast fear into their hearts, so they fled in confusion and great fear.

As for the watchmen whom Saul had placed to watch the armies of the Philistines from the hill of Gibeah of Benjamin, they came down and told Saul all that they had seen, and how the Philistines were afraid and terrified with a great terror and fled and were scattered.

Saul naturally understood that someone had gone and done something that terrified the Philistines, so he ordered a counting and numbering of his men. Indeed the numbering was done, and it resulted in the discovery of the absence of Jonathan and the man who was his armor-bearer.

Ahiah was the high priest at that time, and the Ark had been moved from “Kirjath-jearim” to Gibeah of Benjamin, where the camp of Saul and his men was. So Saul asked the priest Ahiah to stand before the Ark to ask the Lord what Israel should do.

Ahiah indeed began to pray and sought God’s counsel, but with the confusion of the Philistines and the increase of their shouting as they withdrew, Saul was relatively reassured. And, again in an unjustified haste, he ordered the priest to stop praying and lifting his hands to God. This shows his pride and his lack of concern to submit to the voice of God.

Saul raised the battle cry, thereby driving all the people with him to war and to set out toward the place of the Philistines, who in their fear hurried to come out of the pass of Michmash; and in their crowding, each of them began to kill the one near him so that safety would be written for him alone ... so they were killing one another.

As for the Hebrews who had been occupied by the Philistines at Michmash or around it, they joined Saul, who with his son Jonathan drew near to them, and they fought with them the rest of the Philistines. So did all the Israelites hiding from the Philistines in the caves of Mount Ephraim when they heard of the defeat of the Philistines; all were strengthened and pursued the fleeing Philistines.
Beth-aven: the house of idols, located between Bethel and Michmash.

The Lord gave deliverance to His people by means of a small number of men, and after the battle had been at Michmash in the lands of the Israelites, it moved to a place called Beth-aven west of Michmash.

God is the maker of victory, and it is for you to follow through and complete your victory over Satan. When God lifts some sin from you, your holding fast to His commandments must increase and you must complete your spiritual striving, so that Satan fears and flees from you.
Distressed: distress and bitterness of soul.

Before this victory, Saul did not want to give the Philistines any opportunity to reorganize their ranks, and for this reason he swore before God and his men that none of them should taste food or drink until the end of the day, so that they might complete their victory in their pursuit. Before this oath none of the men could break it, but distress, exhaustion and hidden murmuring came upon them. Of course this was not a wise action on the part of Saul, who did not take into account his men’s need for rest and food to sustain them.
Several mistakes into which Saul fell by this decision appear from this:
1- He did not care to hear the voice of God from the mouth of Ahiah (v. 19).
2- He neglected his men’s need for food and burdened them with fasting, so that they almost collapsed from hunger during the battle.
3- The men’s severe hunger led them to fall into an error, for they slaughtered on the blood and ate, although God forbade the eating of blood, as will appear in the following verses.
4- He regarded the Philistines as his enemies, when he should have said the enemies of God, for it is by the power of God that he prevails over them and not by his own power (v. 24).
The forest: an area of trees in the midst of a valley, and it also comes in the sense of a difficult road.

Saul and his men advanced into an area where trees were abundant, and bees had made hives for themselves in these trees and filled them with honey until it overflowed and fell from the trees and covered the whole ground of the area in its abundance. Yet the people, despite their weariness and exhaustion, did not dare to put forth their hand and eat of this honey, for fear of their oath before God and before Saul.
The end of the rod: a staff.
His eyes were enlightened: his strength returned to him.

Jonathan was not present when his father Saul bound the people with the previous oath, and for this reason, when he and his armor-bearer caught up with the people at the forest, he stretched out his staff to the fallen honey of the bees and ate of it and regained his strength and vigor. One of the people saw him eating of the honey and told him that his father had bound the people with an oath and with the falling of a curse on the man who eats before the end of the battle, which had exhausted the people, distressed them and wearied them greatly.

Jonathan did not flatter his father but said sincerely, “My father has erred by this oath and caused distress to everyone.” He gave himself as an example, that when he ate of the honey he regained his health, so how had his father made this error, for if the men of the children of Israel had eaten of this honey they would have regained their strength and been able to finish off the rest of the Philistines.
Aijalon: the last city in the tribe of Dan, located on the border of the Philistines.

Saul’s men followed the Philistines and pursued them a long distance from Michmash to “Beth-aven,” and from “Beth-aven” to “the forest,” and from the forest to “Aijalon,” which is the last city on the border between the lands of the Hebrews in the tribe of Gad and the lands of the Philistines; but the people had reached the utmost degree of weariness and exhaustion.

Saul rushed in and swore and made a covenant that no one should taste food until the battle was finished, and by this he wearied his soldiers. So be wise and seek God’s counsel before you rush into any commitment or vow, and if time permits you, seek the counsel of your spiritual father.

entries.section: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

paragraphs.text: No sooner had the battle ended than the hungry people turned to the spoil of the Philistines, the animals, and took some for themselves and slaughtered and ate on the very ground on which the animals’ blood was shed, which is contrary to the Law (Lev 17:10-16). In their haste and hurry they did not wait until the animals had drained all their blood, and they did not slaughter them on a high place that would allow the blood to drain downward, so their eating was mixed with the blood of the animals, which is considered contrary to the Law.

entries.section: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

paragraphs.text: Out of fear of God’s wrath and punishment, some of the men went to Saul and told him of the people’s error when they ate the sacrifices with their blood. Saul answered that what the men had done was treachery against the Lord, and he asked the men to roll a great stone to make an altar of it.

entries.section: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

paragraphs.text: Saul commanded his officers to spread out among the people and tell them that whoever wants to slaughter and eat of his spoil should bring what he wants to slaughter to this high stone (the altar) and then eat what is pleasing to them, without sinning against God or angering Him. The people responded to Saul’s word, and all of them slaughtered on this stone.

entries.section: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

paragraphs.text: In acknowledgment of the work of God, Saul built another altar to the Lord on which to offer burnt offerings and thank offerings, and this was of course through the priest “Ahiah.” The expression “he began to build an altar to the Lord” distinguishes it from the first stone, which he made for slaughtering the spoils of war for the people. Saul had begun to build it and did not finish it, and this is the first altar that Saul built to the Lord.

entries.section: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

paragraphs.text: Saul wanted to exploit the victory to the end and take the spoil of the Philistines, so he met with the leaders of his people and proposed that they continue the battle by night and attack the lands of the Philistines until the morning of the next day in order to destroy them and take the rest of their spoil. Because the people had eaten and rested, Saul agreed to their proposal that he do what he saw to be right, but “Ahiah the priest proposed that they stand before God to know His will before beginning to do anything.

entries.section: (4) Eating the sacrifices with their blood

paragraphs.text: Saul asked the Lord, by means of the high priest, about his proposal and whether God would stand with His people and deliver the Philistines to them, but God did not answer him anything, that is, He did not say yes or no. Of course Saul did not continue the battle, since the Lord did not give him approval.

Note: Inquiring of the Lord by means of the high priest was done through two precious stones, the “Urim” and the “Thummim,” on one of which was written yes and on the other no. If the first stone was lit up, the answer was God’s consent, and if the other was lit up, the answer was God’s refusal, but if neither lit up, this meant that God gave His people no reply.

In the exhilaration of joy and the need of hunger, the people ate the sacrifices with their blood ... So it is good for a person in his joy not to break God’s commandments by stumbling behaviors such as dancing, drinking wine or wearing improper clothing ...

It was strange that God did not answer His people with yes or no, and for this reason Saul concluded that God was angry with them and that one of the men of the people had committed a great sin that was the cause of this, and this is what made Saul speak to his people about it.

In a new haste on Saul’s part, he swore by the living Lord, the Savior of Israel, that if the guilty person who was the cause of God’s not answering were found, he would put him to death, whoever he might be, even if it were Jonathan his son. As for the people who were listening to Saul, they did not answer him, and no one uttered a single word ... because they knew that the cause was Jonathan, but he was beloved by all.

Saul decided to cast lots to find the guilty one, and so as not to exempt himself or Jonathan his son, he decided to cast the lot in more than one stage. The first stage would be between himself and his son on one side and all the people on the other; if he and his son were cleared, he would then cast the lot on the tribes and then the clans until he reached the sinner, which was the system followed at that time. As for the people’s answer, it was submission to what their king proposed to them.
Give a perfect lot: show us the truth and declare what is true.

Before casting the first lot, Saul addressed God in a quick prayer, saying, “Lord, declare the truth, and let this lot be according to Your will to reveal the person who has erred.” When the lot was cast, the people came out of it innocent, and Saul and his son Jonathan remained. Then Saul asked for the lot to be cast a second time to determine the person; Saul was cleared, and the lot took his son Jonathan.

Saul was surprised by the result of the lot, which was something he had basically ruled out, and for this reason he asked Jonathan for an explanation of the error he had committed. Jonathan answered him with what had happened, that he had eaten a little honey (although he did so without knowing his father’s prohibition), and he went on to say that since the lot had taken him, he was ready to die, because it was the will of God. By this Jonathan accepted death without any fault of his, because he did not know his father’s oath, and in this he is a symbol of Christ, who died on the Cross without sinning in order to redeem His people. Jonathan gave victory to his people and accepted to die for them, and Christ gave the victory over Satan by the Cross, by His death for His people.

Notice with me, beloved, how Jonathan did not defend himself by saying that he did not know of his father’s command or that his father’s command was wrong in the first place, but in wonderful submission offered himself to death, believing that the lot that fell on him was a divine ordering and therefore he must respond ...!!! Defend yourself gently and leave the matter in God’s hand, and when you do so you will find God glorified, sending one to defend you and revealing the truth, as we shall see now in what happened.

Saul did not draw back but issued the sentence of death on his son Jonathan, using the expression “God do so and more also,” which is an expression meaning that God would do something harsher than death if he did not carry out the sentence of death on his son.

The people defended Jonathan with a strong and moving defense, since on the one hand they loved him, and on the other hand Jonathan was the cause of the defeat of the Philistines and the deliverance of Israel, and this would not have happened had it not been for God’s support of him. The people swore in the face of Saul that no harm should befall Jonathan, not even the falling of a single hair of his head. The expression “the people rescued Jonathan” means that by their strong and vigorous defense they saved him from death. Most likely Saul offered sacrifices for his haste in the oath, and Jonathan also offered sacrifices for his unintentional error.

Since Saul received no answer from God to continue the battle, he and his men withdrew, and so the Philistines went each to his own town. But the wars with the Philistines continued, as appears in the following verses and in (ch. 31), in which Saul will die.
The Philistines: they dwelt on the southern border of the land of Israel.
Moab and the children of Ammon: descendants of Lot, who dwelt east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea.
Edom: descendants of Esau, who dwelt on the southern border of the children of Israel in the mountains of Seir.
Zobah: a city of the Arameans.

The kingdom was fully established and settled for Saul over Israel, and he had no opponent. Saul took advantage of the people’s rallying around him and waged a group of small wars on his enemies surrounding the borders of the land of the children of Israel, and the Lord gave him victory over the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites and the Philistines, who are all the pagan peoples on the borders of Israel. In all his wars Saul was fierce and strong, so he was also able to smite the mighty Amalekites, who anciently dwelt in Sinai and, in his days, in the south of Palestine, and he prevented all the plunderers and spoilers from attacking the lands of the tribes.

These three verses are an introduction to Saul’s family and his small and large household ... The introduction began first with his male children: Jonathan his firstborn, and the second, Ishui, who is also called “Abinadab” (ch. 31:2), and his third son, “Melchishua”; there was also a fourth son called “Ishbosheth” (2 Sam 2:8). His two daughters were “Merab” and “Michal,” whom David later married. Saul’s lawful wife was “Ahinoam,” and he had another concubine, “Rizpah.” His uncle was “Ner” and his cousin “Abner,” to whom he entrusted the command of the army; as for Saul’s grandfather, his name was “Abiel,” and he was also called by another name, “Ner” (1 Chr 9:39), which is the name his son, that is, Saul’s uncle, also bore.

At the close of the chapter, the inspired text tells us that all the days of Saul’s reign over Israel there were wars with the Philistines, and it also mentions that Saul was a good commander, for he would attach every strong and mighty man to his army, which showed the strength of Israel.

It was a beautiful quality in Saul that he attached every strong man to his army, so you should hold fast to everything that strengthens you in your spiritual warfare against Satan, such as the Holy Bible, repentance, Holy Communion, prayer and every opportunity for spiritual meetings ...
The victory over the Amalekites and God’s rejection of Saul
Samuel reminded Saul that God was the One who anointed him to fulfill His will. He said this before asking of him what God had commanded in the following verses.
Amalek: a mighty people who dwelt in Sinai and the south of Palestine.

God reminds Saul of what Amalek did when he resisted the people of God in the wilderness of Sinai and tried to destroy them, but God intervened and supported Joshua and Moses, so they overcame Amalek (Ex 17), and now the time has come to punish wicked Amalek.

For this reason the Lord commanded that Amalek be smitten and avenged upon, and that all he has be killed, men, women, children and beasts, to remove evil and everything connected with it, so that the people of God might know the gravity of evil and its punishment and keep away from it.
Footmen: that is, one who walks on his feet and does not ride a horse like the horsemen.

Saul obeyed at once and began to gather a great army in the town of Telaim, which is located south of the land of the tribe of Judah, and he numbered the people gathered for war, who were two hundred thousand footmen from all the tribes. The inspired text mentions the number of the men of Judah separately, which was ten thousand men, a small number in comparison with the size of the great tribe, and this shows that the tribe of Judah was still murmuring at the choice of Saul as king from a small tribe, the tribe of Benjamin, so their cooperation with them was limited.

It appears here that the number of Saul’s army had become great, two hundred thousand, whereas it is mentioned in (ch. 13:15) that the number of his army was 600 men. The meaning of this is that not a few years had passed between these two events.

The Amalekites had no town or city, for they were like roaming Bedouin, and what is meant by the city of Amalek is their land where they had settled and pitched their tents. As for Saul, he hid with his soldiers around them, awaiting the best time to attack them.

There was a kinship between the Jews and the Kenites, because Moses married the daughter of Jethro, who was of the Kenites (Ex 3:1), and his son Hobab accompanied them in the wilderness of Sinai (Num 10:29), in addition to the fact that Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite helped the children of Israel by killing Sisera, their enemy (Judg 4:11). For this reason Saul asked the Kenites, who were dwelling beside Amalek, to depart from them lest they be destroyed with them in the war, and they departed.
Havilah: a wide land that occupied the region from present-day Kuwait and extended toward the land of the Arabs to the south, that is, the south of Palestine.
Shur: it is the wilderness of Shur, and it was west of Havilah and extended opposite Egypt on its east.

Saul waged war and attacked all the land of Amalek with his great army, and it was a war extending from the southeast of Palestine to the far west opposite Egypt, because the Amalekites had no fixed cities but were spread out in the desert exactly like Bedouin.
Agag: a title of the kings of Amalek, like Pharaoh for the kings of Egypt.

Saul was victorious in his war and was able to capture Agag, the greatest of the kings of Amalek, and kill all the people with the edge of the sword, but he disobeyed the Lord’s command to devote everything to destruction, and spared Agag and did not kill him. He also sorted out the spoil he had obtained and devoted to destruction (that is, slaughtered and killed) everything in it that was bad and worthless, but what was good and fair in his eyes he kept and did not destroy, and held it for himself and his men. Perhaps he spared Agag to satisfy his vanity by having a captive king under his hand, or out of pity for this king, and both are disobedience to God. The sparing of the sheep was for the purpose of possessing them and eating of them, and not, as he will claim, that he would offer sacrifices of them to God (v. 15). This shows the extent of his preoccupation with material things and possessions more than with obeying God. And if someone asks why animals that have not sinned are killed, we say that sin is the cause of the ruin of man and of all creation, and then we ask why Christ died although He was innocent! He died to lift sin and its effects from us, from man and from all creation, so that everything may be blessed.
However great the power of evil, it is nothing before the power of God, so do not fear the wicked, but hold fast to the truth and trust that God protects you and crushes the demons under your feet.
It repented Me: God was no longer pleased and grieved because of Saul’s actions.
He was grieved: he was greatly pained because of Saul’s disobedience.
He has turned back from following Me: he did not follow what I commanded.

The Lord spoke in a vision to His prophet Samuel and told him of His grief because of Saul’s disobedience and that He had rejected him as king of Israel, because Saul despised the word of the Lord and did not devote to destruction the king of Amalek or the good of the spoil but kept them. Of course this was Saul’s second great error after his first error at Gilgal, when he presumed against the priesthood and hastily offered the sacrifice, which is the work of the priests only. As for Samuel, the faithful servant of his people, he grieved greatly when he heard this and continued all night praying earnestly to God to have mercy on his people and forgive Saul.
Carmel: about 11.5 km south of Hebron (the present city of Al-Khalil).

Samuel did not taste sleep all night, and because of his burning heart he rose very early to meet Saul and asked where he was, and learned that he had gone to Carmel after the battle and set up a pillar or memorial of his victory over Amalek, and then moved on to Gilgal near Jericho. This shows that Saul had begun to boast in his glories and victories in pride, although he had disobeyed God and become rejected by Him.

When Samuel arrived at Gilgal, Saul met him joyful and exulting at his coming and at his victory over Amalek, and addressed him, saying, “Blessed are you, O man of God, for I have carried out what God commanded me, and the Lord has given me victory.”

Samuel did not return the greeting because of his anger at Saul, but exposed Saul’s disobedience and asked him, if he had carried out the Lord’s command, what then of the bleating of the sheep and the lowing of the cattle that he hears?!!

Saul answered him, not realizing the extent of the error committed, that they had taken this spoil from the Amalekites and the people had decided not to destroy all of it but kept the best of it after they had also destroyed much of it.
And in a naive attempt by Saul to appease Samuel, he told him that the reason for not killing the cattle was to offer them to the Lord as sacrifices.
This shows Saul’s pride, his lack of repentance and his justifying his error by the following:
1- He attributed the error of sparing the sheep to the people and not to himself, although it was he who commanded them to do so. So he is not repentant of the sin.
2- He made an excuse for disobeying God and sparing the sheep, which was offering them as sacrifices to God.

3- He said “the Lord your God” in his speech with Samuel, as if he were saying: if we are pleasing your God, why are you angry? And he did not say “the Lord my God,” which means his separation from God and his not thinking of Him.
Decisively Samuel said to Saul, “Enough speaking, and now listen to what the Lord has sent me to say to you this night.”

Samuel began the word of the Lord to Saul by reminding him of his beginning, that he was of the smallest of the tribes and the smallest of the clans and nothing at all, but God chose him and made him king over all and the holder of the greatest position and honor among all the people. God also was the One who sent him and charged him with the mission of fighting the Amalekites and gave him victory over them, and God’s request of him was clear, to kill all human beings and beasts and spare none of them.
You swooped down on the spoil: you rushed in with a desire to possess the spoil.
And now you preferred to keep the spoil, and what you did was a great evil which angered the Lord against you and made Him reject you.
The best of the things devoted to destruction: the firstlings of the cattle and sheep which God had devoted to destruction.

Saul did not offer anything new in his speech, but said, in a new self-deception and an attempt to lessen the accusation, that he had done nothing but God’s command to fight Amalek and be victorious over them, and that their king “Agag” was captured and all his people killed, and he had not spared of the cattle except their firstlings and best so as to offer them as sacrifices to the Lord at Gilgal. Of course this was an error, because God does not accept sacrifices from animals which He had previously asked to be devoted to destruction. This shows Saul’s persistence in pride and in justifying himself and his complete distance from repentance and seeking God’s mercies. Saul said to Samuel “the Lord your God,” and did not say “the Lord our God,” and this shows his separation from God and his lack of sonship to Him.

To convince Saul of the gravity of his error, Samuel asked him a question of rebuke, saying to him, which is better with God: to listen to His word and carry out His commands exactly as He said them, or to offer sacrifices while disobeying Him?! And Samuel answered his own question, that listening and submitting to God’s commands is far better than offering rams and sacrifices.
Divination: an attempt to know the unseen by means of Satan.
Teraphim: small statues or miniature models of pagan gods which the pagans keep in their houses to seek blessing from them.

Samuel continued his speech and rebuke to Saul, making clear to him that what he had done was rebellion and defiance of the Lord’s command, and that by his foolishness and lack of submission he was as if he had fallen into the sin of divination or idolatry, and because he rejected obeying God, the Lord also rejected him from leading this people.

Many people do exactly as Saul did: they hate others and wrong them and then give much money and many gifts to the Church ... Do not be deceived, beloved, but first learn to love others and forgive them, and after this offer what you wish to offer, and know well that God cannot be deceived or bribed.

After Saul’s failed attempts at defense, and his attempt to pin the accusation on the people, and in the face of Samuel’s clear and frank words about Saul’s violations of all God’s word and his announcement of God’s judgment on him and his rejection as king of Israel, Saul began to offer an apology and declared his error and his breaking of God’s commandments. He offered an excuse worse than the offense, namely that the king and victorious commander feared the people and allowed them, and by this apology he was only adding a new offense to his offenses. He begged Samuel to forgive him and to go with him before God’s altar set up at Gilgal so that he might worship the Lord repentant and sorrowful, although his real intention was not repentance and submission to God, but that Samuel should accompany him as he entered the house of the Lord so that the people would be sure that he was still king and God was pleased with him, which was the opposite of the truth.

If you err, do not try to justify yourself, but in humility express sorrow for what came from you, and you will receive God’s forgiveness and the respect of others, for they will feel that you are bearing responsibility, so they will trust you and deal with you at ease.

Samuel refused Saul’s plea and was decisive in his words, and made clear to Saul that the matter was not in his hand but in the hand of God, who had rejected him, and therefore he too could not go against God and His commands.
The robe: the outer garment.

Samuel wanted to depart from Saul and from the place, and when he turned to go on his way, Saul seized the hem of his outer garment tightly and the skirt of the garment was torn. Samuel took the tearing of his robe as a prophetic sign and told Saul that just as his garment had been torn in two, so God would remove Saul from his people Israel and give the kingdom to another person, who is better than he before God. The word “neighbor” means of course the person of David the prophet, whom Saul loved at first and gave in marriage to his daughter Michal, as we shall see in the events of the book (ch. 16:21, ch. 18:20).
The Strength of Israel: the God of Israel, who counsels and guides him.

Will not repent: He does not draw back from His decision to reject Saul, because He is God who knows all things. God’s repenting in (v. 11) is an expression meaning His displeasure with Saul, because God chose him when he was humble, but he became proud and disobeyed God, so God rejected him; and when God rejected him, this was not a hasty decision, but God announced His decision with the utmost wisdom, understanding and justice. God uses words that we know as human beings, namely repentance, but what is meant by God’s repenting, as we mentioned in (v. 11), is His displeasure.

Samuel continues his speech to Saul, saying that God is the One who announced your rejection and your removal from the throne of the kingdom, and God is far above lying or repenting, for He is not like a man who takes a decision in an hour of anger and then repents afterward, but is an almighty God of all knowledge, and His declared will has no turning back.

Saul confessed his error, but he cared more about his appearance before the elders and the people than about God’s punishment of him and rejection of him, so he pressed Samuel to return with him and worship before God for the sake of his honor and appearance and so that no one would know of the divine punishment and God’s rejection of him. His purpose was not repentance but keeping up his appearance as king. And he did not say “the people of God” but “my people,” which shows his arrogance, his selfishness and his lack of submission to God, for he ascribes the people to himself and not to God.

In the face of Saul’s continued pressing, and perhaps because of the kindness of Samuel’s heart, we find that Samuel did indeed turn back and return with Saul to the house of the Lord, where Saul worshiped.

After Saul’s worship, Samuel did not forget God’s command to devote to destruction, and for this reason he gave the order to bring Agag king of Amalek. As for Agag, when he learned that Samuel had summoned him, it did not occur to him what he would do to him, but he rejoiced and thought that he would be released from captivity, and for this reason he said to himself that at last the specter of death would depart from him.
Childless: the woman who has lost her son.
Before the Lord: before the house of the Lord, to carry out God’s command before His house.

When they brought Agag before Samuel, Samuel said to him, in an introduction before issuing his sentence, that just as your sword was the cause of killing many men and young men and made their mothers childless, weeping for their children, so today your mother will be childless and weep for you all the days of her life; and after that Samuel commanded that Agag’s head be cut off, and all this was done at Gilgal before Samuel left.
Agag is a symbol of the great sin which a person must cut off from his life, however much it is bound up with things dear to him, because obeying God is better than anything.
Samuel returned to Ramah, which was his town and place of residence, while Saul went up to his house and family in his place of residence at Gibeah of Saul.

The meeting between Saul and Samuel at Gilgal was the last of the meetings that brought them together, and Samuel did not see Saul again all his life, since he knew the Lord’s decision concerning him, but he wept much in his prayer for Saul and over how the first king of Israel had become rejected. The expression that the Lord repented that He had made Saul king is meant to confirm God’s rejection and the appointment, in the divine purpose, of another man to reign over Israel. The meaning of God’s rejection of Saul is His refusal that he be king over His people, but Samuel continued to weep over him, asking for his repentance, that perhaps he might repent as a human being and not lose his eternity, but unfortunately he continued in his evils until the end of his life.

Be obedient to God’s commands in declaring the truth and being firm with those who err, for pity on evil increases it and makes others stumble, so that it becomes a sin ... And do not do your own will but the will of God.
The anointing of David as king
Horn: from the horns of sheep, and it was used as a vessel for the anointing oil.
Bethlehem: located about 9.5 km south of Jerusalem.

God spoke to Samuel, asking him to stop weeping and making petition for Saul after He had rejected him as a result of his disobedience and contempt for His commands, and He commanded him to take a horn and put in it “the holy oil” and go with it to “Jesse,” who lives in the city of Bethlehem, to anoint one of his sons as king.
And God says, “I have provided Me ... a king”: God in His fatherhood chooses a king submissive to Him, to carry out His commandments and lead His people in the way of righteousness.

Samuel, in his human weakness, was afraid of Saul, the present king, lest he kill him if he learned that Samuel would anoint another king, and he said this to God. But God, in His long-suffering, did not rebuke Samuel for his human weakness, but gave him a solution, which was to take a heifer and go with it to Bethlehem as though he had gone to offer a sacrifice, which was acceptable and well known of Samuel, who traveled much in the land and offered sacrifices in every place. This was an exception that Samuel made, because the sacrifices were all offered in the house of God. Samuel’s saying that he would offer a sacrifice is not a lie, because he would indeed offer it before all the people, but he would anoint the new king secretly.

The secret anointing of David is a symbol of our present life, for we have all been anointed with the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Holy Myron, but our kingship and coronation will be revealed in eternity (Rom 8:18) after our death, which is symbolized by the death of Saul, and after we pass through the sufferings of this present time, which are symbolized by the sufferings David endured from Saul.

God continues His speech with Samuel and says to him, “Invite Jesse and his house to attend the sacrifice, and you shall anoint the son whom I shall declare to you, and I will tell you all that you shall do.”

Samuel carried out God’s word and came to Bethlehem, and when the elders of the city saw him they were afraid because his visit was sudden, and they thought that he had come to announce an error or punish someone, so they asked him, “Do you come in goodness and peace, or for another purpose?”

Samuel reassured them and said to them ... “I have only come to offer a sacrifice to the Lord, and there is no bad news in my coming,” and he asked them to sanctify themselves before the offering of the sacrifice, and likewise he asked “Jesse” and his sons, and invited everyone to the sacrifice. The sanctification was done by a person bathing, washing his clothes and examining his conscience ...

The priest cries out in the Liturgy, saying, “The holies are for the holy,” before the people come forward to partake of the Holy Mysteries. Examine yourself, beloved, and sanctify yourself by repentance and purifying your conscience, and you will receive the blessing of union with the Body and Blood of Christ.
When they had come: Samuel, Jesse and his sons went to the house of Jesse, and this was at Samuel’s command, so that he might secretly accomplish the anointing of the new king.

Samuel offered the sacrifice on an altar in the midst of the city but went to eat of it in the house of Jesse, of course with a prior purpose in his mind, and while he was in the house of Jesse, Samuel saw Jesse’s firstborn son “Eliab” and said in himself, “This is the Lord’s anointed.”

God made clear to Samuel that Eliab was not the new king as Samuel had thought because of his tall stature, and He declared to him that man looks at the outward appearance of the king, but God chooses the pure heart, so that the king may govern His people with godliness and righteousness.

In these three verses Jesse presented his seven sons before Samuel, beginning with “Abinadab,” his second son, then “Shammah,” his third son, to the last of the seven, but with each of them God declared to Samuel that he was not the one chosen to be anointed king.

Since the Lord did not choose any of these seven, Samuel asked “Jesse,” “Are these all your children?” and “Jesse” answered him that there remained only the youngest, who was charged with keeping the sheep. Samuel asked “Jesse” to bring him, and quickly, expressing his concern for the coming of this young one by saying that he would not sit down to eat until he arrived.

Indeed Jesse sent and summoned his youngest son “David,” and he came, and Samuel describes him as beautiful in appearance and form, his complexion tending to whiteness, and his eyes also colored. And when the youth David came in, the Lord declared to Samuel that he was the chosen one and asked him to arise and anoint him.

We see here that David, the youngest, left with the sheep, whom no one expected to be the one chosen by God, is indeed chosen by God because of his faithfulness in tending the sheep, for he killed the lion and the bear and risked himself to keep the sheep (ch. 17:34). David represents all those despised and rejected by the world whose hearts are pure and faithful, for they are advanced before God. He also symbolizes the Gentiles, who were rejected by the Jews, but Christ, who came for the salvation of all, accepted them, and many saints came out of them. David here also symbolizes Christ, despised, born in the manger, persecuted by the priests, scribes and Pharisees, and crucified, yet He is the Savior of the whole world and the King of kings. It also appears from this that God’s view differs from people’s view, so He chose David, whom even his father did not feel to be suitable for this office. So do not judge by appearance, and give room for prayer to hear God’s voice and His choice.

Indeed Samuel arose and anointed “David” with the holy oil before all who were present, and immediately the Spirit of God came upon David as the anointed of the Lord and king of Israel all his days. As for Samuel, after he had completed his mission, he set out returning to Ramah, his place of residence, after he had anointed David and eaten of the sacrifice.

David believed in the grace of God that had come upon him to be king, but when he did not find himself declared crowned over the kingdom, but Saul who was reigning, perhaps he understood that he needed a period of preparation for the kingship, in which God would prepare him, so he was not troubled and lived his normal life and did not demand any rights of kingship. Perhaps this preparation appears in:
1- His learning to shepherd the people through his shepherding of the sheep.
2- His learning meditation and solitude with God, who would support him in his life and in his office as king.
3- His learning to play the lute to praise God and thank Him for everything, so that he would not be troubled by the sufferings that might pass over him.
4- In his victory over the lion and the bear he felt the power of God supporting him.
5- His playing the lute for Saul let him see the royal palace and learn how the king conducts the affairs of the kingdom.
6- In his victory over Goliath and killing him, his faith in the power of God who was with him was confirmed.
7- Saul’s jealousy of him taught him to make excuses for others, to have pity on them and to love them.
8- His endurance of sufferings and exile when Saul pursued him made him not attached to the delights and luxury of the kingship, and he remained holding fast to his love for God.
9- His exposure to being killed by Saul many times made him rely on God and trust in His protection of him.
10- Saul’s falling into his hands during the pursuit taught him complete forgiveness and respect for others.

Do not judge by appearance, lest your judgment be wrong. Seek God and be deliberate in judgment if you are responsible for choosing a person to bear a certain responsibility, and be long-suffering until God reveals to you the suitable person. And do not interfere in what does not concern you and judge others, so that you fall into condemnation.

entries.section: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

paragraphs.text: After Saul had erred more than once and despised God’s commands, and the Lord had declared his rejection, the Holy Spirit left him completely, and by God’s permission an unclean spirit suddenly came upon him and he became a dwelling of Satan, and this spirit kept troubling Saul and tormenting him from time to time.
This does not mean that God sent him an unclean spirit, but because of his evil God forsook him, so the unclean spirit entered him, and God allowed this to show the result of pride and evil.

entries.section: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

paragraphs.text: With the repeated attacks of the evil spirit on Saul, his servants suggested to him that he send his men everywhere in the kingdom to search for a man skilled in playing the strings, so that if such a man were found and played his melodies while the unclean spirit was active and tormenting Saul, the spirit would be calmed and Saul would be at rest and his soul would be well. Perhaps this suggestion was considered a kind of treatment of agitation by calm music, which often succeeds ... But he did not know that all this was a prior divine arrangement so that Saul would meet David the son of Jesse. And no one dared to confront the king and call him to repentance so that the unclean spirit would leave him.

entries.section: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

paragraphs.text: Indeed Saul commanded his men and servants to search for a man skilled in playing, and one of Saul’s acquaintances who was present said that he knew a man whom he had seen, one of the sons of “Jesse” of Bethlehem, and this son was not only a good player of music but also a bold man and a warrior, with the speech of the wise, and handsome in appearance, and above all this the Lord was with him and blessed him.

entries.section: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

paragraphs.text: When Saul heard this testimony he did not search for anyone else but sent messengers to Bethlehem asking “Jesse” to send his son who kept the sheep. Indeed “Jesse” sent his son David to the king and sent with him a gift consisting of bread, wine and a kid of the goats, for he was a generous and distinguished man and thought it good to send his son with a gift for the king.

entries.section: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

paragraphs.text: David came in to King Saul in his council, and the Lord gave him favor in the king’s eyes, so he loved him greatly from the time he saw him and made him one of his close men, making him his armor-bearer, which means that he was constantly beside Saul. And Saul sent a messenger to “Jesse,” David’s father, asking him to leave David to him because he loved him and trusted him and made him one of the nearest men of the people to him. Of course Jesse could not refuse such a request, but considered this an honor for any father in all Israel.

David’s presence in the royal palace was an opportunity for him to become acquainted with the system of government and its management, to learn everything useful for ruling and avoid the errors that harm the people, so that this would be a preparation and groundwork for him when he actually takes the leadership of the people.

entries.section: (2) David plays the lute for Saul

paragraphs.text: Whenever the unclean spirit attacked Saul, David would play the strings of his lute, and the unclean spirit would depart from the king and he would be refreshed afterward. The reason for the removal of the unclean spirit was not merely the playing of music, but the basis was the presence of David the righteous, so that Satan feared him and departed from Saul.
If you are faithful in your work and in bearing responsibility, God gives you favor in the eyes of those in authority, and even gives you dignity as well, which you can use to draw them to God.
David kills Goliath

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Socoh: 14 miles southwest of Jerusalem, beside the southern border of the tribe of Judah, that is, near the Philistines.
Azekah: a city neighboring Socoh.
Ephes-dammim: located northeast of Socoh at a distance of four miles.
The Philistines gathered for war against Israel and made for themselves a camp in which they drew up their ranks between three places, which are Socoh, Azekah and Ephes-dammim.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The valley of the terebinth: the valley of acacia trees.
As for Israel, they gathered under the leadership of Saul in a valley in which acacia trees abound and drew up in ranks for war opposite the army of the Philistines.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Both sides stood on a hill, and each army could see the other completely and even hear it, and a valley separated the two sides. Each of the two parties feared to go down into the valley lest the other strike it, and when the time grew long, Goliath took this opportunity to come forward and ask for a champion to fight him, as will appear in what follows.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Champion: one who fights with his sword face to face with another champion.

A man from the ranks of the Philistines, whose name was Goliath, came forward. He was from one of the five great cities of the Philistines, which is the city of Gath, and his height by present-day measures was more than three meters, and of course his breadth was proportionate to his height, since he was a man of war.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Scale armor: on the armor there are scales of bronze like the scales of a fish.

This man was dreadful in his clothing, war equipment and weapons. He covered his head with a helmet of bronze and wore armor protecting his chest, also of bronze, and the surface of this armor was covered with bronze rings resembling fish scales. This armor was massive, for its weight reached 55 kilograms, considering that the weight of the shekel ranges from
11-14 grams approximately.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Greaves: thin sheets of bronze wrapped around the leg to protect the fighter.
Javelin: a small spear, shorter in length than the spear and longer and thicker than the arrow.
Goliath wore on his legs something like a bronze stocking to protect his legs, and carried on his back between the shoulders a small bronze javelin.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The spear: it is the lance, and its shaft was of wood and its head of pointed iron.

Goliath also carried a huge spear with a large, broad wooden shaft resembling the beam of the loom used in weaving, which is a broad, heavy piece of wood. His spear did not have a single iron point like the other spears but a group of points like a fork, and the weight of the points of his spear was about seven kilograms of iron ... He had a shield, which is usually round and which the fighter holds with his left arm to ward off attacks, and in the case of Goliath a man was assigned to carry the shield for him until there was fighting, and then Goliath would carry it himself, and perhaps the reason for having a man carry the shield for him was the weight of his clothing and war equipment. And of course, dear reader, if we review what was written in the description of Goliath, we know that we are before a huge human tank, for in all the history of mankind there has been no one whose height reached three meters.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Goliath came forward and called in a loud voice to the drawn-up army of Israel, saying to them, “Why do you fight with all your men? For I am here representing all the Philistines and you are all Saul’s men. So why do you not choose from among you a man to fight me face to face instead of shedding the blood of men in war? If this man is able to defeat me, all the Philistines will become servants to you, but if I defeat him and kill him, all of you with your people will become servants to us, the Philistines.” He said this confident that there would be no one who dared to stand before him.

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: I defy: I challenge.

With the arrogance of one confident of victory, Goliath continued his speech, saying, “I have challenged all the Philistines and have not found a single man among them to come out to meet me and fight me.”

entries.section: (1) Goliath taunts the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The offer that Goliath made was a new offer, not customary among peoples in wars, and his huge and awesome appearance with all that he wore was terrifying to whoever saw him. For this reason all Saul’s men were afraid and kept silent, and of course not a single man of them came forward.

Do not fear Satan, who uses the wicked to threaten and terrify you, for they are worthless before God however strong they appear. Seek God’s help and trust that He is able to rescue you from their hands, and fight for you and glorify you.

entries.section: (2) Jesse sends David to visit his brothers

paragraphs.text: This verse takes us back to the family of Jesse, who was from Ephrath, “Bethlehem,” of the tribe of Judah, and he had eight sons, the youngest of whom was “David,” whom Samuel anointed as king; he also had three sons in the war, who were the eldest, “Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah.” The man wanted to be reassured about his sons, but he had grown old and aged and was not able to go himself to check on them.

entries.section: (2) Jesse sends David to visit his brothers

paragraphs.text: David had been staying with Saul as his armor-bearer (ch. 16), but when the battle began, and because he was too young to be counted among the men of war, he went to his father’s house to tend the sheep, though from time to time he would go to Saul to play the lute for him when the unclean spirit attacked him.

entries.section: (2) Jesse sends David to visit his brothers

paragraphs.text: As for the field of battle, there was no fighting there, but Goliath kept coming out and advancing and taunting and challenging all the people and the men of war for forty days, coming out twice every day, morning and evening, and of course no one dared to meet him.

entries.section: (2) Jesse sends David to visit his brothers

paragraphs.text: Ephah: a measure holding about 22.9 liters, and equal to about 10 kg of parched grain (freekeh).
Token: a sign or anything that confirms that he met his brothers, because writing was not widespread in those days.

The father Jesse charged his youngest son David with the mission of going to the place of battle to check on his brothers and supply them with food, represented by the parched grain as well as ready-to-eat bread, and the generous man did not forget to present to the captain of the thousand, who was the commander over his brothers, ten cheeses as a gift. And “Jesse” asked David to bring back on his return tokens from his brothers by which he could be sure of their well-being and that they were still alive.

entries.section: (2) Jesse sends David to visit his brothers

paragraphs.text: Saul was still in the valley of the terebinth with his men, facing the army of the Philistines, but without any real fighting worth mentioning. The expression “fighting with the Philistines” means that they were in a state of readiness for war.

How beautiful it is that you take care to ask about your loved ones and to visit those who are absent from the Church, to check on them and encourage them to attend, for a question of love has a great effect on hearts.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: The barricade: the barricades are the obstacles that the drawn-up army sets before it to hinder the enemy, and they may be of logs cut from trees, or earthen barriers, or stones.

David left the sheep with a hired keeper and set out early, carrying the bread, the parched grain and the cheeses, as his father had commanded him, and this shows his distinction in obedience, for it was swift, and this qualifies him for his office as king in his obedience to God. When he reached the area of the barricades, the men were drawn up in ranks, singing the stirring songs and shouts of war.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: Both armies stood facing each other, but David left all that he had brought with a man of the army who was assigned to keep deposits, called the keeper of the baggage, to give it to the soldiers at a later time, and went quickly to check on his brothers.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: David reached the front lines and met his brothers, and brotherly conversation went on between them, and while he was there Goliath came out to repeat what he said every day of taunting the people of God, and none of the people answered him. David of course heard him, and also noticed the fear of all the men and their drawing back.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: In the face of the people’s great fear, Saul promised a reward to whoever would confront Goliath. First, the king would enrich him with a large monetary reward that would make him one of the great men of the kingdom; the second gift was that this man would be given his daughter in marriage, so that the king himself would become his relative; and the third reward was that his father’s house would be exempted from taxes and from the service of the king and from any other forced labor. Yet no man came forward to fight Goliath.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: Uncircumcised: that is, he was not circumcised (purified) like the rest of the males of the people of Israel.

David addressed the men around him, saying, “What shall be done for the man who kills Goliath and takes away the reproach from the people of Israel?” and he asked in a tone of disapproval, “Who is this pagan, uncircumcised Philistine that he should insult and taunt the people of the living God by his words?...!” David’s question was based on zeal and enthusiasm for his people and for the name of God.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: The men answered David with the three rewards of the king which he had promised in (v. 25).

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: Eliab heard David’s words with the men, so he became angry with him and rebuked him, saying, “Why have you come down to the field of battle, and why have you left your work of keeping the sheep?” and he accused him of the pride that drove him to learn the news of the war in order to boast of it among his young companions. Of course Eliab was wrong in all that he said, and accused his brother in it of curiosity and of seeking to raise his own standing.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: As for David, with wisdom he absorbed his brother’s anger, saying, “What have I now done?” or is it just talk, conversation, and question and answer? And with intelligence also he removed from himself the suspicion that he was thinking of fighting Goliath, so that his brother might be reassured.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: No sooner had David turned his back, moving away from his eldest brother, than he kept asking here and there and repeating his saying about how “this uncircumcised one taunts the people of the living God,” and the words were passed from man to man until the men told Saul of David’s bold words, full of confidence, so Saul sent and brought David before him. From this appear some virtues that qualified David to prevail over the mighty Goliath:
1- Obedience: which appeared in his swift obedience to his father (v. 20).
2- Wisdom: in his answer to his eldest brother “Eliab” and his not being disturbed by his rebuke (v. 28).

3- His zeal for the name of God, for he did not fight Goliath to prove his strength because he was his personal enemy, but because of his daring to insult the name of God (v. 10), unlike Saul, who considered the Philistines his enemies and not the enemies of God (ch. 14:24).

4- Self-giving: he was ready to give his life to redeem his people when he agreed to fight Goliath, and his asking about the king’s reward for whoever defeats Goliath was an understanding of everything surrounding the matter of Goliath and not an attachment to a reward, because nothing is dearer than a person’s life, and if he dies no reward will benefit him (v. 27).

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: When David met Saul, he spoke to him first, reassuring the king and trusting in God who supports him, and told him that there was no need for anyone to fear this uncircumcised one or feel humiliated, for he was fully ready to go and kill this Philistine.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: Despite the king’s great need of any volunteer to go and fight Goliath so as to remove the shame from his people, his love for David and his pity for him on the one hand, and his realistic view of the matter on the other, made him advise David to give up the matter, pointing out to him his young age and that Goliath was a man experienced in war all his life. For Saul thought that David’s words were merely youthful impulsiveness on his part.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: David’s enthusiasm did not wane in the face of Saul’s words, and in an attempt to convince him that he was not the tender lad but had the heart of a fighting man, he began to tell Saul a story that had happened to him: that one day, while he was tending his father’s sheep, a mountain lion and also a bear came out against him, and the lion was able to snatch a young sheep in its mouth. Of course in such circumstances the shepherd thanks God that the lion did not come near him personally and that the loss is considered a slight loss since it was a single sheep, but the shepherd with the fiery heart did not do this; rather he took his staff and chased the lion desperately and struck it and knocked it down and rescued the sheep from its mouth, and when the lion rose again from its faint, David seized it again by its beard and kept striking its head until he killed it, and he killed the bear also.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: David continued his speech: “Your servant has killed a lion and a bear, which are among the most ferocious of animals, so likewise will be the fate of Goliath the uncircumcised Philistine, who has permitted himself to taunt the people of the living God, and God Himself, who delivered me from the lion and the bear, will give me victory over Goliath and rescue me from death.” In the face of this courage and faith of David, Saul could do nothing but agree, and he prayed for God’s blessing on his steps.

entries.section: (3) David among the men of war and hears Goliath’s taunting

paragraphs.text: As a kind of appreciation and reward, Saul rose and took off his war clothes and put them on David, and also gave him a bronze helmet and armor, and after that David took Saul’s sword as well and tried to move. It was the first time in his life that he moved in war clothing, and he found them very heavy and hindering him from moving, and he told Saul that he could not walk, so he put the clothes off him, that is, took them off.

Here a question appears: where is the brave Jonathan, who had earlier attacked the Philistines alone with his armor-bearer (ch. 14)? Why did he not come forward to Goliath?! This shows how difficult it was to confront this huge monster of a warrior, so Jonathan feared him.
And David here is a symbol of Christ, whom no one else could overcome Satan and bind him by the Cross.
Be humble if someone rebukes you even if he is not right, for your long-suffering and love absorb the anger of others, so you win them and keep your peace.
Smooth stones: pebbles.
Shepherd’s bag: a sack or pouch in which the shepherd carries his food and carries it on his shoulder.
Sling: a strip of cloth in the middle of which stones are placed in preparation for hurling them.

After David took off the heavy war clothes and became light in movement, he took the staff that shepherds carry and chose five stones (pebbles) from the ground of the valley and put them in the shepherd’s bag hung on his shoulder, and took his sling in his other hand and advanced in the low valley between the two armies toward the huge Goliath.

Goliath also advanced toward David, and when he found him without war clothing and its equipment, and also young, slight of body and delicate of features, he despised him in himself and mocked him, and regarded David’s coming out to meet him as unworthy of his position and strength, so he began to curse David and revile the God of Israel, and said to David in his mockery, “Do you think I am a dog and not a warrior, that you come out against me with a staff instead of a sword or a spear?”
In anger Goliath threatened David to terrify him and said, “Come and advance toward me, and I will make you a tasty meal for the birds of prey of the sky and the beasts of the earth.”

David said to Goliath his famous and well-remembered word, declaring in it his strong faith in the God of Israel and in the power of His holy name, which is: if you come to me relying on your weapons, sword, spear and shield, I take refuge in the name of the God of the heavenly hosts and the God of Israel, whom you have despised and whose people you have taunted insolently.

Then David said, “Now God will deliver you into my hand, and by His power I will kill you and cut off your head; indeed God will give me victory over all your people, so that all your people will become food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, and your people first, and all the peoples of the earth second, will know that the God of Israel is a God able to do all things and that no command is too hard for Him. And it will be a lesson to all who are watching, present at this encounter, that victory is not by human weapons and the instruments of war, but God alone is the One who delivers you into our hands despite your apparent strength and your many numbers.”
It sank: it was embedded in his forehead.

When Goliath advanced in his steps toward David, David also quickly advanced toward him and put in his sling a stone from the five stones and stretched out his arm to hurl the stone, and indeed the stone flew through the air on its way to Goliath’s forehead and sank into it.
