The shock of the stone was so violent that it made this mighty man lose his balance, and he fell on his face to the ground. And so David prevailed over Goliath without a sword, and threw him to the ground and killed him.

From this it appears that however strong a person is, he has a point of weakness, even if only one, and Goliath’s point of weakness was that his forehead was not protected, so David was able to hunt him with a small pebble by the dog sling which he used to drive dogs away from his sheep. So do not be disturbed by the strength of enemies, because God is able to overcome them easily.
Drew it out of its sheath: brought it out of its scabbard.

This verse gives the detail of the summary that came in (v. 50). After Goliath fell to the ground, David ran quickly to him as he lay on his face and drew Goliath’s sword from its scabbard, raised it with both hands and brought it down on his neck, cutting off his head and killing him, and before the terror and severity of the surprise the Philistines trembled and fled.
Shaaraim: one of the cities of Judah in the valley of acacias.
All the people rose after the Philistines who fled to their cities “Gath and Ekron” and killed many of them and pursued them to the valley near their cities.
It is noted that the tribe of Judah is mentioned by name separately from the rest of the tribes, in honor of the tribe from which came the victorious David and the coming king of all the people.
Taking shelter: in other translations, “the pursuit.”

After the people had finished pursuing the Philistines, they returned quickly to the place where the Philistines had been encamped and took possession of all the spoil or goods that they had left behind.

As for David, he took care to carry and take the head of Goliath, who had been killed, and brought it to Jerusalem, and likewise he kept Goliath’s sword and the rest of his weapons in his tent in preparation for moving them to the house of the Lord as a memorial of God’s work with His people and His great victory (ch. 21).

David was not disturbed by the hugeness and strength of Goliath or by his weapons, but in faith he advanced toward him and by the power of God was able to kill him. So believe in God, who protects you and works through you, and you will advance to the hardest circumstances confident of your success by His power, and even if many oppose you, they cannot hinder you or overcome the God who is in you.

This verse takes us back to before David’s encounter with Goliath and his killing him. After David’s dialogue with Saul to convince him of his going to the war, and David’s actually going out, Saul asked Abner, the commander of his army, about David, saying, “Whose son is this lad?”
This arouses wonder, for Saul had earlier loved David and made him his armor-bearer, so how does he ask about him now? To answer this question we explain the following:

1- David did not have a permanent residence in Saul’s house, but they would summon him whenever Saul was troubled, and in the last period the unclean spirit had not been attacking Saul, and consequently David’s appearances with him were not frequent.

2- The title of the king’s armor-bearer was more an honorary title for one whom the king wished to honor, and perhaps David carried Saul’s weapons for some days and then left this task to take care of the sheep of his father “Jesse.” Perhaps years passed between David’s playing the lute before Saul and his killing Goliath, in addition to the fact that the unclean spirit made Saul forget many things.
There is another opinion, which is that Saul was jealous of David and showed that he did not know him, out of neglect of him, and Abner followed him in that.

Saul charged “Abner,” the commander of his army, to inquire about David and his lineage, and indeed when David had finished killing Goliath, “Abner” brought him before Saul while he was still carrying Goliath’s head in his hand, and Saul asked him, “Whose son are you, lad, and of whom of the people?” and David answered him that he was the son of “Jesse” of the village of Bethlehem. In David’s answer his humility before the king is noted, for he said, “the son of your servant.”
David, by his victory over Goliath, is a symbol of Christ in the following:
1- David killed the mighty man who taunted the people of God, and Christ bound Satan, who fights and taunts the children of God.
2- David cut off Goliath’s head, and Christ by His death trampled the head of the ancient serpent, that is, Satan.
3- David killed Goliath with Goliath’s sword, and Christ trampled Satan by the Cross and His death upon it, which Satan arranged through the high priests of the Jews.
4- David took a staff in his hand when he met Goliath, and Christ carried the wood of the Cross.
Be humble when you achieve victories, accomplishments and successes, giving the glory to God with thanksgiving, and you will protect yourself from pride and receive more abundant divine blessings.
Jonathan’s friendship and Saul’s enmity toward David

entries.section: (1) The friendship of Jonathan with David

paragraphs.text: Jonathan, the son of Saul, was present at the conversation between Saul his father and David after the battle, and Jonathan loved David greatly; to express the intensity of this love, it is said that he loved him as his own soul. The friendship of Jonathan and David became strong because its conditions were present in both of them, namely:
1- They had one goal, which was the love of God and zeal for His name, which appeared in Jonathan's challenge of the Philistines and David's fight against Goliath.
2- They were alike in strong faith in God, which gave them rare courage against the enemies.
3- Each was ready to sacrifice himself for the other, as would appear in Jonathan's defense of David before his father, when Saul was enraged and rose up to kill his son.

entries.section: (1) The friendship of Jonathan with David

paragraphs.text: As for Saul the king, who also loved David greatly and became attached to him, he did not let him return again to Bethlehem but kept him with his men.

entries.section: (1) The friendship of Jonathan with David

paragraphs.text: As for Jonathan, he expressed his love for David by making a covenant with him to be his friend to the end of his life, and indeed both of them kept their covenant; indeed, the friendship of Jonathan and David became an example for all generations.

entries.section: (1) The friendship of Jonathan with David

paragraphs.text: Robe: a splendid outer garment.
Girdle: a belt.

As a sign of the covenant between the two friends, Jonathan gave a token to his friend David: he took off his own "robe" and gave it to David as a gift, and he also gave his sword, his bow and his leather belt. These are all things very personal to a man, and it is not easy to part with them, but he did this with all love, as if he were giving the dearest thing he had to his new friend.

entries.section: (1) The friendship of Jonathan with David

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave David favor in the eyes of Saul, since the Lord was with David and he prospered in all the tasks the king assigned to him. Therefore Saul gave him a high position in his army, and he became one of the commanders of war. God blessed David even more, and he became beloved by all the servants of Saul and also by all the people of Israel.

If you live in godliness and hold fast to God's commandments, He will give you favor in the eyes of others, so that they love you and you live in good relationships with them, which helps you to succeed in your life and also in serving others and drawing them to Christ.

Saul's love for David did not last long, for some events came that turned everything upside down. After a period of time, when Saul decided to return from the places of war and enter the cities of the people, as was the custom with victorious kings, the people came out to meet them. And indeed the women came out to meet the victorious men, with musical instruments such as timbrels and ringing triangles, and they danced and chanted with singing.
Ten thousands: tens of thousands.

There were always popular poems and songs sung on such occasions and celebrations, so the dancing women began to chant: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. Of course, the women did not intend to provoke Saul, but the words came out this way as an expression of their recognition of David's merit in this great victory over Goliath and the Philistines.

Saul was greatly angered, because of his human jealousy, by the words of the women, and he considered it a kind of insolence and a belittling of himself, and he said, They have ascribed to me thousands and to David they have ascribed ten thousands, so what more can he have but the kingdom? That is, nothing remains but that David should also take the kingdom from me and the rule should become his!!!
After these events Saul began to harbor evil against David, and his former love turned into hatred, jealousy and a desire to be rid of him.

Do not be troubled if they praise another person in your presence and do not praise you; this does not mean that you are belittled. Be positive and learn from the virtues of those they praise, and be content with pleasing God, for He is better than every human praise.
As at other times (literally, as day by day): an expression meaning from time to time.

On the day after Saul's anger at the chanting of the women, a state of agitation came upon him because of the unclean spirit, and as usual they brought David, the lute player, who began to play. Satan (the unclean spirit) exploited Saul's hatred of David and his jealousy of him and drove him to kill David, especially since he was holding his spear. So Saul hurled the spear toward David, who was leaning against the wall, and tried to kill him, but David was able to escape from Saul twice, and the spear struck the wall and did not hit David.

Here we find Saul the king, in whose hand was all authority, fearing David, envying him and trying to kill him, while David flees from before him and God preserves him from all the plots of Saul. From this we conclude how great was Saul's inner weakness, because he was not with God even though he had the authority of a king, whereas David, who seemed to have no authority, had all power with him because God was with him.
This verse reveals to us that although Saul was still the king and David was merely one of his servants, God's departure from Saul and His strengthening of David made it Saul who feared David.

This teaches us, beloved, to acquire the fear of God and His love, and to obtain His favor toward us, for if the Lord is with us, who can be against us... God gives awe and inner strength, so that no one can frighten you or terrify your heart, but He makes all your enemies fear you.

As cunning politicians do, so Saul did with David. He could not harm the hero of the people or kill him, so he gave him a position of honor and limited authority, but kept him away from himself and from his court and made him captain over a thousand. David was faithful in his work, and the Lord gave him success and strengthened him, and he became beloved by all the people.

The news of David's success reached Saul, and his fear of him increased even more, for he had come to stand as the foremost man of the people, since everyone loved him, from his own tribe and from all the tribes of the people. For the people love the leader who mingles with them and lives among them, like Christ, who lived in the midst of the crowds and suffered their sufferings (Heb 2:17).

Jealousy grew greatly in Saul's heart with David's success and the people's love for him, so a very cunning idea went around in his mind for getting rid of him and killing him: to offer him a great honor, namely giving him his elder daughter "Merab" in marriage, on condition that David be the commander of his army in fighting the Philistines. Thus David would be exposed to death in these wars and would be killed by the hand of the Philistines, while Saul's hand would remain clean of his blood. Here we see David's humility: he did not demand his right to marry the king's daughter without a dowry, for he had already paid it by killing Goliath, since Saul had promised this, but he obeyed.
In humility and self-denial, David answered Saul that he was not worthy of this noble kinship, saying, Who am I, and what is my family, that I should be worthy of becoming the king's son-in-law?

At the time set for the marriage, we are surprised that Saul's daughter was given to another man, unknown, from the town of "Meholah" in the Jordan valley, named "Adriel". We do not know the reason for this change; perhaps Saul broke his promise in order to vex and humiliate David among the people. We see here that while Saul breaks his promise to David and does not give him Merab, God rewards him with many rewards, which are:
1- Success in his wars with the Philistines, so that he appeared as a great warrior leader.
2- The friendship of Jonathan, the son of Saul, toward him.
3- The love of Michal for him, which would stand with him against her father, as will appear later.
4- The love of the people and their rallying around him.
On the other hand, after the marriage of "Merab", "Michal", the younger daughter of Saul, loved David, and when Saul's men learned of it they told him, and he welcomed the matter greatly.
A snare: a trap and a net.

Michal's declaration of her love for David came in keeping with what Saul had previously prepared in his heart to be rid of him at the hands of the Philistines, so he offered David kinship by marriage and the wedding.

Saul's speech to David was not direct but through the men of his court, since it was not proper for the king to offer his daughter to David himself. Indeed the men went and spoke to David to encourage him toward the idea of becoming the king's son-in-law, the king who loved him and preferred him over the rest of the men. When the men spoke such kind words to David, he answered them that it was not easy for a man like him to become son-in-law to the daughter of the king of Israel, since he was a poor man and not one of the wealthy of the people.
Foreskins: the male genital part, uncircumcised.

The men carried everything David had said to Saul, and Saul seized the opportunity to be rid of David. He sent David a message through his men, saying that he did not care about money as a dowry for his daughter, but wanted David to bring a hundred foreskins of the Philistines as the dowry for Michal. Saul's purpose was that David would fight the Philistines and die in the war, and so he would be rid of him.

The king's men informed David of the king's request, and because David was courageous, the word pleased him and he made light of the task. He gathered his men, and before the time set by Saul for accomplishing this task had ended, David, trusting in God, was able to attack the Philistines and kill two hundred men, that is, twice the number Saul had asked for, and he brought their foreskins to Saul. This was the dowry of Michal, with which David married her.

After these events Saul became sure that God supported David in all his affairs, and his daughter Michal was also attached to David, so Saul's anger, jealousy and fear of David increased, and Saul's enmity toward David grew.

The princes of the Philistines began to go out and attack the people of God again and again, but each time they went out God gave victory to the people of God. David and his men were more successful and distinguished in these wars, so that the name of David was greatly loved and revered among all the people.
Although the Law provides that a bridegroom is exempt from war for a year (Deut 24:5), David gave up his right in order to defend his country and fight the Philistines.

We see through the events of this chapter how evil Saul's heart was and how all his schemes were to be rid of David, and we also see how God turned evil into good, and all things led to the exaltation of David's name among the people in preparation for his becoming king. This reminds us of what Joseph said to his brothers, that they meant evil against him, but God turned the evil and used it for the good and blessing of Joseph (Gen 50:20). So make your heart steadfast and leave it to God to deal with all the plots of evil around you, even if threats and plots surround you, for God is able to turn them to your good and to protect you in all your steps as long as you hold fast to His commandments. Saul's attempts to kill David

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: After Saul had been planning secretly within himself to be rid of "David", he could not keep the matter hidden within himself, especially after David's successive successes, and so he declared to his son Jonathan, and also to the officers of his army who were close to him, his desire to kill "David!"

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: But God, who protects those who trust in Him, put a wonderful love in Jonathan's heart toward David, so Jonathan hastened to tell David what Saul wanted to do and advised him to hide so as to be safe from his father and his men. Jonathan did not try to push David to flee altogether from the face of Saul his father, because he loved him and wanted the kingdom to benefit from him as a military commander; he had hope of calming his father toward him so that he would treat him kindly, but when he despaired of this, he encouraged him to flee, as will appear later.

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: Jonathan also told David that he would go with his father to one of the fields, where he would speak with him, trying to dissuade him from his intention to kill David, and Jonathan agreed to inform David of the result of his conversation with his father.

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: This conversation took place, of course, in one of the fields, as we understood from the previous verse. Jonathan began his words to Saul his father by saying that "David" had not sinned against Saul for even one day; on the contrary, all his works had been good in the eyes of the people and in your eyes too, for he risked his life and went to kill "Goliath", whom all the men feared, and so he was an instrument of God's salvation for His people. You yourself saw it and rejoiced over the man, so why do you commit today this great sin and sin against God and against your own reputation by killing this man without cause?

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave grace to Jonathan's words in the heart of his father Saul, and the king responded and swore to his son by the name of the living God that he would not kill David or do him harm.

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: Jonathan hastened to David's hiding place and told him the whole of the previous conversation with his father and how it ended, and he brought David with him to meet Saul. David was before Saul as before, beloved by him and in his service.

entries.section: (1) Saul's order to kill David and the success of Jonathan's intercession

paragraphs.text: When the Philistines again tried to attack the children of Israel, David and his men went out against them and defeated them, and they all fled from before him, and David sang his fifty-ninth psalm.

May you defend the oppressed if you have the opportunity, even if you bear some blame from people or lose anything. Put yourself in the place of the oppressed so that you feel for him and defend him, and know that God has defended you, who were oppressed and condemned to death because of the sin into which the devil made you fall, and He died for you and redeemed you... So from today take an interest in every oppressed person whom you can defend or to whom you can render a service.

entries.section: (2) New attempts to kill David and his escape from them

paragraphs.text: These two verses are the same scene that happened in (ch. 16:14), of the unclean spirit suddenly seizing Saul and his attempt to kill David (ch. 18:11), and David was able to escape.

entries.section: (2) New attempts to kill David and his escape from them

paragraphs.text: We find that Saul had returned to his evil nature and began again to plan to be rid of "David". He ordered some men to watch him all night and to kill him when the sun appeared, but some men loyal to David learned of the matter and informed "Michal", his wife, who in turn warned David to flee from his house that very night or he would be killed in the morning. Indeed David heeded the advice of his wife, who was able to smuggle him out through a window of the house. David began a journey of fleeing from place to place before the pursuits of Saul, and he had no fixed dwelling place until the death of Saul; in this he is a type of Christ, who had nowhere to lay His head.

entries.section: (2) New attempts to kill David and his escape from them

paragraphs.text: Teraphim: the image of an idol, or small figures that people kept to bring good luck. After Michal was assured of her husband's escape, she came up with a new trick: she placed in the place of David's bed an image the size of a man, put under its head a piece of goat's skin as a pillow, and covered it with a garment as a kind of disguise.

Michal's keeping of idol figures is a strange thing that shows her heart was not upright toward God. She certainly kept these figures without David's knowledge, and perhaps she wished that these figures would grant her offspring.

entries.section: (2) New attempts to kill David and his escape from them

paragraphs.text: Saul learned that "David" had not gone out in the morning as usual and that the men had not been able to kill him, so he sent his men to seek David that he might come down to him. As for Michal, in order to use up time and give her husband a greater chance to escape, she sent the men back to her father with the excuse that he was sick and could not leave his bed.

entries.section: (2) New attempts to kill David and his escape from them

paragraphs.text: Saul's anger grew very strong, so he sent his men again to David's house, commanding them to bring him even if he were very sick, that he might carry out his evil counsel of killing him. When the men broke into his house, they found in the bed nothing but the image and the goat's skin at its head.

entries.section: (2) New attempts to kill David and his escape from them

paragraphs.text: When the matter was uncovered, Saul reproached his daughter for deceiving him and smuggling out her husband, and she gave him an answer that would save her from his anger and revenge, namely that she had done so under David's pressure and his threat to kill her.

Believe in God, who is able to protect you however much the wicked try to harm you, for He gives you favor in the eyes of some of those around you and moves circumstances so that you escape from evil, and so the power of God appears, and you thank Him and live your life to glorify His holy name.

entries.section: (3) David's refuge with Samuel and Saul's continuing attempts

paragraphs.text: Naioth: located on the outskirts of Ramah, and Samuel made it the seat of a school of the prophets; perhaps David learned there at the hands of Samuel.

When David fled, leaving his house, he headed for Ramah and stayed where Samuel lived, and as soon as he found him he told him all that Saul had done to him and how he was planning to kill him. So Samuel took him to "Naioth" and settled him there.
How good it is for a person in his distress to take refuge in his father of confession, to hear the voice of God and to keep away from evil.

entries.section: (3) David's refuge with Samuel and Saul's continuing attempts

paragraphs.text: Prophesying: praising God.

Saul learned of David's hiding place with Samuel in "Naioth", so he sent some of his men to arrest him. But when these messengers arrived at "Naioth" they found the company of the prophets praising God, with Samuel the prophet leading them in it, and instead of arresting David a spiritual state took hold of them and the Holy Spirit moved them, so they joined the prophets in what they were doing and began to praise God themselves also. That is, the Holy Spirit came upon the messengers and changed them from a state of evil and vengeance against David to a calm spiritual thought, namely the praise of God.

entries.section: (3) David's refuge with Samuel and Saul's continuing attempts

paragraphs.text: Saul learned what had happened to his men whom he had sent, so he sent a second group to bring David, and the Spirit of God, the Holy, came upon them and they did as their predecessors had done; and he sent also a third group, and they too prophesied.

entries.section: (3) David's refuge with Samuel and Saul's continuing attempts

paragraphs.text: Sechu: located north of Ramah, at a distance of 5 km.

Saul's patience ran out after the many missions he had sent to bring David, so he decided to go himself. Before reaching Ramah he stopped at "Sechu", beside a well known and great well in it, and asked more carefully about the place of Samuel and David, and the people told him that they were in "Naioth."

entries.section: (3) David's refuge with Samuel and Saul's continuing attempts

paragraphs.text: Saul went on the road to Ramah and Naioth, but on the road, before he arrived, the Spirit of God came upon him, and he too began to praise God as he was on his way there.
We find that God was calling Saul to repentance and to casting out jealousy, envy and the attempt to kill David, and He warned him of this in many ways:
1- Jonathan's intercession and his attempt to turn him back from his hatred.
2- Michal's smuggling out of David and her support for him.
3- The prophesying of Saul's messengers, and then his own prophesying when he tried to arrest him at Naioth.
4- The attack of the Philistines on the land of the Jews while he was pursuing David, so that he was forced to leave him and go to fight them (ch. 23:27).
5- His falling twice into David's hand, but David forgave him and let him go (ch. 24, ch. 26).

entries.section: (3) David's refuge with Samuel and Saul's continuing attempts

paragraphs.text: When Saul arrived at "Naioth", the Spirit of the Lord worked in him even more, so he humbled himself and took off all the garments of the king and also his military dress, and remained in his undergarments, and he went on praising God all day and night, until he fell and lay prostrate from exhaustion. The people marveled and said, after they had seen him... Is Saul also among the prophets?! This last saying, however, became a proverb used in mockery of a person who may do a great deed that people do not expect of him.

We note that this is the second time Saul prophesied, for he prophesied on a previous occasion after he was anointed king (ch. 10:10). Thus God turned Saul's heart to calm concerning David, and he began to prophesy the word of God, but because of Saul's persistence in pride he returned again to hating David and trying to kill him.

It is mentioned in (ch. 15:35) that Samuel would not come again to see Saul, yet he saw him here. If we look closely we find that Saul did not come to take counsel from Samuel, and that is what Samuel meant, that he would not meet Saul again in order to counsel him. What happened this time is that Saul came to search for David and saw Samuel, but not with the purpose of benefiting from Samuel.
God prevented Saul from killing David as a protection for David and to keep Saul from falling into sin, so He turned his heart to prophesying instead of evil and killing.

May you pay attention to God's attempts to keep you from evil and seize these opportunities for repentance, for they are love from God, who seeks your repentance, because if you do not do this you are exposed to destruction in the end, as happened with Saul. Jonathan's covenant with David and his defense of him before Saul

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: Although David had seen Saul among the prophets praising and glorifying God, he was not reassured about him and preferred to flee, because he knew what was in Saul's heart. So he went down from Naioth, near Ramah, to Ramah, where he met Jonathan, and he opened his heart to him and asked him in protest, What have I done to your father, and why is he angry with me, and what is my crime for which he seeks my death?!

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: Jonathan, the loving one, answered, also in protest, that this would never happen, and to reassure David's heart he told him that his father Saul told him all his affairs and thoughts, however small, so if he wanted to kill him he would surely tell him.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: As the Lord lives and as your soul lives: an expression of an oath for emphasis.

David confirmed his words to Jonathan with an oath so that he would believe him, that his father was determined to kill him and that only one step separated him from death. But Saul also knew the extent of Jonathan's love and friendship for David, and therefore he decided to hide this particular matter from him so that his heart would not grieve, and also so that he would not prevent him from killing David.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: Jonathan wanted to express his love and loyalty to David and also to reassure his heart, so he said to him, Whatever you ask of me, I will do it, and I promise you this.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: When Jonathan told David that he would carry out everything David asked of him, "David" indeed began to ask Jonathan to help him in his plan. The Jews celebrated the new moons as spiritual feasts (Num 28:11-15), offering sacrifices and making feasts, and of course the king prepared a monthly feast from which all his commanders and men ate, David among them. So David asked Jonathan to hide for three days in one of the fields and not to attend his father's feast.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: If the king asked about David and his empty place, Jonathan was to answer that he had permitted him to go to his father's house in the village of Bethlehem to offer with his family the sacrifice that his people were accustomed to offer every year; and indeed it was among the customs of the Jewish clans to offer memorial offerings at the new moons.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: If your father's answer is agreement and approval, this will be a sign of peace and that he does not harbor evil against me; but if he becomes agitated and angry and his wrath grows fierce, know that your father intended evil against me, that is, my death.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: You have brought your servant into a covenant with you: David's thanks for the humility of Jonathan, the king's son, and his entering into a covenant with his servant David; and this is also humility on David's part, because he forgot that he was the king and remembered only that he was Jonathan's servant. In this, Jonathan, you will have done me a great kindness, since you will have saved innocent blood from your father's hand, especially as you are my friend and the Lord is witness to the covenant of our friendship. But if you see me as guilty or deserving of death, then kill me yourself rather than hand me over to your father.

entries.section: (1) David tells Jonathan frankly what is in Saul's heart

paragraphs.text: Again Jonathan answers David, saying, "Far be it from you," which means that I forbid you to say this about yourself, that you are a doer of evil. But my friend, do you think that if I knew that a danger threatened you from my father, I would hide it from you?!?.! That is, he reassured him that he would not die.

If you sense evil in some place, or a sin into which you will fall if you go to that place or meet certain people, flee and keep away so that you do not fall into sin; this is wisdom and strength, not weakness, for what matters is that you keep yourself in purity and peace.

David asked Jonathan again, But who will tell me and inform me if Saul's answer carries evil? But before Jonathan answered him with anything, he asked him to go out together outside the city to the field, meaning to an empty place.
O Lord God of Israel: an oath in the form of a prayer.

Jonathan began his words to David by addressing God, that is, to call God as witness to the truth of his words in order to reassure David, which is a style resembling an oath. The content of the words was that tomorrow, during the king's feast at the new moon, if he learned that Saul loved David and wished him good, he would tell him so; but if he did not tell him, may God do to Jonathan every evil, "may He do so and more also". But if he sensed that his father was harboring evil toward him and truly wanted to kill him, he would also tell him and let him flee from his presence. He prayed that the Lord would be with David and give him victory, as He had been with his father in the early days and gave him victory over his enemies.

After Jonathan pledged to tell David what was in Saul's heart and promised to help him flee in the case of his father's anger, he now asks a covenant from his friend "David": that when God gives him the kingdom and he becomes a man of influence, he should not only spare Jonathan and promise not to kill him, but should also care for all of Jonathan's offspring and house, in the event that he alone holds power after God has destroyed all his enemies.
Let the Lord require it: it means, let the Lord take vengeance.
Jonathan repeated his reassuring words to David, giving him a covenant of peace and safety, and he even asked, in the form of a prayer, that God take vengeance on all of David's enemies.

Jonathan also made "David" swear by their love that he would keep his promise toward Jonathan and the people of his house, and David did this. As for the expression "he loved him as he loved his own soul", some see that it describes Jonathan's feelings and others see that it describes David's feelings toward Jonathan; combining the two opinions is better, since the two men loved each other intensely, as the following events will reveal.

It is noted that Jonathan "renewed" the covenant with David, because it was known in that time that when the rule came to a new king who was not of the offspring of the old king, the first thing the new king would do was to get rid of all the rest of the family of the former king.
It is noted here Jonathan's faith that God was with David and that he would become king after his father; therefore he asked him to care for his offspring after him.

How beautiful are the covenants of love between people... between every husband and wife, or two brothers, or two friends, that each offers love to the other, for this encourages the giving of love and its steadfastness. Love is what shatters the plots of the devil and the problems he invents every day, so that each one finds an excuse for the other and forgives him, and even has compassion on him and supports him.

entries.section: (3) The plan that Jonathan made for David

paragraphs.text: Tomorrow is the new moon: that is, the king's feast at the beginning of the month.

The stone of parting: a place and a sign, meaning the place where we part and which both of us know. Jonathan proposed to David that he be absent from his father's table on the first two days of the month, the two days on which Saul gives the feast to his men, and of course everyone, Saul included, would notice David's absence. On the third day you will come to this place from which we shall now part, and its sign is this stone.

entries.section: (3) The plan that Jonathan made for David

paragraphs.text: Suddenly: you come, lad, toward Jonathan to pick up the arrows.

I will go out as if strolling and hunting some animals, and I will shoot three arrows with my bow, as if I wanted to hit a target, and then I will send the lad who follows me to pick them up. I will use with him a way of speaking like a code for you to understand, David. If I say to the lad in a voice that you hear, Here are the arrows, they are near, come and take them, you will understand that matters are well and nothing will harm you, so come out of your hiding place. And he confirmed his words with an oath, As the Lord lives, that he would do what he said.

entries.section: (3) The plan that Jonathan made for David

paragraphs.text: But if I say to the lad that the arrows have gone far ahead of you, so go away to pick them up and bring them, this means that you, David, are in danger and you must flee, and the Lord sends you on your way and gives you His peace.

entries.section: (3) The plan that Jonathan made for David

paragraphs.text: Jonathan wanted to reassure the heart of "David", so he made the Lord a witness to his words that he would not betray him, and that the covenant he had made on himself was an everlasting covenant.

Take care to rescue everyone who is in distress, show him love and help him as far as you are able; then you will receive blessings from God and He will rescue you from every distress, and you will receive mercy on the last day.

The first of the month came and David carried out Jonathan's plan and was absent from the king's table, at which the king sat in his usual place, his face toward the entrance of the hall and his back toward the wall at the head of the table, and Abner, the commander of his army, also sat there, while Jonathan stood, perhaps to welcome the men as they entered, and David did not attend the feast.

On the first day Saul noticed David's absence but did not comment on anything; rather, he made an excuse for him and said to himself, Perhaps David did not come because of some unexpected excuse, or perhaps he was not physically clean (and this is one of the conditions for approaching and eating of the sacrifice offered to God) (Lev 7:19-21).

On the second day of the feast David's place remained empty, so Saul asked his son Jonathan about the secret of David's absence from the feast on the two days. Saul's contempt for David appears, for he did not mention him by name but said "the son of Jesse." His question was not out of love for him but to seize an opportunity to kill him.
Let me get away: allow me to be absent from the feast and go to Bethlehem.

Jonathan answered his father with the same words he had agreed with David to say (vv. 5, 6), that he went to Bethlehem, where his father offers a sacrifice for the whole clan, and that he had permitted him to go ......

Jonathan's answer kindled anger and great wrath in Saul's heart, and he could not hide his wrath but burst out, cursing his son Jonathan and describing him as disobedient and rebellious. As an insult he attributed these qualities to his mother, as if he had inherited them from her, and he told him that in choosing David as a close friend he had chosen for himself one who would be the cause of shame to him and to his whole family.

The shame of your mother's nakedness: Saul thinks that if he does not kill David, David will become king, and one of the characteristics of wicked kings is that they take the wives of the former king and make them concubines and lie with them.

Saul continued rebuking Jonathan and said that as long as "David" lived he would be the coming king, and therefore you will not inherit the kingship and the rule, and the kingdom will be lost from our family, and there is no solution for us except that you bring "David" here so that he meets his certain fate, which is death.

Thus anger and the desire for possession blind a person to the divine will, as if Saul were able by his schemes to change God's purpose and arrangement. So do not let your anger rule you, and do not make a decision while you are angry, for the wrath of man does not work the righteousness of God.

Jonathan remained faithful to his covenant of friendship and loyalty to his friend David; his father's anger did not frighten him, but he continued to defend his friend, explaining that he had done nothing wrong that he should die.
Hurled the spear: that is, turned the face of the spear toward him.

When Saul heard Jonathan's defense of David, he was angered all the more, and this time he did not use words but took the spear and tried to aim it at Jonathan to kill him, and Jonathan knew and became certain that his father's intention was to kill David and be rid of him.

Therefore Jonathan rose in anger from his father and left the place of the feast without eating anything from it, and he grieved greatly for his friend David because of the troubles that awaited him from his father, and he was also angry with his father because of his heart full of evil.

entries.section: (5) The meeting of David and Jonathan and then their parting

paragraphs.text: On the morning of the third day of the month, Jonathan went out to the field agreed upon with David, with his arrows and his bow and a young lad to collect the arrows. He ordered the lad with him to start running, but Jonathan shot his arrow with force, and the arrow passed beyond the boy and fell farther than he. Perhaps he took a young lad so that he would not understand the plan agreed between him and David, who was in hiding.

entries.section: (5) The meeting of David and Jonathan and then their parting

paragraphs.text: Jonathan called to the boy in a loud voice so that David would hear that the arrow had gone farther than the boy, and he spoke the same words that he had agreed with David (v. 22), and then ordered the boy to go back with the arrow and bring it to him. It is noted in Jonathan's words to the lad that he gave him three commands, "Make speed, hasten, do not stay", all of which are words directed to David so that he would understand from them what he must do, that is, hasten to flee from the face of Saul, who wanted to kill him.

entries.section: (5) The meeting of David and Jonathan and then their parting

paragraphs.text: Of course the lad understood nothing of all these words, which were meant for David. Then Jonathan gave the lad his bow and arrows and ordered him to go back, so that he could meet his friend David alone.

entries.section: (5) The meeting of David and Jonathan and then their parting

paragraphs.text: David came out from the place where he was hiding and went toward Jonathan his friend and bowed before him three times, in acknowledgment of Jonathan's merit in preserving his life, and out of David's respect for Jonathan because he was the crown prince, completely forgetting that he himself was anointed by God as king. This shows his great humility and that he did not exploit his strong friendship with Jonathan. Then each embraced his friend and wept, and David wept even more than Jonathan, perhaps because his circumstances were harder than his friend's, since from now on he had to flee and hide from Saul's violence.

entries.section: (5) The meeting of David and Jonathan and then their parting

paragraphs.text: After a little while Jonathan spoke and told David that he must flee and go far away, and he prayed that God's safety would accompany him. He reminded him of all that they had said and sworn before God, that He is the witness of what passed between them, and how each had given a covenant of peace to his friend and to all his offspring after him. After these events Jonathan returned to the city, while David began his journey of flight.

Love urges you to warn others of the dangers that may assail them so that they may guard against them, especially the wars of Satan and everything that takes them away from God. If they listen to you, you have won their souls, and if they do not listen, you continue to pray for them until God guides them, but you must warn them, for you are responsible before God for this.
David's flight to "Nob" and "Gath"

Nob: located northeast of Jerusalem and 8 km from Gibeah, the town of Saul. It was counted as a city of the priests because the tabernacle of meeting was moved to it after the destruction of Shiloh, although it was not among the priestly cities that Joshua assigned (Josh 21). The First Book of Samuel. The town of "Nob" was the town to which the tabernacle of meeting was moved after it had been for a time in the town of "Shiloh", and consequently the high priest "Ahimelech the son of Ahitub", the son of "Eli", also moved to it; he was the same as "Ahijah the son of Ahitub" or his brother (1 Sam 14:3, 18), and "Abiathar" the priest, his son, helped him in the service (1 Chr 15:11, Mk 2:26). When Ahimelech saw David he was amazed and afraid at his unexpected visit, and because he was alone and without a retinue of men, as ought to have been the case since he was a military commander, and he asked him the reason for his sudden visit and his coming alone ...

When the Book of Chronicles or the Gospel of Mark mentions that David met Abiathar the high priest at Nob, what is meant is that he was the son of Ahimelech, for he was with him and would become high priest after him. Christ did not say that Abiathar was the one who gave David the bread, but said "in the days of Abiathar."
David's coming to Nob was to ask for the prayers of Ahimelech and his son Abiathar, in addition to asking them for food and a weapon, as will appear in the following verses.

David answered Ahimelech with a lie, for he feared to inform him of Saul's pursuit of him and his seeking to kill him (and of course this was a point of human weakness into which David ought not to have fallen, but God shows us pictures of human weakness so that we also may learn from them). David told him that he was sent by the king on a secret mission that he could not disclose, as the king's command, and he answered him about the young men that he had appointed for them places to hide here and there. God forgave David his lie and his not turning to Him in prayer or asking Samuel, because he always returns to Him quickly in repentance and does not persist in his sins like Saul, for indeed his heart is like the heart of God.
What is there under your hand?! With this question David expressed his need for food, and then asked Ahimelech for five loaves for himself and the young men, or anything available and at hand to eat.
Common bread: that is, ordinary bread that it is lawful for any person to eat.
Holy bread: what is meant is the showbread of the table of the presence, which none but the priests eat.

Ahimelech answered David that he had no ready bread that the men could eat, but the bread available and present at the moment was the showbread, which none but the priests eat. But as a kind of flexibility, to save the situation and to make David's and the king's mission succeed, "Ahimelech" indicated that David could take the bread and eat it with the young men if they were physically clean and had not touched their wives.

Today also it will be sanctified in the vessel: the new bread placed in the vessel on the table of the showbread is sanctified by being placed in it; that is, after my taking the common bread, holy bread remains in the tabernacle of meeting. Common in a way: the bread had been taken off the table, and therefore in a case of great need such as David's it was possible for them to eat it, lest he and his men faint on the way, on condition of their cleanness.

David assured Ahimelech the priest that he and his men were clean and had not touched women for two days, since they left "Gibeah of Saul", and that the young men's vessels also were clean, untouched by anything unclean, and therefore the matter became lawful, with no evil in it.
After "David" had reassured "Ahimelech" the priest, he took the bread from him, which was the old bread that the priest had taken off the table and replaced with new bread.

Among the beautiful things David did was that the first place he decided to take refuge in was the house of the Lord and the first person he spoke with was the priest. Perhaps we too should do this, so that the Church is the first place we turn to, for God's blessing in His house is what supports you in all the steps of your life, gives you favor in the eyes of all whom you meet and guides you to good conduct.

This verse mentions a man who would have a role in the later events (ch. 22). This man worked for Saul as chief of his herdsmen, and it happened that he was present in the tabernacle of meeting, since a vow was upon him or a necessity called him to be there, which is what the inspired text expressed by the phrase "detained." We know from his name that his origin was Edomite, that is, of the offspring of Esau, and he had become a Jew, so he was one of Saul's followers. The First Book of Samuel

"David" hastened to make a second request of Ahimelech the priest, which was that he supply him with any weapon, and he gave his excuse for not carrying his weapon, namely his haste in leaving according to the king's command, which made him forget his weapon.

Ahimelech answered David that he had no weapon except the sword of Goliath the Philistine whom he had killed before. The people had kept this sword in the tabernacle of meeting as a memorial of God's work with them, and Ahimelech had hidden it in a corner of the tent and placed before it the "ephod", which is one of the priests' garments and has been spoken of often before. David took the sword and said that there was none like it, for two reasons:
1- Because it was well made, since this mighty man Goliath used it.
2- Because it reminds him of God's work and His protection of him from Goliath, so he always remembers God's support of him when he has this sword with him.

We note that when David killed Goliath, which was the greatest offering a person could offer to God at that time because it was in place of his life, God blessed him and afterward gave him the sword of Goliath to fight with, and preserved him in all of Saul's pursuits of him. So when a person gives something to God, God blesses him and gives him more and more.

entries.section: (2) David's flight to "Gath" and his feigning madness

paragraphs.text: We have already pointed out that "Gath" is one of the five great cities of the Philistines, and its king was Achish. "David" went to it in an unexpected step, but he went to it as a political refugee, to use the expression we use now. David's thinking was that Gath was the place where Saul would not search or attack that great city for the sake of David. It was an unusual courage on David's part to flee to Gath, because he was exposed to death there, but he may have said to himself that Achish would receive him out of spite toward Saul, because he was an enemy of Saul, and if he saw that David had left Saul and joined him, he would gain a hero with whom to fight Saul; yet fear remained within him that Achish might arrest him and kill him.

entries.section: (2) David's flight to "Gath" and his feigning madness

paragraphs.text: We understand from the text that Achish accepted David to take refuge in his city, or at least paid no attention to his presence, but the leaders of his people and his counselors did not like that, so they spoke to Achish, reminding him that David was the man who had brought shame upon the Philistines by killing Goliath, and that he was the hero of Israel for whom the women chanted.

entries.section: (2) David's flight to "Gath" and his feigning madness

paragraphs.text: These words reached "David", and he feared greatly that "Achish" would be influenced by his aides and their words and would kill him, and therefore he came up with a new idea, which was to feign madness and insanity. He began to let his spittle run down his beard and to scratch with his nails on the doors like madmen.

We note that to save his life David resorted to human means and did not turn to God, who is able to save him from evil. He began first by lying to the priest, then taking refuge in the cities of the enemies without seeking God's opinion, and with his human thinking he also pretended madness to save his life, forgetting what he had said earlier to Goliath, that his strength was in the name of the Lord of hosts!! ... My beloved brother, do not resort to lying at times of danger or pressure on you, but turn to God and leave the arrangement to Him. Stand firm in your faith even if thought fights you that matters will become complicated, for God is able to solve all your problems if you trust in Him.

entries.section: (2) David's flight to "Gath" and his feigning madness

paragraphs.text: The purpose of the men in speaking with "Achish" was to bring David to him so that he would try him and pass the sentence of death on him, but here we see God's work to protect "David", for He put it in the heart of "Achish" that David had become a madman, so how could he bring him into his council or into his house; he rebuked this conduct in himself before his men and indeed refused to do anything with David.

David was praying in all these situations, and he prayed Psalm "34"; for this reason God saved him despite his human weakness in lying, because he was a righteous man and wronged, and God defends His weak children who take refuge in Him.
The men rally around David and Saul kills the priests

entries.section: (1) David goes to Adullam and then to Mizpeh of Moab

paragraphs.text: David left Nob and Gath and headed to his own country, Adullam, located 12 miles southwest of Bethlehem in the land of Judah. When his brothers and all his father's relatives heard, they went to him, and with them also went all the men who were distressed by Saul or who were suffering financial hardship and could not pay. The number of those gathered around him was about 400 men, whose motives differed: his family feared Saul, who might take revenge on them out of spite toward David, while the rest of the men were driven by distress to follow David, since they saw in him a deliverer from Saul's injustice and their hard circumstances, especially as poverty had increased among the children of Israel because of the repeated attacks of the Philistines and their plundering of the people. By David's competence as a leader he was able to turn them into a fighting army that he led himself. We see here the benefit of the Philistines' uprising against David in Gath, that he was compelled to leave it and return to his country and be subject to God and under His protection, and God blessed him with the rallying of 400 men around him, so that he became a great force; and at Adullam he chanted Psalm (57). David here is a type of Christ, for the weary and distressed gathered around him as sinners and tax collectors came to Christ, and He took away their sins and they became a great army, which is the flock of Christ that enters the Kingdom. As for Saul, who reigned with apparent power over the kingdom, he is a type of Satan, who reigns over the world, but his end is destruction, as Saul was killed in the battle with the Philistines (ch. 31).

entries.section: (1) David goes to Adullam and then to Mizpeh of Moab

paragraphs.text: David continued his flight with his men and his family. He left the land of Judah and crossed the Jordan to its east, where the land of the Moabites is, and met their king in his town "Mizpeh of Moab" and asked him to let his father and mother stay in this town to protect them from Saul's violence, until he could work out his affairs and know what God wanted for him in the coming days; and indeed he left them as guests of the king of Moab, while he hid in one of the fortified places in the lands of the Moabites. David took refuge in Moab because one of his grandmothers, Ruth, was a Moabite (Ruth 4:17), so there was a bond of kinship between him and Moab. In addition there was enmity between Saul and Moab, since Saul had fought them and defeated them (ch. 14:47).

entries.section: (1) David goes to Adullam and then to Mizpeh of Moab

paragraphs.text: Gad the prophet: mentioned in the incident of the numbering of the people (2 Sam 24:11-15) and in (2 Chr 29:

25) in the arrangement of the musical service. Some think that he was one of the disciples of Samuel the prophet in the school of the prophets, and that Samuel charged Gad to follow David because he knew that he was the man of God and the true king. God visited "David" through one of His prophets, "Gad the prophet" or the seer, as the prophets used to be called anciently, and "Gad" informed David that he must leave the stronghold, which was one of the strongholds of Moab, and return to the land of Judah. David obeyed the message and came to a place in the land of Judah called "the forest of Hereth", a wooded region southwest of Bethlehem.

Listen to the voice of God even if it is contrary to what you are thinking, for God arranges all things for the salvation of your soul, and accept God's guidance in humility. David was a prophet, yet he accepted the guidance of Gad the prophet, and in this God leads you and protects you and no one can harm you.

The fame of David and his men spread, since their number was large and noticeable, and the matter reached Saul the king, who gathered with his men and servants in his town Gibeah, and under the shade of the tamarisk tree he addressed them, filled with wrath and envy. He said to them, You are of the tribe of Benjamin and of the sons of my clan, and it is I who gave you vineyards and fields and made you captains of thousands over all the people and captains of hundreds, so has David the son of Jesse given you anything in return?! Of course Saul's words to his men were meant to win them to himself and to incite them against David, that he was poor, and that even if he became king Saul and his men expected that he would honor the men of his tribe of Judah and not the men of Benjamin.

Saul's weakness appears from this, because he relied on himself in pride and not on God, so he went seeking support from his tribe against David. As for Moses, who relied on God, his disciple Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim while Moses was from the tribe of Levi, and Moses did not set up his sons as leaders. And David also, when he became king, had a wide heart, and received Abner the commander of Saul's army, and Amasa and others ...
You have conspired against me: you have plotted against me.

Saul continues his speech in order to win the sympathy of his men, saying to them, Why then did you not rally around me, and why have you plotted against me, and I find no one who pities me or sympathizes with me, when my son (Jonathan) has gone and allied himself with my enemy "David", and they have set up a plan against me to kill me and an ambush for my destruction, and none of you told me of the agreement made between them. Of course Saul's words were a lie by which he wanted to incite the men against David in order to kill him, and to arouse pity for himself over the alleged plot. All this confirms Saul's weakness, for since he had departed from God he went on stirring people up against David and feeling that he was wronged and neglected by his clan, and the truth is that his heart was empty of God, and therefore he suffered from smallness of soul.

Doeg the Edomite was the man who was in the tabernacle of meeting when "David" met "Ahimelech" the priest (ch. 21:7), and he was the one who began to answer Saul here in order to declare his allegiance to him and his hostility to David. He began to relate to him the details of David's meeting with Ahimelech and how Ahimelech gave David bread and also the sword of Goliath, and he added that Ahimelech inquired of the Lord for him, in order to show Ahimelech's sympathy with David and to stir up Saul against Ahimelech. Doeg and his work and lineage were spoken of before in (ch. 21).

Do not seize opportunities to win the love of others by condemnation and by stirring people up against one another, for in this you are an agent of Satan, spreading evil and disputes among people and challenging God, so you lose His mercy and divine punishment awaits you.

entries.section: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: After the denunciation of "Doeg", Saul was very greatly enraged, so he sent his servants with a message to bring Ahimelech the priest and all the priests with him from "Nob", the city of the priests and the tabernacle of meeting at that time. When they came before Saul, Saul began to speak in a manner that showed contempt for Ahimelech, for he did not mention his name but called him by his father's name, in a tone of wrath and threat of evil, and Ahimelech answered him in humility, "Here I am, my lord."

entries.section: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Saul spoke directly to Ahimelech and the priests, charging them with conspiracy and with helping David against the king by giving him bread and the sword and praying for him to remain hidden and lying in wait for the king. Of course Ahimelech meant no evil against the king when he helped David, for David was fleeing from the king and not lurking for him or wanting to do the king any harm.

entries.section: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Ahimelech began to speak in his own defense in a logical and sober manner, and we can summarize his defense in two main points:

A- The character of David: he described him as a valiant man of courage with none like him among the people, and also as the king's son-in-law, his confidant, who always has a place at the king's table, that is, a person far removed from any suspicion.
B- His lack of knowledge: this is Ahimelech's second defense, that he knew nothing of the quarrel between David and Saul, or David's flight, or David's conspiring against the king.
In all this Ahimelech was telling the truth, and he asked Saul not to charge him or his family of priests with any of these false accusations.

entries.section: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The runners (guards): soldiers trained for swift movement, from whom came the royal guard that stood before Saul.

Despite Ahimelech's strong defense of himself and his truthfulness in all that he said, Saul's wrath and anger blinded him, as if he had heard nothing, and with injustice and tyranny in his opinion he pronounced the sentence of death on Ahimelech and all the priests, and asked his men standing with him to carry out his unjust sentence, justifying his sentence by the priests' conspiracy with David and their concealing the truth. But the men could not do this abominable deed and stain their hands with the blood of the priests of God Most High, who were honored by all the people, whom God commanded to be honored, who offered the sacrifices, interpreted the laws and led the people even in wars. It appears from this that the runners were more righteous than the king, respecting the priesthood and refusing injustice.

entries.section: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The ephod: white linen cloth that was among the priests' garments.

Saul noticed the disobedience of his special guard and their refusal to kill the priests, and this did not turn him from what his heart was stirred up with, so he looked to "Doeg the Edomite" and asked him to carry out the same order. This wicked man, who did not belong to the people of God at all but was of the offspring of "Esau", responded, and indeed he killed 85 priests wearing the linen ephod of the priests.

entries.section: (3) Saul kills the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The matter went beyond every limit, for this wicked man also went to "Nob", the city of the priests and the present place of the tabernacle of meeting, and killed all the remaining priests with their wives and innocent children, and even the animals did not escape from this hideous massacre. Saul here, because he was a follower of Satan, ruins himself, because he ruins a city that belongs to him and not a city belonging to the enemies, just as the wicked person ruins his own senses and thoughts by himself instead of resisting Satan.

Anger is blind and leads a person to the worst sins. Examine yourself and do not make a decision in your anger, but flee from anger and control yourself and your nerves and ask God for calm, lest you commit a mistake that is hard to mend.

entries.section: (4) The flight and escape of Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech

paragraphs.text: Abiathar the son of Ahimelech did not go with the priests to meet Saul, but remained at Nob inside the tabernacle to complete the service, and this was the reason for his escape and not being killed. After he saw all that had happened, he left "Nob" and fled to "David", who was also fleeing from the face of Saul, and when he found David he told him all the evil that Saul had done to the priests and how he had shed innocent blood.

entries.section: (4) The flight and escape of Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech

paragraphs.text: David spoke with "Abiathar" the fugitive priest and told him that when he saw "Doeg the Edomite" at Nob, as he took the bread from his father Ahimelech, he expected that this wicked Edomite would be a troublemaker and would report to Saul what he had seen and add to it to kindle his wrath. David offered Abiathar an apology and expressed sorrow that he was the cause behind all these sad events, and this shows his humility.

entries.section: (4) The flight and escape of Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech

paragraphs.text: David then asked Abiathar to stay with him, and of course this was what the man expected from David, and to reassure the man David gave him a covenant and a promise of protection, saying to him that whoever seeks to kill you seeks to kill me, the intended meaning being that David would never allow this. Thus there joined David the last priest remaining from Saul's dreadful crime, and Abiathar remained a priest with David all the days of his life. David's welcome of Abiathar shows his heart that was wide for all the persecuted, and God blessed him, as he alone came to have a priest who inquired of God. Through this evil that Saul did, God's word was fulfilled in the destruction of the house of Eli the priest because of his leniency with his two sons (ch. 2:31-36).

In proportion to Saul's evil was David's nobility of character, so he welcomed Abiathar to live with him and protected him. Be loving and helpful to others however wicked and selfish and abusive of others those around you may be, for you love people for the sake of God, who loved you and redeemed you and counts as great every love you offer to others and rewards you for it. David fights the Philistines, and Saul pursues David

entries.section: (1) David delivers Keilah from the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Threshing floors: barns, that is, storehouses of wheat or barley.

Keilah: a town located in the territory of the tribe of Judah near the border of the Philistines, three miles from the cave of Adullam and eight and a half miles northwest of Hebron (present-day Hebron.) Some men came to "David's" place and told him that the Philistines had raided the Jewish town of "Keilah" to plunder the wheat or barley harvest that the people of Keilah had stored. It is noted that they did not go to Saul, who had turned away from protecting the people and whose first concern was to kill "David."
The Philistines' attack on the Jewish land was because of:
1- God's forsaking of Saul, so that he became weak and unable to protect his country.
2- Saul was occupied with resisting David and pursuing him rather than protecting his people, so that he ruined some of his own country, such as Nob (ch. 22).
3- Saul's loss of his great military commander David.

entries.section: (1) David delivers Keilah from the Philistines

paragraphs.text: David did not rush or take the initiative to go up to war and deliver "Keilah", but began by asking God, perhaps by sending a messenger to Samuel or through Abiathar the priest, who carried with him the Urim and Thummim, and the Lord's answer to him was that he should go to war to deliver "Keilah." Thus David learned not to move or do anything except after asking God, so as not to err as he had erred when he went to Gath. Perhaps he understood here why God, through the guidance of Gad the prophet, had brought him back to the territory of the tribe of Judah: it was to use him in rescuing Keilah and as a preparation for his reigning over all the children of Israel.

entries.section: (1) David delivers Keilah from the Philistines

paragraphs.text: However, David's men who accompanied him were very afraid to go up to war, and said to him, We are now in the land of Judah, that is, inside the kingdom, and yet we are very afraid, so how can we go up and fight an army of the Philistines?

entries.section: (1) David delivers Keilah from the Philistines

paragraphs.text: David went again to ask God in order to reassure his frightened men, and God's command to him was as clear as the first time, that he should go to Keilah to deliver it, and God declared to him that He would be with him and would deliver the Philistines into his hands, that is, give him victory over them.

entries.section: (1) David delivers Keilah from the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Indeed David went and defeated the Philistines and took their cattle and delivered the people of Keilah from their injustice and theft; David needed this victory greatly in order to raise his morale and the morale of his men and to feel that the Lord was with him and had not left him.

Be careful to ask God and seek His blessing before any work you undertake, and He will lead your life and you will dwell in reassurance, and do not be disturbed if distresses meet you, for He makes you overcome them and succeed in everything.

This verse is an explanatory introduction to what comes after it, and it tells us that when Abiathar fled from "Nob" he took his ephod with him, and the ephod of the high priest had on it the breastplate and the two stones, the Urim and Thummim, which are used to know God's opinion when He is asked.

Saul learned the news of David's victory over the Philistines and his dwelling in "Keilah", and Saul considered that this was his great opportunity, since David had left the wilderness and the caves and shut himself up in a city with walls and gates, as if he had entered the trap himself. Saul set it in his heart to attack David at Keilah and called all the men of war from all the people to attack David there.

We see here Saul's evil. It was his responsibility to defend Keilah and deliver it from the Philistines, but he was negligent, so David made up for his deficiency and defended it and rescued it from the Philistines, and Saul did not thank him for that; on the contrary, he considered it an opportunity to arrest David and kill him. Saul's saying that God "has delivered him into my hand" means that God left him to fall into my hand, and this is a mistaken view, the exact opposite of the truth, for God was with David and was protecting him, so he defeated the Philistines and delivered Keilah, but because of his evil Saul sees matters in an inverted way, and everyone who departs from God loses wisdom and discernment and sees matters in an inverted way.

David learned of Saul's affair, and how he had prepared and summoned the men to go out to kill him, so he asked Abiathar the priest to bring the ephod; what is meant by bringing the ephod is that the high priest puts it on, with the Urim and Thummim stones upon it, in order to ask the Lord about some matter.
David stood before God and facing the new high priest Abiathar and began to ask God two questions:
1- Will Saul indeed come to Keilah and storm it in order to kill me?!
2- Will the people of Keilah betray me and deliver me into Saul's hand?
The Lord's answer was yes concerning Saul's coming down to Keilah.
David repeated his second question again, and the Lord's answer also was that the people of Keilah would hand him over to Saul and would not defend him.

Although David had rescued the people of Keilah from the evil of the Philistines, he learned from God that they would betray him and hand him over to Saul. So, beloved, do not put your hope in a human being and do not expect the reward of kindness from them, but conduct all your dealings with God, and you will always gain and He will not forsake you.

After David listened to the voice of God, he took his men, whose number had increased to 600 men after being 400 (ch. 22:1-2), and left Keilah for the wilderness again, and they went wherever God guided them and not to a fixed place. Saul learned of the matter again and of David's leaving Keilah, so he too gave up going out to pursue him. God prevented David from remaining in Keilah and fighting Saul for the following reasons:
1- Lest, after he defeated the Philistines, he think that it would be easy to defeat Saul, and so become proud and forget that God is the source of his strength.
2- So that he would not fight his people, over whom he would soon be king, and become hostile to them when they were his own kin.

entries.section: (3) Jonathan meets David and renews the covenant with him

paragraphs.text: The wilderness of Ziph: a place very high above the sea, about 6 km south of the city of Hebron.

David fled to the desert and took refuge in some abandoned fortresses or natural mountain caves, and Saul tried repeatedly to pursue him, but God did not allow him to be harmed. David learned that Saul was seeking him, so he sometimes took refuge in an area where trees were dense, which was called the forest (Horesh).

entries.section: (3) Jonathan meets David and renews the covenant with him

paragraphs.text: Jonathan, the friend nearest to David's heart, longed for him, so he went to him in the forest and encouraged him with kind words and advised him to trust in God, who strengthens him.

It is noted that Jonathan's love for David is what drove him to seek him out, although this posed a danger to him, for if his father Saul learned of it he might kill him, since he would consider him a supporter of his enemy.

In the time of the crises that surround people, and begin by encouraging them and strengthening them and drawing their attention to God, the refuge, the strong fortress and the comforter in distresses, and God will help you and guide you as He guided Jonathan to David's place.

entries.section: (3) Jonathan meets David and renews the covenant with him

paragraphs.text: In confident words Jonathan completed his encouragement of David, and with the eye of faith he told him that whatever his father did he would not harm David, and that Saul himself knew this for certain and also knew that David would rule Israel after him. In a humble tone Jonathan said that he would not forsake David but would be his second man, his helper, which is the heavenly expression for "his right arm", in managing the affairs of the kingdom on whose throne God would seat him.

entries.section: (3) Jonathan meets David and renews the covenant with him

paragraphs.text: The two men repeated what they had done before in (ch. 20), making a covenant of friendship and love before God, and Jonathan returned to his place while David remained in the forest.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: The hill of Hachilah: a hill located south of the wilderness and southeast of the city of Hebron.

In an unexpected turn of events, the people of Ziph went to Saul the king in the city of (Gibeah) and told him of David's hiding place and specified it precisely, and they offered Saul to go to them to arrest David, and they would help him in that and hand him over to him.

We find no justification for the people of "Ziph" doing this except that perhaps they feared that Saul would strike them as he had struck the priests before, or their attempt to draw near to Saul to receive material rewards from him, and in this they are a type of Judas Iscariot, whom no one asked to harm Christ, but who went by himself and sold Him to the Jews. Even if the people of Ziph were afraid of Saul because of David's being with them, if they loved David and not themselves they would have asked David to leave them for any other place. David chanted Ps (54) when the Ziphites did that.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: Saul was greatly relieved at hearing this news and praised the people of Ziph and prayed for blessing upon them, and he considered this deed of theirs a personal favor offered to him, and that they were a people who had been moved by compassion for him, in the sense that they felt for him and sympathized with him.

Saul uses the name of the Lord for blessing but is ignorant of its power because his heart is far from God; it is a verbal use and not from his heart, as many today use holy expressions that have great effectiveness if they understood their meaning.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: The thousands of Judah: the lands in which the thousands of Judah live, that is, the great clans of Judah.

Saul asked the people of Ziph to go to their city and spy out news of David to determine the place where he dwells and spends the night, "where his haunt is", and to make sure also of the person who had seen him and where exactly he had seen him, for he had learned of David's cleverness and how he changes his places and is skillful in hiding. After they learn all the places where he hides, they should return and inform him of them, and when he is sure he will go up and search through all the regions of the land of Judah.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: The wilderness of Maon: located south of the city of Hebron at a distance of 13 km.

The men of Ziph went ahead and made sure of the matters and returned to Saul to accompany him on the way to David's place; David was moving from place to place, and the inspired text mentions that at this time David had left the area of the forest and gone to another place, a low desert valley known as the wilderness of Maon.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: When Saul arrived in the area, David's watchmen knew of Saul's movements and informed David, so he left the open plain and went to the rocks in the same area, that is, the wilderness of Maon, to take refuge in them. Saul also heard of this and the pursuit continued.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: The plain, or valley, of the wilderness of Maon was surrounded by some heights called mountains, so Saul took one side of these mountains to camp in, and David took another side to take refuge with his men behind it, and David was always fleeing from the attacks of Saul's men, who had tightened the noose on him greatly and had almost succeeded in capturing him.
