entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: And here the divine help comes, for in this very difficult time for David and his men, God allowed the Philistines to attack the people of Israel and occupy some lands, and a messenger from the people came to inform Saul of this news.

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: The Rock of Escape (literally, the Rock of Slippery Places): a smooth rock.

Of course the last incident was far more important than continuing to pursue David, and therefore we find Saul the king and those with him went to gather men for war against the Philistines. The place where Saul received the news was a smooth rock, and therefore its name was given to this place, "the Rock of Escape."

entries.section: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

paragraphs.text: David left the place quickly after Saul and his men departed, and went to "Engedi", which is a spring of water about a mile west of the Dead Sea and 35 miles from Jerusalem. This place had many hiding places and natural caves.

Be reassured: when your situation grows narrow and all doors are closed, cry out to God, who arranges for you ways out that you do not expect, as He arranged the attack of the Philistines to turn Saul away from pursuing David. God moves all circumstances for your deliverance from your enemies and keeps you in all your ways.
David cuts off the corner of Saul's robe and forgives him

entries.section: (1) Saul pursues David and then falls into his hand

paragraphs.text: Wild goats: plural of the ibex, an animal a little larger than a young goat, which has horns and lives in the mountains.

These two verses are considered a continuation of the previous chapter, so we learn that Saul finished his mission on which he went to pursue the Philistines (ch. 23:28), and some spies told him of David's new place, so he took with him three thousand chosen men known for their strength and went with them after David to the mountainous region in the wilderness of "Engedi" (ch. 23:29).

entries.section: (1) Saul pursues David and then falls into his hand

paragraphs.text: Sheepfolds: pens for sheep.
Recesses: the inner depths of the cave.
To cover his feet: to lie down and sleep.

Saul reached a place with many sheepfolds and found a natural cave hewn in the mountain, and the hand of God led him to enter it. He wanted to take some rest, not knowing that David was lying in wait in the same cave, but in a deeper part than where Saul sat, since Saul slept at the entrance of the cave.

entries.section: (1) Saul pursues David and then falls into his hand

paragraphs.text: His robe: the outer garment.

Saul slept at the entrance of the cave, and neither he nor his men could see the dark depths of the cave, whereas David and his men, who were hiding in the depths of the cave in the dark, could easily see Saul and his men, because they were at the entrance of the cave, plain in the light of the sun, especially as they were talking and their voices were clear, while David's men were in complete silence. Here David's men spoke to him, saying that this was his opportunity to take revenge on Saul, for God was the one who had sent him to you that you might kill him. But David did not listen to the evil counsel; instead he seized the opportunity of the sleep of Saul and his men and rose with courage and cut off a piece of the cloth of his robe to show by it his forgiveness of him.

Be patient and do not rush after the advice of others even if they love you; perhaps their advice is evil and has no good in it for you and its consequences are bad... Be calm and seek God and His counsel in your prayer before venturing on anything.

entries.section: (1) Saul pursues David and then falls into his hand

paragraphs.text: His heart struck him: that is, he rebuked himself greatly.

Although David had not harmed Saul in any way, his sensitive conscience rebuked him and he regretted even this small act, for he felt that it was a matter of respect not to cut anything from the garments of the king anointed by God, even though his intention was good and not evil. He rebuked his men, saying, "How can I stretch out my hand against one whom the Lord chose and anointed as His king over His people?"!!

entries.section: (1) Saul pursues David and then falls into his hand

paragraphs.text: David continued to calm his men, for they wanted to kill Saul, the cause of their misery, but David was decisive in preventing them from harming him until Saul finished his rest and then set out from the place to continue his pursuit of David, not knowing that he was behind him inside the cave

If you have an opportunity to harm one who has wronged you greatly, do not respond to thoughts of evil and harm him, because Christ forgives you all your sins, so why do you not forgive also? ... Make excuses for others and pray for them, confident that your forgiveness and love will affect them, even if after a while, but in any case it is very precious to God.

After Saul went out of the cave and had gone a sufficient distance, David also went out behind him and called to him in an audible voice, so Saul looked behind him and saw David, who in remarkable humility bowed to the ground before Saul. In this conduct David was not only humble but also bold, for instead of fleeing he went to face Saul and speak with him.

David rose and began his speech to Saul, saying to him, Why have you given your ear to those who say to you that David is your enemy who wants to be rid of you and kill you, when I never intend to harm you? For God sent you today to the very cave in which I am hiding, and the men incited me to kill you because you pursue me, but I had pity on you and said to myself and to my men that I could not come near you or touch you, since you are the Lord's anointed and king over His people. We see here his humility in calling him "my lord" and his respect for God in honoring the king anointed by Him.

After David had addressed Saul before, calling him "my lord" (v. 8), he now calls him by the title "my father", which is wisdom on David's part, urging Saul to treat him as his son and not as his enemy, and it also confirms the purity of David's heart toward Saul. Then David showed him the cut-off corner of the robe to prove that he could have killed him but did not and that he harbored no evil for him, but he reproached him, saying, You are my lord and my father, so why do you try to kill me?

I will never undertake this deed and stretch out my hand against the king, but I leave my whole affair to God the just, and He will carry out the judgment He wills, and the Lord will avenge my weakness.

David cites a well-known proverb to confirm his words; the meaning of the proverb is that the wicked are the ones who do evil, but I am not one of them that I should do as they do and take vengeance on you for myself.

David continues his speech, and in the utmost humility he comes with a form of astonished protest, asking Saul, After whom have you gone out to fight or pursue ... Is it against a great army or a mighty king that you have gone out? You have gone out only after a dead dog in which there is no movement, or a small, trifling insect that does not deserve all this from you.

David affirms that God the Judge is the one who will judge him and judge Saul and decide between them, because he is wronged and Saul moves with jealousy, envy and evil to kill him, and God is able to rescue him from all of Saul's plots to kill him.

David's plea was extremely wise, bold and humble, for he bows to the king and calls him again "my father", and at the same time he confronts the king with his error in a wonderful boldness... If only we would ask God for the spirit of wisdom, that we may know when to be silent and when to speak with a boldness not devoid of humility, and in all circumstances seek the glory of God and be in inner peace, wishing no evil for anyone but seeking God, and He will defend us and protect us.

After Saul heard David's words, he was deeply moved by his love, forgiveness and humility, and he raised his voice in weeping in shame before David, so that he said to him, "Is this your voice, my son David?" David by his love had stirred the feelings of fatherhood within Saul, and Saul felt his grave wrong toward David in pursuing him and trying to kill him.

Saul confessed his guilt and error, and before David's humility and forgiveness of him and his not taking revenge on him, he said to him, You are more righteous and pure than I, for I went out to kill you, and you did not repay me for my evil with evil, but moreover you offered good and kindness in return for my evil, and you did not kill me although I was under your hand and your sword and God had delivered me to you. But unfortunately this emotion was temporary, because Saul afterward returned to his evil and pursued David; he was not steadfast in God but subject to the unclean spirit that moved him, and he did not repent a true repentance.

Saul also wanted to praise David for his conduct, so he said to him, You have done, David, what no one can do, which is that a man should let his wicked enemy go on the way of life, and therefore I ask God to repay you with every good for this deed of yours ... Perhaps Saul remembered all David's previous service to him and his love and submission, which was crowned today by his wonderful forgiveness in leaving him to live and not killing him.

Then Saul comes with a new confession that one can hardly believe he said, for he said to David, I now know for certain that God will give you the kingdom of Israel and that you will be established on the throne and that the pillars of the kingdom will also be established.

Some see that what Saul said here was in the spirit of divine prophecy and not from his heart, since the events will prove that he would return to pursuing David a little later. He may also have concluded this from Samuel's rebuke to him that his kingdom would not be established, and he heard from his son and those close to him how great David's righteousness, godliness and strength were, in addition to what he now sees with his own eyes of David's strength and forgiveness.

Saul asked David for a covenant and a promise, to swear by the name of God that he would not take vengeance on his offspring and his clan after his death, and indeed David obeyed and swore as Saul asked of him. The chapter ends with each of them going his own way, but we understand that David was not fully reassured about Saul, for he did not go to the city but went up to the stronghold.

Although Saul was certain that his kingdom would pass away and David would reign after him, he did not offer repentance and return to God and imitate David in his righteousness; rather his concerns were still material, namely that David's name be erased, for he feared that when David became king he would destroy his offspring and everything connected with him, as kings do to glorify their own names, so that their name alone would be the one that exists and they remove the names of those before them. So his concern was still worldly and not spiritual.

If you feel your error, do not try to justify yourself, but apologize for your error and try to make up for it by good deeds that you do in the future, and cling to God, and you will have true repentance. David and Abigail

This chapter begins with the news of the death of Samuel, the first spiritual father of David the prophet, and here we would like to recall some things about this man who had a great influence on his people:
1- Samuel the prophet was the greatest of men among the people of Israel after the figure of Moses the prophet.
2- Samuel the prophet was the last of the judges and was a judge for his people from his youth.
3- After the beginning of the monarchy he left judging and went on traveling through the land in continual spiritual visitation.
4- He was a man zealous for the name of God and was also bold before Saul's errors.

Therefore we understand how all the people gathered at his death and farewell as the most important spiritual leader who served them with sincerity and love, and he was buried in the city of Ramah, where his house was. As for David, with the loss of Samuel his loneliness grew intense, so he preferred to go as far from Saul as possible and headed for the wilderness of "Paran", located in the south of Palestine. The life of Samuel - the first of the prophets of the Old Testament after Moses and the last of the judges.
- His father was called Elkanah, and was a Levite from Zuph (1 Sam 1:1), and he lived in Ramah, therefore it was called Ramathaim-zophim.

- His mother "Hannah" was barren, so she prayed to God and asked for a son and vowed him to the Lord, and God answered her request and she bore Samuel in the year 1149 B.C., and when she weaned him she brought him to Eli the priest in the temple of the Lord at Shiloh (1 Sam 1, 2:1-11). - Samuel's calling and God's declaration to him that He would judge the house of Eli forever in the year 1137 B.C. (ch. 3:1-18), that is, his age was about 12 years.

- Samuel grew, and all the children of Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that he was established as a prophet of the Lord. - A little after this Eli and his two sons died in the year 1127 B.C., and the domination of the Philistines over the children of Israel began, and their seizure of the ark (ch. 4:1-22). - After the death of Eli, Samuel became the holder of religious authority and judged the people in the period between

- After the return of the ark (ch. 6), Samuel called the people to Mizpeh to confess their sins and fast before the Lord (ch. 7), and the Philistines attacked them and God gave them victory through Samuel's prayers (ch. 7:3-14), and the Philistines were afraid to attack them for most of Samuel's life.

- His headquarters was Ramah, but he went about the land to judge the people, and he founded the school of the prophets (ch. 7:15-17, 19:18-20). - Samuel grew old and appointed his two sons as judges, but they perverted justice and took bribes.

- The people asked Samuel to set a king over them, and he rebuked them, but God agreed and asked him to anoint Saul, and he anointed him (chs. 8-10). - He renewed the kingdom for Saul at Gilgal (ch. 11:14, 15), then exhorted the people and rebuked them for asking for a king, and gave them the sign of thunder and rain in the summer (ch. 12). - His rebuke of Saul for offering the sacrifice in place of Samuel and his declaration that God would raise up a good king in his place (ch. 13). - Samuel's rebuke of Saul after his victory over Amalek because he spared their king and took their spoil, although God had commanded the opposite; then Samuel's killing of Agag, king of Amalek, and his declaration to Saul that God had rejected him, and then he left him, and Saul grasped his robe and it tore, and Samuel declared that God would tear his kingdom (ch. 15). - His anointing of David as king at God's command (ch. 16). - David took refuge with him in flight from Saul and stayed with him at Naioth, and Saul pursued him (ch. 19). - He died and was buried in Ramah and all the children of Israel mourned him (ch. 25:1) in the year 1059 B.C.

The life of Samuel as a type of the life of Christ. (1) The birth: Samuel's birth was by a miracle because his mother Hannah was barren, and the birth of Christ was the greatest miracle because His mother was a virgin.

(2) His name: the meaning of the name Samuel is the name of God, and one of the names of Christ is Emmanuel, that is, God with us. (3) Childhood: Samuel was brought up in the temple and was called by God at the age of twelve, and Christ was accustomed to visit the temple every year, and at the age of twelve He sat among the doctors, discussing with them and convincing them (Lk 2:42-47). (4) The office: Samuel was a prophet and a leader of the people, that is, a king, and a priest who offered sacrifices in an exceptional way (ch. 7:9, 15, 16), and Christ was the Prophet of whom Moses prophesied and the King of kings and the High Priest of the New Testament.
(5) Judging: Samuel was a judge who judged for the people in all their problems, and Christ is the just Judge who judges on the Day of Judgment.
(6) Shepherding: Samuel moved among the lands to shepherd his people and judge for them and guide them, and Christ is the Good Shepherd who went about everywhere doing good.

(7) Prayer: Samuel prayed for his people, and they asked him to do so, especially in wars or when they sinned, and he promised them that he would not cease to pray for them (ch. 12:20-25), and Christ often withdrew alone to pray and even spent the whole night in prayer for His people, and He prayed even while on the Cross (Jn 17:6-26). (8) Discipleship: Samuel established a school of the prophets in Naioth so that the prophets might be discipled in it, and Christ took for Himself 12 disciples and 70 apostles, declaring the importance of discipleship.

(9) Humility: Samuel lived a simple life as one of the people in his food, clothing and dwelling, so that Saul did not recognize him when he met him at the gate of the city, and Christ was born in the manger and lived a poor life throughout His life, having nowhere to lay His head, and He said to the whole world, Learn from Me, "for I am meek and lowly in heart."
(10) Rebuke: Samuel rebuked the people when they asked for a king, and rebuked Saul when he offered the sacrifice and spared Agag, and Christ rebuked the scribes, the Pharisees and the lawyers.

(11) Miracles: he showed a miracle before the people by the occurrence of thunder and the falling of rain in the season of the wheat harvest to show them their error in asking for a king, and Christ performed many miracles to help His people and to declare His divinity.

(12) Appearance: Samuel appeared to Saul after his death and rebuked him, and Christ appeared after His death and Resurrection to His disciples and to many, to confirm His Resurrection and Ascension to heaven.

We begin to get to know Nabal the rich man, the owner of many possessions and thousands of sheep. He was of the offspring of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, the man famous for his courage when he spied out the land with Joshua (Num 13:30), and Nabal lived in "Maon", a village of the villages of "Carmel" south of Hebron. Despite his wealth, the inspired text describes the man as hard-hearted and evil in his deeds, unlike his wife Abigail, who is described as wise and intelligent in addition to the beauty of her face. It is also among the wonderful paradoxes that the meaning of the name Nabal is "fool", a name that fits the coming events perfectly.

Shears his sheep: the shearing season is the one in which the shorn wool is sold and the owner of the sheep receives large sums, so it was a season of joy and of holding feasts and giving to the needy, like the cotton-picking season in Egypt.

David and his men learned that Nabal and his men were shearing the wool of the sheep at Carmel, so he sent ten of his men as delegates for him and asked them to reach Nabal and give greeting and ask politely after Nabal in the name of their master David, and so the men did when they met Nabal, praying for his well-being and the well-being of his house, his family, his possessions and all that was under his hand.

The words here are spoken by the men on the tongue of David the prophet, who began his message with "I have heard that you have shearers", and he continues his words that when Nabal's men were tending their sheep at Carmel beside David and his men, they suffered no harm; on the contrary, they protected them and provided protection for your sheep, and perhaps your young men are the best informed of this, so that they may tell you of it, and perhaps my young men may find favor in your eyes on this good occasion, so that in your generosity you give whatever gift you see fit for us. After David's young men said this message they fell silent, waiting for Nabal's reply.

Note David's gentle manner, which began with a blessing and then referred to the good day, and in humility called himself a son of Nabal before asking his request. If only we would learn always to begin our speech with gentle words and a wish of good for the one we address. By this manner you can win many and soften hearts.
Break away: flee.

In pride, harshness and folly Nabal answered David's servants, and said to them in mockery, scorn and disdain for the person of David, "Who is David?", as if he were a nobody and he knew nothing about him, despite David's fame among all the people. He even described him as a servant, though David was never a servant, and he also accused him of being a runaway servant because he was fleeing from Saul, although David was wronged and everyone knew Saul's evil. This means that David did not deserve kindness but punishment; should he take his bread and his water and what he had slaughtered for his shearers and give it to David and his companions, whom he did not know who they were?!

By this saying Nabal also reveals his great stinginess despite his wealth, for it was the prevailing custom that a person would not turn away anyone who asked for bread, but he had no pity on the need of David and his men, especially as he knew well David's goodness.
Gird on ... his sword: each one made his sword ready for war.

David's men returned to him and told him all that they had said, and Nabal's reply to them, which angered David greatly, so he rushed in anger, ordering his men to take up arms, for he had made a decision to go up against Nabal and kill him, and he took with him four hundred men and left two hundred of his men with the baggage.

If Nabal in his folly brought all this on himself, David also, with his anger that had mastered him, came close to committing a great folly himself by killing Nabal, and had he done so he would have been accused all his life of being a highwayman and a bloodthirsty murderer ... So beware of being the harsh and hasty Nabal or of being David in a moment of his wrath and anger that blinded him.

One of Nabal's young men hastened to Abigail his wise wife and told her all that had happened and how harsh Nabal had been in his answer to David's servants and men. The man continued his words to Abigail, explaining how David's men had been kind and had not harmed them while they were tending the sheep of "Nabal"; more than that, they had been as guards for them and had kept outside harm from them.

The man continues his words to Abigail and says, Now that you know all that has happened, you must arrange the matter and do what is necessary so that we do not all perish, for David and his men are coming to kill us without fail and no one of the house of Nabal will escape; and Nabal is a "son of Belial", that is, a harsh and sharp person with whom no understanding is possible, and who listens to no one.
Bottle of wine: a leather vessel for keeping wine, like a waterskin.
Parched corn: green wheat that is not fully ripe.
Cakes of figs: dried figs.

Abigail moved quickly and ordered her husband's servants to prepare two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep slaughtered and ready to eat and five measures of parched corn, and also large quantities of dried raisins and figs, and she had all this loaded on donkeys and set it in her heart to go with all this to meet David and offer this vast quantity of food to his men. She ordered her young men to go on before her and did not tell Nabal what she had determined to do.
The covert of the hill: that is, beside it, where the mountain acted as a covering and shelter for those walking in the valley.
On her way to meet David, David also had gone out with his men to punish Nabal, so they all met midway.

These two verses are words David spoke to himself out of his distress at what he had heard from his men and before he met Abigail. He said in an audible voice, expressing his anger and justifying to himself and his men what he was determined to do to Nabal, speaking of Nabal's strange and provoking deed, that he repaid David's good work in preserving his possessions and sheep with evil, mockery and scorn. He took an oath upon himself and swore by God in a manner known in those days that he would leave Nabal nothing of his property or his men and young men, and the expression "one who urinates against a wall" means any adult male who can urinate voluntarily.

Among the important means by which you express your love for others is offering gifts, so you win their love, especially if they are in distress or anger or enmity, for love breaks hatred and restores peace.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: Abigail saw David and his men coming toward her on the same road, so in wisdom and humility she immediately got down from the donkey out of respect for David, and even bowed before him at his feet, then pleaded with him to hear her and allow her to speak, and she said to him that she bore this fault that her husband had committed. We note that Abigail was a rich lady with standing in society, but for the sake of making peace she humbled herself and bowed to the ground and offered gifts to remove the spirit of anger from David and to protect her husband and herself and all their men.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: Abigail began her plea to rescue her husband with a petition to David not to carry out his purpose of killing Nabal, whom she described as dull and foolish, and she showed that this is indeed his name, for Nabal is a name meaning fool, and she expressed regret that she had not been at the place of the meeting when David sent his men to Nabal, and therefore she had not seen any of them.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: As the Lord lives: a form of oath used anciently.
As your soul lives: a prayer for a person's life.

Abigail swore by God and adjured David and prayed for his life, and asked him not to kill her husband and stain his hands with blood, and said that her meeting with David and her speaking with him was a divine will by which God intended that David should not carry out what he had planned. Then she continued and said another prayer for David, that all his enemies be as foolish as Nabal, and likewise everyone who seeks evil for David.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: Then Abigail offered what she had brought of food as a gift to David for him and his young men to eat, and politely she described it as a blessing, that is, she ascribed it to God, the giver of every grace and blessing, and did not ascribe it to herself, and she said that this gift was offered to the servants and not to David, so as to magnify David's station.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: And after she put her husband's guilt on her own head, she also asks David to forgive her trespass, and she prayed that God would establish him over the whole house of Israel, especially as he fights the battles of the Lord and has all right in what he does and has committed no evil until now, and it is better that he remain so, without taking vengeance for himself by killing Nabal.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: The hollow of a sling: a wide piece of leather in which the stones are placed to be hurled by the sling far toward the target.

Abigail declared that Saul had risen to pursue David, but he could not harm him because God preserved him, and she wished that David's life would be within the bundle of God, that is, in God's protection and in a life that pleases Him, and thus, in a gentle way, she calls him to keep away from evil, because his life must remain pure with God. And on the contrary she wished that God would cast David's enemies far away from him like the stones hurled far by the sling.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: Because of David's greatness and righteousness and because of God's rejection of Saul by the mouth of Samuel, the people expected David to be the coming king, and perhaps some of them had heard of his being anointed king by the hand of Samuel, and therefore Abigail prophesied to him that he would be king, and when the divine promise is fulfilled and he is king over Israel, nothing will stain his reputation or his history, nor will he be described as one who shed blood without necessary cause or as one avenging his own honor. Abigail ended her speech with David by asking that, when God fulfills His promises to him and sets him as king over Israel, he not forget her deed and her prayers and her prophecy to him of his coming station.

Abigail gives us all an example of wisdom and of the sweet, gentle tongue that turns away anger and prevents evil. If only we would take from her a lesson in dealing with the angry, agitated person, and look at him as a poor man who does not know what he is doing, so that we remind him of his virtues and offer him love, care and an apology in humility, and so soften his heart and restore his calm.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: Before David praised Abigail's soundness of mind and her wisdom in all the words she spoke with him, and how her speech prevented him from committing evil and taking revenge for himself and staining his hand with Nabal's blood, he first gave thanks to God, the giver of every blessing, who in His care sent Abigail to prevent him from committing this crime; so also the spiritual person sees the plain hand of God in all the affairs of his life and thanks God for them.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: David thanks God also for another thing, which is Abigail's coming out to him on the road, because had she not come out David would have killed her herself with her husband, since in his anger he swore to kill Nabal and all his family and servants and men in his raid upon him.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: With feelings of thanks David accepted from Abigail the gifts she had brought to him to feed his men, and prayed for her blessing and bade her farewell and sent her in peace to her house, and in a gentle courtesy to her and to her deed he reassured her that he had heeded her words and turned from what he would have done; and the expression "I have lifted up your face" means "I have heeded your words and honored your coming."

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: Abigail returned to her house and found "Nabal" her husband celebrating with his men the celebrations of the sheep shearing and making them a very great feast, and everyone ate and drank wine, and when she found Nabal very drunk she was wise also in telling him nothing.

Nabal's evil appears from this, for he spent lavishly on the feast that he enjoyed with his friends, while he refused to help the needy such as David; he is stingy toward others and immersed in his desires.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: In the morning of the next day, after Nabal had recovered from his drunkenness, Abigail told him all that had passed between her and David in conversation, and how David had sworn to destroy Nabal and all his men, and the man was terrified by the words and the color of his face left him, so that he looked like a dead man, and his heart turned to stone from fear; for although his wife had set right his errors, he was still very afraid of David.

entries.section: (5) The conversation of Abigail and David

paragraphs.text: After ten days that Nabal spent in fear, he died, and God allowed this as a punishment for his evils mentioned before.

entries.section: (6) David's marriage to Abigail and Ahinoam

paragraphs.text: David learned of Nabal's death, so he blessed the Lord, and considered that Nabal's death was God's vengeance upon him for having reproached him, and David thanked God, who had kept him from evil.
And because David admired Abigail's wisdom and her good conduct, he sent some of his men to her to propose marriage to her.

entries.section: (6) David's marriage to Abigail and Ahinoam

paragraphs.text: The messengers of "David" indeed went to Abigail and spoke to her the words of "David" in asking to marry her, and she rose in humility, and before answering a word she bowed to the ground before them and said that she was not worthy to marry "David" but was like a handmaid ready to wash the feet of his servants.!!

entries.section: (6) David's marriage to Abigail and Ahinoam

paragraphs.text: Abigail rose with five maidens of her servants and rode on the donkey and went behind the servants of "David", and reached him, and he married her. The inspired text also mentions that David married Ahinoam of the town of Jezreel, so she became his third wife after Michal the daughter of Saul and then Abigail the widow of Nabal. In (ch. 27:3) the inspired text mentions Ahinoam before Abigail, so Ahinoam may be the second wife and Abigail the third. Polygamy was permitted in the Old Testament because of spiritual weakness, but the original state in which God created man was one wife (Gen 1:27), and Christ restored humanity to this state in the New Testament (1 Cor 7:2, Mt 19:3-10).

entries.section: (6) David's marriage to Abigail and Ahinoam

paragraphs.text: Gallim: one of the villages of the land of Benjamin near Gibeah.

Saul learned of the marriage of "David" to Abigail and Ahinoam, and this was against the honor of Michal his daughter, so Saul annulled her marriage to him and gave her as wife to a man named "Phalti", but we also know that after David took the rule he took back his wife Michal from "Phalti" (2 Sam 3:13-16).

David chose Abigail as a wife for her wisdom, humility, love and gentleness; therefore, my brothers, preparation for marriage is adorning oneself with the Christian virtues that qualify for forming a marital relationship on a spiritual level of understanding and affection, and not by passing material preparations, which may deceive some but lead to failed marital relationships.
David forgives Saul for the second time and takes his spear and his jug

entries.section: (1) Saul goes out to pursue David

paragraphs.text: Once again the people of Ziph volunteered to go out and inform Saul of David's new hiding place. They had informed him before in (ch. 23:19) when he pursued David, but he left him because of the Philistines' attack on the land. And the second time, at En Gedi (ch. 24:1), it was probably the Ziphites who informed him, when he entered the cave in which David was. The Ziphites, of course, wanted to gain some benefit from this in one way or another, so they went to Saul's residence at Gibeah and told him that they were certain David was in a region called "the hill of Hachilah," which is mentioned in (ch. 23:19).

entries.section: (1) Saul goes out to pursue David

paragraphs.text: Immediately Saul gathered three thousand men of Israel, chosen for their skill in war, and went out with this small army to look for David in the wilderness of Ziph, at "the hill of Hachilah."

entries.section: (1) Saul goes out to pursue David

paragraphs.text: Saul encamped with his army on "the hill of Hachilah," while David was hiding in caves inside the mountain in the wilderness opposite the hill of Hachilah. Of course David heard the commotion of Saul and his men and learned that he had come out after him.

entries.section: (1) Saul goes out to pursue David

paragraphs.text: Trench: a protective barrier for defense.

To be more certain, David sent out spies, and when they returned he knew for sure that Saul had come out to kill him. So David himself went out stealthily, and from a hidden place he looked at the site where Saul and his men were gathered, and he saw Saul himself, with Abner, the commander of his army, relaxing behind a trench for protection.

Saul was still pursuing David and had not learned from David's earlier forbearance toward him, nor from God's deliverance of him out of his hand. Do not be persistent in evil; rather repent, and do not go on in evil, lest God abandon you and allow you to be disciplined, and you suffer greatly.

entries.section: (2) David goes down to Saul's place

paragraphs.text: Zeruiah: she was David's sister by his mother, and Abishai and Joab were her sons.

David spoke with Ahimelech the Hittite and with Abishai the brother of Joab, and asked the two of them, "Who will go down with me to the place where Saul is?" And Abishai answered that he would go down with him.

entries.section: (2) David goes down to Saul's place

paragraphs.text: David crept down by night to Saul and the people gathered around him. It appears that Saul was fast asleep, he and those with him, including Abner, the commander of his army, who was primarily charged with guarding Saul. Saul's spear was stuck in the ground by his head. God allowed this deep sleep in order to show David's forbearance, as we shall see. And we see here how Saul relied on his own strength and on his strong protection in the hand of the great military commander Abner and the armies around him, and forgot that protection and strength are from God, so God showed his weakness before David.

entries.section: (2) David goes down to Saul's place

paragraphs.text: Delivered your enemy: that is, He has given him into your hand.

It was never expected that the matter would be so easy, and so Abishai dared to speak to David, saying: The Lord has delivered Saul into your hand this day so that you may take vengeance on him; so let me strike him with his spear once, a single piercing blow that will kill him and end the days of his pursuit of you. But the forbearing David answered him with a refusal, explaining that Saul was still the king whom God had anointed, so how could he kill the one whom God had chosen, and if he did this, could he escape the wrath of God?

entries.section: (2) David goes down to Saul's place

paragraphs.text: David was confident of God's justice and that He does not tolerate the wrong done to His children for long, so he declared that God would intervene in His own way and take vengeance on him: either he would perish in one of the wars, or God would cause him to die in His own way.

entries.section: (2) David goes down to Saul's place

paragraphs.text: David repeated his words, that he could not stretch out his hand against Saul, the Lord's anointed, but he asked Abishai to take Saul's spear from beside him, and also the water jug set aside for his drinking. They indeed took the spear and the jug, and no one noticed them, for by divine providence a deep sleep had fallen on everyone. And David and Abishai returned to their first place.

Rise above taking your right into your own hand, and lift your grievance up to God, and trust that He hears the cry of the wronged and feels for him, for He is the hope of him who has no hope and the helper of him who has no helper. In this way you keep your peace and your love for others, and your faith increases in God, who seeks the salvation of all and disciplines them in the fitting way that leads them to repentance.

David withdrew and crossed over, returning to his first place, and went up to the top of a hill. The distance was great enough that no one could throw a dart at him, and at the same time his voice would be heard and he would be easy to see, since he was standing in a high place.

David called out in a loud voice more than once to the people and to Abner, asking him to answer and respond to him. And Abner answered, inquiring about the voice that was calling. Perhaps Abner's question carried a note of astonishment and displeasure at this call: who dares to call out to the king? It seems that Abner did not answer quickly, since he was deep in sleep and did not expect anyone to call to the king and the commander of his army.

David addressed Abner, and began his words with a question followed by a rebuke. He said to him: Are you not supposed to be the bravest of the men of Israel, and is there not a man like you in courage who can be entrusted with the king's life and guarding? Why then were you negligent and overcome by sleep, and did not do your duty? For a man came by night to kill the king, and you knew nothing of it. How then can you be a faithful servant over the life of your lord?

You have done evil, Abner, by this carelessness and unfaithfulness toward your lord the king. You and those with you who guard the king deserve death for this negligence and for not keeping safe your lord and king, Saul, the Lord's anointed. For the spear and the water jug were taken, and you did not stir to protect the king.

Be faithful in your responsibilities, whether guarding or any work that you do, so that you complete it with faithfulness and precision for the sake of God and not of men, and God will reward you for your faithfulness, in addition to which people will be pleased by it.

Saul recognized David's voice and wanted to be sure of it, so he asked him again about his voice. Saul's words were in a fatherly tone, even though he was wicked and was trying to kill David. And David answered that it was indeed he.
David continued his speech, asking: Why, O king, have you come out after me seeking my death? What evil have I done, and what crime have I committed, that you should decide my death?
Let Him accept an offering: that is, may God accept the offering.

David began to present his case to King Saul with humility, describing himself as a servant appealing to his master, and he said to him: If it is God who has sent you out after me because of some fault I may have committed, then tell me and give me time to offer a sacrifice for my sin to God, perhaps He will accept it and forgive me. But if it is men who have slandered me to you without any real offense, then let them be cursed before the Lord, for by doing this it is as though they have driven me out from before the Lord and His worship, so that I should take refuge with other people who serve other gods.

Note David's courtesy in speaking with Saul. Although he knew Saul's evil and his hatred toward him, he attributed the evil to others who were speaking evil about him to Saul, in order to give Saul an opportunity to turn back from his evil.
Partridge: a mountain bird that hunters chased in order to eat it; when it grew tired of flying it would come down to the ground and be easy to catch.

David used here a manner of forbidding, the meaning of which is that it is unthinkable for the king to shed his blood before God, because he is innocent and his blood would cry out from the ground like the blood of Abel. He continued, expressing his amazement at how the great king of Israel could come out after a weak servant of his servants. He applied to himself the title of the flea as a way of belittling himself, and he also described himself as that mountain bird which hunters chase, yet which has no worth or price.
David's excellence in this dialogue with Saul appears in the following:
1- His humility, and his describing himself as a flea or a partridge.
2- His confidence in himself, as he boldly declares that he is innocent.
3- His courtesy, as he attaches the evil to others who incited Saul to it, in order to give him a chance to turn back.
4- His readiness to declare his apology for any fault he had done, and to offer repentance and a sacrifice.
5- His attachment and longing for communal worship with his people in the house of the Lord.

By the work of divine grace Saul was moved by David's words and quickly reconsidered. He began his apology by acknowledging his error in going out after David, and promised him not to harm him, especially as David had preserved his life and had not killed him. With remorse he also acknowledged his foolishness and error and that he had lost his reason, and he asked David to return from his flight to his home and his clan in safety.
Apologizing with humility when one is at fault is a beautiful virtue adorning the true Christian, so do not let your pride stand in the way of your apology when you are at fault.

David did not trust Saul completely, for he had previously promised David safety and then broken his covenant. So David did not come down to give Saul his spear, but asked one of Saul's men to come over and approach David to take the king's spear.

David prayed that the Lord would give and reward everyone according to his righteousness and faithfulness. Of course he is referring here to himself, and he also points out that he had been faithful toward Saul, since when the opportunity was given him to kill him he did not do so.

And as David did with Saul, David asks and prays that he too might find grace in the eyes of God, and that He would deliver him from his enemies or from every tribulation to which he might be exposed.
And David here puts his trust in God, who does not go back on His promises and protects His children, whereas men like Saul are, sadly, not dependable in their promises.

This chapter ends contrary to how it began, and the picture changes completely, for Saul prays a blessing for David, whereas at the beginning of the chapter he blessed the Ziphites, David's enemies, who were trying to deliver him up to him. The expression "you shall both do great things and also still prevail" is meant to say that you may always be able to pardon and forgive. And both departed: Saul returned to his city, and David went on his way.
David's refuge with the Philistines

entries.section: (1) David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath

paragraphs.text: With Saul's repeated attempts to kill David and his continual pursuit, David did not trust his promises, which he had given before and then broken. So for the second time David thought that there was no escape for him except to flee to Gath, one of the great cities of the Philistines. He had fled to Gath the first time, and the king's men tried to stir the king up against David, so he feigned madness and the king let him go (ch. 21:10-15). By this he would avoid Saul's pursuit, since Saul would not think of waging war with the Philistines for David's sake. And indeed he took his six hundred men with him and crossed the border to "Achish," king of "Gath."

The men following him numbered 600, in addition to their wives and children, a large number, and perhaps David felt that it was hard for their life in the caves and hideouts to continue, so he thought of taking refuge in a city of the Philistines.

And perhaps David did not consult God before going to Gath because he was forced to use cunning so that the king of Gath would not rise up against him, and God, for the sake of his righteousness throughout his life, kept him safe with the king of Gath and delivered him from embarrassing situations, as we shall see in the following chapters.

It appears to us that it would have been better for David to remain pursued by Saul in the land of Judah, relying on God's promise to keep him and make him king, rather than taking refuge with the idolaters, especially since God's voice to him through the mouth of Gad the prophet had been, "Abide not in the hold; depart, and get thee into the land of Judah" (ch. 22:5), meaning that God was able to keep him while he was a pursued stranger in the land of Judah.

entries.section: (1) David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath

paragraphs.text: Achish allowed David to dwell in "Gath" with his two wives, "Ahinoam" and "Abigail," and all his men as well. Perhaps Achish, the king of the Philistines, considered David and his men a force not to be taken lightly, one that would add great strength to his army, and because he knew of the enmity between David and Saul, he regarded David as an ally who would help him against Saul.

entries.section: (1) David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath

paragraphs.text: Saul learned of "David's" flight to Gath and his settling there, so he gave up on him and did not go out to pursue him afterward, for fear of the Philistines.

entries.section: (1) David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath

paragraphs.text: David did not want to stay long in "Gath," since it was the capital of the king and he and his men would always be under watch there, and for fear of slanders or problems that his men might cause. So he preferred to leave for somewhere farther away so that he might have a greater measure of freedom that would allow him to worship God with his men, because his being in Gath might expose him to pressure from its king to burn incense to the idols with the rest of his royal court. In addition, if he succeeded and grew strong and his men increased, or if he won victories in any raids, the king of Gath might become afraid of him through the slander of some of his royal court. So he came forward and asked the king to give him a place in one of the villages.

entries.section: (1) David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath

paragraphs.text: Ziklag: it lies ten miles north of Beersheba.

The Lord gave David favor in the eyes of King Achish, so he granted his request and gave him the village of "Ziklag," which lies on the border. It had originally been part of the land of Judah, and the Philistines seized it in one of the wars, and it remained in their hands throughout Saul's life; afterward the kings of Judah recovered it and it became part of their lands and kingdoms. The inspired text tells us the period that David spent in this town: it was a year and four months.

God gave David favor in the eyes of King Achish, so that he did not suspect him and received him as his guest. So trust that if you please God and keep His commandments, He will give you favor in the eyes of all, even your enemies, so that they live at peace with you and you grow in your relationship with God without hindrance.

During David's stay in Gath he raided some of the pagan tribes, whose life was largely of a nomadic character. These tribes and their small lands were spread out from the borders of Shur, which is south of Palestine, to the east of Egypt. The most important of these peoples were the Geshurites, the Gezrites, and the Amalekites, peoples whom God commanded to be fought, all of them.

David's wars and raids were comprehensive: he destroyed all the inhabitants of these places and was able to take their spoil of sheep, cattle, donkeys, and camels, besides the fabrics and garments. Perhaps the purpose of these raids of David was:
1- To destroy the pagan peoples dwelling on the southern border of the tribe of Judah, thus securing the land of that tribe, to which he belonged.
2- To obtain spoil sufficient for the needs of his men for their livelihood.
3- To make Achish believe that he had attacked the Jews, so that he would become loyal and subject to him, as will appear in (v. 10).
Whither have ye made a road today: an interrogative expression whose meaning is "whom have you raided today," as it appears in the Septuagint.

"Achish" asked David about the peoples he had raided, and David answered cunningly, with an answer that had more than one meaning. David answered him that he had raided the south of Judah and the south of the Jerahmeelites, who are Jewish peoples, and also the south of the Kenites, friends of the Jews, from whom came Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, and Heber the Kenite, the husband of Jael, who killed Sisera (Judg 4). David's answer suggested that he had raided the southern outskirts of these peoples, but he had not done this; rather he raided the peoples who lie south of these regions, and by this cunning he wanted to suggest to Achish that he had raided the Jewish peoples themselves, and so become an enemy of the Jews and a vassal of the Philistines. David's raiding of the lands neighboring the tribe of Judah was a common practice at this time, as a securing of the borders of the land by seizing the lands adjacent to them.

This verse comes on its own as an explanation for David's killing everyone he raided, so that none of these peoples would come and report to Achish that David had used the land of the Philistines as a base from which to kill these pagan tribes and not the Jews, as he had led Achish to believe.

David's trick worked on Achish, who believed that he had raided his own people and rejoiced greatly at this. He thought that by this deed David had become hated by his people Israel, many of whom he had killed, and that he would therefore become a mighty servant of strength, subject to him, whom Achish could use in wars.

God is able to give you strength however hard your circumstances may be, like David's being with the Philistines, his enemies, and his victory in his raids and the provision of his men's needs. So do not worry, for God arranges your needs and opens ways for you to live and rejoice with Him.
Saul's consulting the medium before the war

A short time after the preceding events, the Philistines decided to wage war against the people of the children of Israel, so they gathered all their armies to prepare for this war. Among the preparations made by "Achish," king of Gath, was that he spoke with David to secure his going out with him in the fight against Israel. This shows the measure of Achish's confidence in David, that he would ally himself with him against his own people, so much so that Achish's words did not take the form of a question but of a command.

Of course the situation was hard for David, and so he answered with wisdom and with an open-ended answer. He said to Achish, "You shall know what your servant can do," and he did not specify what he would do, but Achish understood from David's answer what he wanted to understand, namely David's agreement and allegiance to him. So Achish replied to his words that he trusted him with great trust, so much that he entrusted his life to him and would make him his personal guard.

When circumstances put you in a position to lie, do not rush, but ask God's help, and He will give you wisdom and you will give an answer that has no lie in it, and it will rescue you from the awkward situation. Only be careful to keep God before your eyes, so that you fear Him and hold fast to His commandments and seek His help, and He will never leave you and will always give you wisdom. The First Book of Samuel

entries.section: (2) Saul asks the Lord about the war

paragraphs.text: Familiar spirits: kinds of demons.
Those with familiar spirits: the sorcerers who make use of demons in their evil works.
Wizards: those whom demons accompany and follow in their lives, so that they perform wonders and tell them hidden things.

This verse is a parenthesis in the events, but it is an introduction to what Saul would do afterward. It tells us of the death of Samuel the prophet, who represented the voice of God, and points to his exalted standing in all Israel's mourning for him and his burial with honor in his city, where he had lived all his life. As an introduction also to what is coming, we learn that Saul in the days of his early reign had put away those who had familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the soothsayers from all his kingdom, in keeping with God's Law (Deut 18:10, 11).

entries.section: (2) Saul asks the Lord about the war

paragraphs.text: Shunem: it is the present town of Sulam, and it lies 3.5 miles north of Jezreel in the land of Issachar. Gilboa: it is now the village of Jilbun, and it lies in the Gilboa mountain range, which forms the northeastern part of the mountains of Ephraim, near the Jordan, opposite Shunem.
The two armies gathered in two positions with a plain between them, the valley of Jezreel. The Philistines were north of this valley, while the Israelites were south of it.

entries.section: (2) Saul asks the Lord about the war

paragraphs.text: Because of the great numbers in the Philistine army, Saul was greatly afraid and went to inquire of God. But he had killed all the priests at "Nob," and none of them escaped except "Abiathar," who fled to David and carried with him the ephod and the stones of the Urim and Thummim. For this reason Saul received no answer from God in any form: not by dreams, nor by Urim and Thummim, since these were with Abiathar, nor by prophets, since he no longer had a prophet with him. And Saul's turning to God was out of fear of the Philistines, and not out of piety or faith in God.

Do not cut off the means that lead you to God, which are prayer, the Holy Bible, your relationship with the Church, and the sacraments, lest tribulation come upon you and you find no accustomed means that bring you to God, and you fall into bewilderment and trembling.
A woman that hath a familiar spirit: a soothsayer who consults demons and makes people think they are the spirits of the dead.
The First Book of Samuel. Endor: one of the cities of the tribe of Manasseh, lying about 9.5 km southeast of Nazareth.

Despair and distress took hold of Saul's soul when God did not answer him, and instead of repentance and remorse he turned to a greater error. He commanded his men to seek out for him any woman who practiced sorcery and was known to have contact with demons, so that he might go to her and ask her about the war. And his servants pointed him to a woman who practiced sorcery and divination and lived at Endor.

Bring up: because evil and righteous spirits were in Hades in the Old Testament, but the former in torment and the latter in rest, awaiting Christ's redemption to raise them to Paradise. Saul took two men of his followers and went with them to the woman by night so that no one would see him, and he disguised himself to hide his identity, and he asked two things of her: first, that she tell him the future by means of the familiar spirit, and then that she bring up for him the spirit of the person he would name to her.

God may delay His answer to your petition because of His divine wisdom, or His voice may not be clear to you in something you ask of Him. So beware of the helpers of Satan, and do not deal with an astrologer, a sorcerer, or a fortune-teller, even as a jest or for amusement, for by doing so you despise God Himself and hand yourself over as an easy prey to the enemy of good.
The woman answered Saul that everyone knew what Saul had done, gathering and killing every sorcerer and soothsayer in the kingdom. "Is this a trap and a test for me, so that you may destroy me?"

Saul swore to her by the name of the Lord to reassure her and gain his purpose, and when she asked him whom he wanted her to bring up, he told her that he wanted the spirit of Samuel the prophet so that he might speak with him. In Saul's oath there is an appearance of religion, but his heart was far from God, for how could he swear by God that no harm would come to her, when what he was doing was against God's Law, which commands the stoning of sorceresses (Lev 20:27)?

The woman was expecting one of the demons with whom she was accustomed to deal to appear, but Samuel's appearing with the splendor of the saints' appearance terrified her greatly, so that she cried out from the severity of the shock and surprise. And she learned from Samuel's spirit that the one speaking with her was King Saul himself, and in alarm she asked him why he had deceived her. Samuel's appearance was by God's permission and not by the power of divination, as a final warning to Saul, that perhaps he might repent.
From this it appears that the one who appeared to the medium was the spirit of Samuel and not a demon calling itself by his name, as shown by the following:
1- The alarm of the medium, who did not expect the spirit of Samuel himself to come.

2- Samuel told Saul by a prophecy from God that he would die tomorrow, that the children of Israel would be defeated before the Philistines, and that David would become the king after him. And all this was fulfilled.
3- Samuel's saying to Saul, "Why hast thou disquieted me," because the spirits of the righteous are with God and are not occupied with anything else.
4- The testimony of the medium that she saw gods ascending, that is, a powerful spirit different from what she was accustomed to see of the spirits of demons.
5- The testimony of the Holy Bible itself to this in the Book of Jesus ben Sirach: "And after his death he prophesied, and showed the king his end" ... (Sir 46:23).

Saul wanted to reassure the woman again, so he said to her, "Be not afraid," and asked her what she had seen. She answered him that she had seen something great and new to her, namely gods ascending out of the earth. By the word "gods" it is meant that she may have seen the spirits of saints or angels who accompanied Samuel in his appearing, or perhaps it was Samuel alone, but from the splendor of his form she used the expression "gods" in the plural, which is the expression used by all the pagan sorcerers of that time.

Saul asked her more closely what his form was, and she told him that he was an old man, that is, advanced in age and days, covered with a mantle. This was in fact Samuel's clothing during his ministry on earth, and so Saul was afraid and expressed his trembling by bowing to the ground.

The spirit of Samuel spoke, rebuking Saul for what he had done by his urgent desire to call up his spirit, which was rejoicing in praise before God and resting in peace, awaiting Christ's redemption to transfer it to Paradise. The First Book of Samuel. The expression "bringing me up" does not mean that Saul had authority to bring up his spirit, nor did the sorceress, because no one has authority over the world of spirits except God alone; rather it is a rebuke from Samuel's spirit to Saul for seeking to speak with spirits.

Saul answered Samuel that he had resorted to this when the Lord had closed all the ways before him and did not answer him by a prophet or a dream, and Samuel had been the last to speak to him with the voice of God. For this reason he sought his spirit so that he might tell him what to do in his war with the Philistines.

Samuel answered him with hard words: how dared Saul ask, when the Lord had departed from him completely? If God had wanted to speak with Saul and inform him of the matter, He would have used one of the other usual means, and not this way by which Saul transgressed the Law, so that he became a complete enemy of God.

The kingdom torn out of your hand: after Saul's death David will take a part of the kingdom, the tribe of Judah, and reign in Hebron, and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul will reign over the rest of the tribes; then Ish-bosheth will die and the whole kingdom will submit to David.

Samuel spoke in the past tense to confirm that the divine plan and God's absolute judgment had already gone forth from Him, to take the kingdom from Saul and give it to David the son of Jesse. The word "neighbour" does not mean physical kinship, but is because David was formerly close to Saul's table.

And all this has come upon you, and God has rejected you, because of your disobedience and your not obeying Him when He commanded you to kill "Agag," king of Amalek, and to destroy all that you took in the war, but you spared Agag and also much of his livestock.
Tomorrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me: that is, in Hades, but the righteous in one place and the wicked in another.

And because of your other evils also, God will deliver you tomorrow, and with you the people of Israel, into the hand of the Philistines, and God will carry out His just judgment, so that you die with your sons and your spirits come to dwell with me. Likewise your army will lose the battle and be humiliated and given up to the Philistines.

Note: before Christ's redemption of mankind, the waiting place of departed spirits was one place, for the righteous, like Samuel the prophet, and also for the wicked, like Saul. But the righteous were in a better state, since they were awaiting the hope of Christ's redemption of them, while the wicked were in a very bad state, since they knew what their final fate was. And after Christ's redemption of mankind on the holy wood of the Cross, the Paradise of delight was opened and the righteous came to be in a place separate from the place of the wicked, which is the heavenly Paradise, while the wicked remained in Hades.

God's judgment and justice must be fulfilled, so do not persist in sin or justify it, but hasten to repentance and you will enjoy God's forgiveness and mercies, for He desires that all be saved. So draw near to Him, whatever your sins may be, for He is a loving Father.

Saul was terrified and completely broke down at the horror of what he heard, and he fell full length on the earth, for he would lose his life, his sons would die also, and he would lose the war. His muscles' slackening also helped to bring about his fall. The First Book of Samuel. And he felt weak, since he had eaten nothing all day. But sadly he did not think of offering repentance and returning to God.

When the woman, the medium, saw Saul's collapse, his weakness and his great fear, she said to him: I have listened to you and obeyed you, and I was at your command, and I put myself in danger and carried out all your orders; so now you also listen to my request, that I set a little food before you, so that you may eat and regain your strength, so that you can return and go back to your place in the midst of your army.

Saul refused to eat because of his great grief, but after the urging of the woman, the medium, and his two servants who had accompanied him to her, he listened to them and rose from the ground and sat on the woman's bed, while she killed her calf and baked flour into unleavened bread in order to honor the king. And indeed Saul ate with his two servants, and then they all departed to the camp of Israel to await the war the next day.

"Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap," so the Lord Christ has warned us, and how much harsher and more bitter was what Saul reaped from what he had sown before. So be careful and do not wrong anyone, and obey God and His commandments, and you will have deliverance and enjoy God's mercies in place of His justice and punishment. And accustom yourself to repentance from now on, because if you do not accustom yourself to it and then meet hard circumstances like Saul, you may not be able to, for lack of habit.
The Philistines prepare for war and David is excluded from taking part in it

Aphek: a place south of Shunem (ch. 28:4). After the Philistines first gathered at "Shunem," they began to move south to be nearer to the armies of the Israelites, and they assembled at the town of "Aphek" to organize their army before the war. Meanwhile the Israelites were stationed in Jezreel by a fountain, probably Harod, and it is most likely the spring of Jalud, which lies southeast of Jezreel.
Lords: chiefs and leaders or kings.
Rereward: the rear of the army.

The five kings of the Philistines advanced with their armies and led hundreds and thousands of men to war, and David too was compelled to go out with them, as King Achish had asked of him. Of course David did not know what to do: if he withdrew, his earlier deception of Achish would be exposed, and if he really entered the war he would be a traitor to God and to his people, which David would never do!!! But he prayed and waited for God to intervene to save him from this predicament.

The kings of the Philistines were five in number, one of them Achish, who had received David into his ranks and allowed him to dwell there, and who now also called him to fight with the ranks of his men. When the rest of the kings of the Philistines saw this, they objected to Achish about David's going out with them in this war. So Achish hastened to defend him, saying that he had been one of Saul's servants but had fled with his men to him, and he had received him and found nothing evil in him throughout his stay with them in the city of Ziklag.

The four kings of the Philistines objected to "Achish's" defense, and they were indeed wiser and more realistic. They explained in their objection that David would turn against them in the war in an attempt to appease Saul again, and would present their heads to him as a gift. For how could David betray his people, when he was a national and popular hero whom the women had earlier sung of after his victory over Goliath? And they suggested to Achish that he require him to stay in Ziklag and not leave it, and that he have no part at all in this war.

Do not be troubled when embarrassing situations meet you, however hard they may be, but lift up your heart to God and ask the intercession of the saints, and trust that God will not leave you but will deliver you and guide you and protect you, so that no harm will befall you.

Achish was compelled to yield to the opinion of the four kings, so he summoned David, and when he came, he began his speech to him in a tone of apology. He first praised him for his uprightness throughout the period of his stay in the land of the Philistines and said that he had found no evil in him, and he had wanted to take him with him to the war, but his opinion did not find acceptance with the chiefs of the Philistines. Therefore David must go back and return to his place at Ziklag and not take part in the war. Of course we see here how it was God's hand and providence that relieved David of the embarrassment and rescued him from the difficult situation, and God also brought him back to Ziklag, which the Amalekites had attacked, to save his household and his wives from this attack (ch. 30:

David hid his true feelings by God's mighty working, and how the apology had come from the Philistines, and he seized the opportunity and showed feigned emotion that he would not take part in the battle with Achish, and how could he remain far from the battle and not fight the Israelites.

Achish repeated his kind words to David and described him as being like a guardian angel from the gods to him, and made clear to him again that the rejection had not come from him but from the rest of the kings of the Philistines.

He also asked him to rise early in the morning with his men and return to "Ziklag," and indeed David did so and went back with his men to the lands of the Philistines and did not take part in the war, while the Philistines prepared to fight in Jezreel.
In the words of Achish, king of Gath, to the lords of the Philistines and to David, we see what shows his being moved and his great love for David, as appears in the following:
1- His oath by the Lord in his saying, "As the Lord liveth" (v. 6), the original of which is "Yahweh," and this means Achish was influenced by David and took this oath from him.
2- His testimony about David before the lords of the Philistines that he is upright (v. 6).
3- His likening David to an angel in his speech with him (v. 9).

Because of the uprightness of David's heart, his enemies loved him and saw no fault in him. So be upright before God, and He will make all those around you live at peace with you, so that you can deal with them in peace and prosper in all your ways.
David pursues the Amalekites and defeats them

David and his men returned and discovered that the Amalekites had taken advantage of his going out to the war and had raided the whole region of the South, including "Ziklag," in revenge on David, who had raided their land before (ch. 27). They also burned the city and took the women in it, as well as the remaining men and the children. They did not kill anyone, but took them as captives and slaves.

When David entered the town, they were shocked at what they saw of fire and destruction, and at its emptiness of women and sons, and they learned what had happened. So they cried out and wept, moved by what they saw, and their weeping went on until they had no strength left in them.
Both Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail, whom David married after the death of her husband Nabal, were also taken captive among the women who were taken captive.

David was greatly distressed by this calamity, and what doubled his distress and grief also was that the men, in their despair and frustration, turned against him and wanted to kill him, believing that he was the cause of everything that had come upon their wives and upon this city which he had left unguarded, and they counted that as negligence on his part. But David laid all his distress and pain before God, and felt His presence beside him, and his soul was strengthened and made strong.
We see that David here was in a severe predicament such as he had not met before, for the following reasons:
1- He was pursued by Saul, who was trying to kill him, that is, he was driven out of his homeland.
2- He was also rejected by the Philistines, because they refused his taking part with them in the war.
3- He lost his wives and sons.
4- His tents and possessions in Ziklag were burned.
5- His men rose against him and tried to kill him, because he was accused of negligence in protecting their wives and children.

If loved ones and friends turn against you, take refuge in God, who is sure in His love and steadfast in His fatherhood, for He never changes. He will support you, and you will be able to win back many of those who turned against you.

Abiathar was the priest who escaped after Saul killed all the priests (ch. 22), and he had fled to David, taking with him the ephod and the stones of the Urim and Thummim. So David called for him and asked God through him whether he should pursue these Amalekite aggressors and whether he would have victory if he overtook them. God's answer came to him that he would prevail and would rescue the captives, the women and children. This was a good act on David's part, since he asked God and did not let his anger and desire for revenge lead him, and in this he learned from the earlier experience when he took refuge in Gath without asking God. We note here that when he prayed, God blessed him and his men submitted to him.

We also learn here not to be troubled by trials if we take refuge in God, because the trial turns into God's testing and the recovery of everything that was lost, and even the gaining of spoil. This is what happened with David, and it happens in our lives also, when we receive blessings from any trial.

The brook Besor: a depression south of Ziklag through which a stream, that is, a small river, runs from the mountains of Edom and empties into the Mediterranean Sea at Gaza, and perhaps it is what is called the river of Egypt, located on Egypt's border.

David took all his men, and when they reached the edge of the brook Besor, exhaustion and weariness overcame two hundred of his men and they could not go on. So David left them and continued on his way and crossed the brook with four hundred men.

Be gentle with people's abilities, and do not ask of them what is beyond their strength or make them feel at fault if they are worn out, for compassion and sensitivity to others are among the characteristics of the Christian!!

God sent new help to David by means of a guide who would help him reach the Amalekites. This help was an Egyptian man overcome by exhaustion and close to death, whom David's men found lying in a field, and they gave him food and drink, and when he had eaten he recovered some of his strength, for it was three days since he had eaten or drunk. This shows David's love and concern for the weak, for he helped this man who was at the point of death before he knew that he would be the one to guide him, and he did this despite his preoccupation with pursuing the invaders.

It appeared from the man's features and clothing that he was a slave and not from the people of this region, so David asked him whose man he was, "his master," and about his original homeland. The man answered him that he was a slave from Egypt and his master was an Amalekite, but he had fallen sick and his master had cruelly left him behind to meet his fate of death in this place?!!
The Cherethites: a people from the island of Crete who migrated east to the Philistine lands and merged with its people.

The man continued his speech, explaining the cause of his exhaustion and weariness, which was that he had taken part with the Amalekites, as a slave of his master, in invading the southern lands of the Cherethites, as well as the southern fields of Judah and the south of the lands of Caleb, and that they had also attacked Ziklag and burned it with fire.

David asked the man to guide him to the place of the Amalekites and their gathering, and the man, fearing for his life, asked David for an oath that he would not kill him or deliver him into the hands of his master, and David promised him this. So the man took him to the place where the Amalekites were gathered, who were celebrating with eating, drinking, dancing, and drunkenness after their victory over the land of the Philistines and Judah, for they thought David, the Philistines, and the Jews were occupied with war.

David waited until night, and after the Amalekites had gone to sleep, he and his men attacked them and kept fighting them fiercely throughout the night and the morning of the next day until its evening, and none of the Amalekites escaped except a small number of men, four hundred in all, who were able to flee on their camels. As for David, he was able to recover his two wives and all the spoil, of which nothing was lost, and he returned with all the sheep and the captives he drove before him, and everyone cried out that this was David's spoil. We note that those who cheered David were the very ones who had called for his death a little while before, so we should learn not to rely on people for anything, for they are changeable, moved by contradictory feelings, whereas reliance on God is the true refuge of the spiritual man.

David returned to the brook Besor, where he had left the two hundred exhausted men, and they came out to meet him after his victory. It was a kind gesture from David to ask about them and be reassured about their health, and he did not blame them for not going with him, since he recognized their physical weakness and their inability to continue the march with him.

Greed took hold of some of David's men, and they thought of the spoil more than their brothers did, so they spoke to David, saying to him that these men had not gone out with us to the war, and therefore it was enough for each of them to take his wife and children, and he should have no share of the spoil. The inspired text described everyone who thought thus as wicked and base.

David's answer, however, was wise. He spoke first about God's work among them and how it was God who gave them the victory and the material gifts, and also kept them from all harm and brought them back safe, so the victory and the good came from God and not from them. For this reason David denounced what they had said, and set a new rule which the generations after him took up: that he who guards the baggage and does not go down to the field of battle with the rest of the men shall have an equal share of the spoil with him who took part in the fighting, for his work was also important in preserving the supplies, and his poor health may be what kept him from fighting, so it is no fault of his that he should be deprived of his share. This agrees with God's Law that he who guards the baggage takes a share like him who fought (Num 31:
